en: Prajāpati indeed conquered this world by means of the threefold Veda; that which is his conquest here, he [Prajāpati] reflected: "If other gods should sacrifice with this Veda, they will surely win this very conquest which is mine. Come now, let me take the essence of the threefold Veda. He took the essence of the Ṛgveda by saying "bhūḥ"; that became this earth. That which was its essence, the vital breath, became Agni—the essence of the essence. By saying "bhuvaḥ," he took the essence of the Yajurveda.

That became this intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Its essence that breathed forth became Vāyu, the essence of the essence. 4. He took the essence of the Sāmaveda as "Svar. That became yonder sky. Its essence that breathed forth became Āditya, the essence of the essence. 5. Then he was unable to take the essence of even a single syllable—of this very syllable "Om. 6. That became Speech; its name is indeed "Om," and its essence is breath (*prāṇa*). 7. These are those eight [syllables]; the Gāyatrī has eight syllables, and the Gāyatra [chant] is based on it.
The Sāman is indeed Brahman, and that is the Gāyatrī; thus one attains the Brahman. Cattle have eight hooves; therefore, it is beneficial for cattle. Thus ends the first section in the first Anuvāka.

When he says "Om," that is Agni; "Vāk" (Speech) is the Earth. When he says "Om," that is Vāyu; "Vāk" is the Intermediate Space. When he says "Om," that is Āditya; "Vāk" is Heaven. When he says "Om," that is Prāṇa; "Vāk" is indeed Speech. He who, knowing this, sings the Udgītha—taking Agni with "Om," he establishes him on the Earth; taking Vāyu with "Om," he establishes him in the Intermediate Space; taking Āditya with "Om," he establishes him in Heaven; and taking Prāṇa with "Om," he establishes him in Speech. This is the Gāyatra chant of Śailana.

They sing: "Ovā3 covā3 covā3 chuṃ bhā ovā" three times. Now, that [singing] is, as it were, turned away and not conducive to long life; it should be sung in accordance with the path of the wind and the waters. For if the wind were to blow only away from oneself, one would perish. When it blows from the east, from the south, from the west, from the north, from above, and when it blows through all the quarters—that is this [wind]. Regarding this, they say: "Now indeed he has come from here, and now he blows in this manner. When it blows gathering heat and whirling around, it is as if it fears destruction. And when...

Indeed, if the waters were to flow away only in a straight line, they would waste away; but when they go forming bends, winding, and creating eddies, it is because they are afraid of perishing. Therefore, this [Sāman] should be sung following the path of both Vāyu and the waters.
Thus ends the second section in the first chapter.

"Ovā ovā ovā huṃ bhā ovā"—by performing [the chant] with these two, one attains the full span of life. Just as one might ascend a tree by means of climbing-steps, even so, joining these two deities together, he ascends and goes toward these worlds. Death follows him as a single entity, namely hunger. Then he utters *hiṅ*; the *hiṅ* is indeed the moon, and the moon is food; by means of food they strike down hunger. Having struck down that very hunger with food, he is completely released from this very sun, saying "Om. This indeed.

The opening of the sky is like the aperture of a chariot; even so is this opening of the sky, which appears covered by the rays [of light]. That which is above the *hiṅkāra* of the *gāyatra* is the immortal; there one should place oneself and the sacrificer. And that which is the rest of the *sāman*, above its *pratihāra*—just as water would mingle with water, as fire would mingle with fire, or as milk poured into milk, even so does this syllable (*akṣara*) mingle with these deities. Thus ends the third section in the first chapter.

Now, they utter this *hiṅkāra* as "hiṃ bhā. *Bhāḥ* is indeed glory (*śrī*), for yonder sun is "bhāḥ. This very limb, following which there is "garbha" (womb), is that which enters the generative organ of women as "bhā"; therefore, from that, a Brāhmaṇa is born who is like a seer (*ṛṣi*), and a Kṣatriya who is a hero and a great archer. This very limb, following which there is "vṛṣabha" (bull), is that which enters as "bhā"; therefore, from that, a virtuous draft-ox, a milch-cow, a stud-bull, and a stallion are born.

This very thing follows the limb called *nyaṅga*, namely that it goes down with the sound "bha. Therefore, he who is wicked moves among those who are superior; therefore, from one who is wicked, something superior is born—either a mule or a female mule. This very thing follows the limb called *kubhra*, namely that it goes down with the sound "bha. Therefore, even though he is not an Ārya, he attains the status of a king. Some indeed perform this as the *hiṅkāra* chant, chanting "hiṃ bhā ovā" as if externally. For prosperity is indeed external, and prosperity is the *sāman*.

"Hiṅkāra"—this is the name. If someone were to say of him at that time, "He has placed his glory outside; he will become worse off," then since when one dies, one is cast into the fire, [the critic would say], "Alas, he will die soon; they will cast him into the fire. And so it would indeed come to pass. Therefore, one should internalize this *hiṅkāra* as "hiṃ vo" within oneself, as it were; thus one does not place one's glory outside, and one reaches a full lifespan. The Fourth Section of the First Anuvāka.

This wicked deity stands here warding off [the deceased], saying: "Indeed, you shall go there where you have committed this evil; for whoever is a doer of merit, he may come here. He should say: "You have seen that which I did; indeed, you would not have caused me to do it, for you yourself would have been the doer of that. She knows: "He speaks the truth to me. For she is a truthful deity; she has no power over him to ward him off, but she merely calls out to him with the truth. Then Ikṣvāku said: "Or..."

Thus ends the fifth section in the first Anuvāka. Gobala Vārṣṇa said: "Who is capable of approaching this Āditya? For he burns this from afar; he is turned downward. Therefore, one should mentally bring him along that eastern path of Sāman and place him above this [world] in that immortality. Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said: "One should indeed approach him together. Who knows whether these waters on both sides, or whether it is the wind that he summons, for he then disperses his rays toward him? Then Ulukya Jānaśruteya said: "Wherever this..."

"This is austerity, this is immortality; if one indeed attains this, one is turned away from death and evil. "Who knows that which is beyond the sun, yet this atmosphere is without a foundation below it? "Now, this is indeed immortality; you shall lead me to this very thing, for I do not disregard this. These are the eight syllables. The Gāyatrī has eight syllables, and the Sāman is Gāyatra. The Gāyatrī is indeed Brahman, and one attains that Brahman. Animals have eight hooves; therefore, it is beneficial for cattle. Thus ends the sixth section in the first chapter.

These are the eight deities; this entire world is just this much. He makes them do this for him. He should not leave room for his evil rival in these worlds; he should exclude him by means of the mind alone. This is declared by a Ṛgvedic verse: "Speech has been measured out in four quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them. Three, hidden in secret, do not stir; the fourth quarter of speech is what human beings speak. Now, those three which are hidden in secret and do not stir—these are indeed those worlds. The fourth quarter of speech is what human beings [speak].

"They speak"—this indeed is a fourth part of speech. For one who knows this, everything has been accomplished by him through his entire speech, through all these worlds, and through his whole being. 5. Just as a clod of earth, having struck a stone that is being split, is shattered, even so is he shattered who speaks ill of one who knows this. 6–7. Thus ends the seventh section in the first Anuvāka;
the first Anuvāka is complete.

Prajāpati indeed conquered this world by means of the threefold Veda; that which is his conquest here is this very thing. He reflected: "If other gods should sacrifice with this same threefold Veda, they will surely win this same victory that is mine. Come now, let me squeeze out this threefold Veda. He squeezed out this threefold Veda; while he was squeezing it, he was unable to squeeze out even a single syllable—namely, this "Om. This, indeed, is full of sap; for one who knows thus, the threefold knowledge becomes full of sap. He...

Having pressed this sap and set it aside, it flowed upward. As it flowed, four gods beheld it: Indra, Candra, Rudra, and Samudra. Therefore, these are the most excellent among the gods, for they were the ones who beheld it. That which was this sap became austerity (*tapas*). The gods gazed upon this sap; they perceived, "It has indeed become austerity. Having felt along this threefold Veda, they found within it this very syllable, *om*, as if it were pressed out.

This very thing is indeed the essence (*sarasa*). With that he mixed it for him, just as one might mix parched grain with honey. They performed fervent austerity; while they were performing austerity, the Veda swelled within them. By means of this austerity and this swollen Veda, they won that very victory which Prajāpati had won. These [sacrificial fires] are all of the measure of Prajāpati: "Ayā3mayā3m! Therefore, the fame of one who performs austerity becomes greater, and his glory increases. He who knows this thus, by means of this very swollen Veda, [wins the same].

When one sacrifices and when one causes another to sacrifice, it is in this very same way that he causes the sacrifice with this Veda. For him who knows this, there is no affliction whatsoever; but he who speaks ill of him meets with affliction. Thus ends the first section in the second Anuvāka.

Regarding this they say: "When it is sung as 'Oṃ' or 'Oṃ', where then is the *ṛc* and where is the *sāman*? Indeed, the *sāman* is "Oṃ" and the *ṛc* is "Speech. "Oṃ" is the mind and "Speech" is speech; "Oṃ" is the breath and "Speech" is indeed speech; "Oṃ" is Indra and "Speech" is all the gods. Thus, all the gods follow after Indra alone. This very syllable is "Oṃ"; by means of it, in a contest for superiority, one may win over the Indra of another. By means of this, Baka Dālbhya indeed won over the Indra of the Ājakeśins and led him away with that very "Oṃ. These [syllables] are eight.

The Gāyatrī has eight syllables; the Sāman is the Gāyatra; the Gāyatrī is indeed Brahman, and one attains that Brahman. Cattle have eight hooves; therefore, it pertains to cattle. Its names are these: Indra, Action, the Imperishable, the Immortal, the Sky, the End, Speech, the Abundant, the More, the All, that which is higher than all, Light, Order, Truth, Consciousness, Discernment, the Undeniable, the Primeval, the Whole, the Entire Speech, and this All—even as a cow, it swells both in the distance and nearby.
Thus ends the second section in the second Anuvāka.

She milks out the separate waters, the earth that yields all desires, the vital breaths joined together, sight, hearing, speech in abundance, the mind as its pervader, the heart as its summit, food auspicious for the Brahmins, the rain-purifier, the fortune of the cows, the highest of the earth, austerity as her body, Varuna as her enclosure, Indra as her excellence, the immortal nectar consisting of a thousand syllables with ten thousand streams; thus milking, she flows over all these worlds. That very syllable "Om" is this Truth; in it the waters are established, and in the waters, the earth.

These worlds rest upon the earth; just as leaves might be pierced by a needle, so too are these worlds pierced by this Imperishable (akṣara). This very [Imperishable], having pierced through these [worlds], flows forth tenfold, hundredfold, thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, hundred-thousandfold, millionfold, ten-millionfold, hundred-millionfold, billionfold, ten-billionfold, hundred-billionfold, and a trillionfold—[an extent] that is inexhaustible, reaching to the end of space. Just as a flood, as it overflows, becomes greater and more extensive, even so does this Imperishable become greater and more extensive. These worlds indeed rise upwards.

Thus supported are these thirteen months. He who, knowing this, sings the *udgītha*, carries these worlds across in this very manner. By means of this syllable "Om," he places yonder sun within his mouth; for this syllable, indeed, is that [sun]. Everything is attained by him, everything is conquered; no desire whatsoever remains unfulfilled for one who knows thus. Now, Pṛthu Vainya questioned the divine *vrātyas*: "They call the pillar that supports the sky the sun; the sun is in the atmosphere."

"Supported by the earth, the earths—bearing a great weight—rest upon the waters. Upon what, then, do the great waters rest? They replied: "The pillar that supports the sky; they say the sun is in the atmosphere. Supported by the earth, the earths—bearing a great weight—rest upon the waters. Truth, the great waters, rest upon. "Om"—this very syllable is truth; upon this the waters rest.
Thus ends the third section of the second chapter; the second chapter is complete.

Prajāpati created living beings; once created, they surrounded him on all sides, seeking food. He said to them, "What is your desire? They replied, "We desire food. He said, "I have indeed created only one Veda as food; that is the Sāman, and I shall bestow it upon you. They said, "Bestow it upon us. He said, "We live most abundantly upon these cattle; I shall give it to them first. He bestowed the *hiṅkāra* upon them; therefore, cattle [utter the sound] *hiṅ*.

The *hiṅkāra* they move about as if desiring to understand; it belongs to humans, therefore they praise, thinking, "This shall be mine, that shall be mine. The *prastāva* belongs to birds; therefore, when they take hold of something, they move as if flying down. The *udgītha* belongs to the gods as immortality; therefore they are immortal. The *pratihāra* belongs to the wild animals; therefore, when they are startled, they move as if running away. Thus ends the first section of the third chapter.

The *upadrava* belongs to the Gandharvas and Apsarases; therefore, they move about as if seizing the *upadrava*. The *nidhana* belongs to the Pitṛs; therefore, they conclude with the *nidhana*. Now, when he bestowed that *sāman* upon them, he bestowed this very Āditya upon them. When he has not yet risen, that is the *hiṅkāra*; when half-risen, it is the *prastāva*; at the time of dawn (*āsaṃgava*), it is the *ādi*; at midday, it is the *udgītha*; in the afternoon, it is the *pratihāra*; when he is setting and turning red, that is the *upadrava*; and once he has set, that is the *nidhana*. He...

"This is equal to all the worlds; because it is equal to all the worlds, therefore it is *sāman*. Indeed, he who knows thus is a knower of the *sāman*; he truly knows the *sāman*. They said, "This is indeed far from us; place it where we may subsist upon it. He brought it toward the seasons. He made spring the *hiṅkāra*, summer the *prastāva*, the rainy season the *udgītha*, autumn the *pratihāra*, and winter the *nidhana*. He made the months and half-months the seven *svara*s. They said, "It is too near."
"Now indeed, let us go right there where we may subsist. He then led it toward Parjanya; he made the east wind itself the *hiṅkāra*.
Thus ends the second section in the third chapter.

He made the clouds the *hiṅkāra*, thunder the *prastāva*, lightning the *udgītha*, rain the *pratihāra*, and the rain that causes offspring and plants to be born the *nidhana*. He made these seven. They said, "Come even closer now; perform it right there where we may subsist. He led it toward the sacrifice. He made the *yajus* formulas the *hiṅkāra*, the *ṛc* verses the *prastāva*, the *sāmans* the *udgītha*, the *stoma* chants the *pratihāra*, the meters the *nidhana*, and he made the *svāhā*-utterance and the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance the seventh.

They said, "Come closer; indeed, do it right here where we may subsist upon it. He led it toward a man. That man made *hiṅkāra* out of his mind, *prastāva* out of speech, *udgītha* out of breath, *pratihāra* out of sight, and *nidhana* out of hearing; and he made semen and offspring the seventh. They said, "He has indeed performed this here, where we shall subsist. One should know: "I am the Sāman itself; in me are these deities.
Thus ends the third section in the third chapter.

The gods are not far away; for as long as one worships the gods through the self, so long do the gods remain present for him. Now, he who knows this thus—"I am indeed the Sāman; all these deities are in me"—for him all these deities become present in that very way. This Sāman is called *devaśrut* ("heard by the gods"), for all the deities indeed hear one who knows this for the sake of merit and goodness; they cause him to perform only what is meritorious and good. Sucitta Śailana used to say: "Whoever desires to perform a sacrifice, let him choose me alone."

"Therefore, the sacrifice itself will lead him [to success]; for all the deities are satisfied following one who sings the *udgītha* while knowing this. Being satisfied, they will act in such a way that the sacrifice leads him [to success]. Thus ends the fourth section of the third chapter;
the third chapter is completed.

The gods, indeed, desired to attain the heavenly world; yet, whether lying down, sitting, standing, or running, they did not reach it by any action whatsoever. Those gods then ran to Prajāpati, saying, "We have indeed desired to attain the heavenly world, but whether lying down, sitting, standing, or running, we have not reached it by any action whatsoever. Instruct us so that we may attain the heavenly world. He said to them, "Go to the heavenly world with the *sāman* and the *ṛc*. They went to the heavenly world with the *sāman* and the *ṛc*.

"They have gone to the heavenly world"—thus [it is called] *prasāma*; therefore it is *prasāma*. And because one eats food, it is *prasāma*. The gods, indeed, when they were going to the heavenly world, went shaking off these bodily remains consisting of the *ṛk*-verses; thus they won the heavenly world. Those [remains] were scattered as far as heaven and remained there. Then Prajāpati, having gathered together these bodily remains consisting of the *ṛk*-verses, honored them;
because he honored them, they became the *ṛc*s. Thus ends the first section in the fourth anuvāka.

This very *ṛc* became this very *śrī*; therefore the gods prospered. Then the asuras seized this *śrī* of theirs, and so it became "asura. The gods said, "The *śrī* that was ours, the asuras have taken; how indeed can we regain this *śrī* of theirs? They said, "Let us sing the *sāman* upon the *ṛc* itself. They returned and sang the *sāman* upon the *ṛc*, and thereby they drove the asuras away from this world. That [was done] at the midday pressing and at the third pressing.

There is a fault in the *narcas* when one sings it in the *ṛc*; by that, he repels his hateful rival from this world. And when he sings the *prātaḥsavana* among the immortal deities, by that he goes to the heavenly world. Prajāpati indeed won this victory through the *sāman*. This victory which is his, he ascended to the heavenly world with it. Those gods approached Prajāpati and said, "Give this *sāman* to us as well. He said, "So be it," and he gave that *sāman* to them. That *sāman* [led] these [gods] to the heavenly world.

It did not desire to carry the world. Those gods approached Prajāpati and said, "That Sāman which you gave us—this indeed does not desire to carry our heavenly world. "Then unite it with evil," [he said]. "What is its evil? "The Ṛc. They united it with the Ṛc. This [Sāman] stood reproaching Prajāpati, saying, "They have indeed united me with evil. He said, "Whoever shall separate himself from this, he alone shall be separated from evil. He who...
With this Ṛg-verse he separates [him] at the morning pressing; thus he indeed turns away from evil. (12.16) Thus ends the second section in the fourth Anuvāka.

Regarding this they say: "When [the Sāman] is sung as 'O-vā-o-vā', where then is the Ṛc and where is the Sāman? While beginning the *prastāva*, he begins with eight syllables. The Gāyatrī has eight syllables; each syllable consists of three morae (*akṣara*), and thus they amount to twenty-four. The Gāyatrī has twenty-four syllables. Having reached this very Ṛc by means of the *prastāva*, he remains singing it, [attaining thereby] that prosperity, that honor, that heavenly world, that fame, and that food which belong to it.
The Third Section of the Fourth Anuvāka.

Prajāpati created the gods; after them, Death, who is Evil, was created. Those gods approached Prajāpati and said, "Why did you not create us with Death as Evil? Had you done so, we would have been invincible. He said to them, "Gather the meters and enter them according to their proper place; then you shall be separated from Death and from Evil. The Vasus gathered the Gāyatrī meter and entered it; it concealed them. The Rudras gathered the Triṣṭubh meter and entered it... [and so on].

The Ādityas gathered together the *jagatī* meter; they entered it, and it concealed them. 6. The Viśvedevas gathered together the *anuṣṭubh* meter; they entered it, and it concealed them. 7. Death perceived them within this *ṛc* that was without tone (*asvarā*), just as one might perceive the thread of a gem within the gem itself. 8. They entered the tone (*svara*); while they were there in the tone, he did not perceive them, but he pursued them by means of the resonance (*ghoṣa*) of the tone. 9. They ascended to this very syllable, "Om"; this very syllable is the threefold Veda.

"Having attained that immortal light which shines yonder through this very knowledge, they turned away from death and evil. In exactly the same way, one who knows this, having mounted upon this very syllable *Om* and attained that immortal light which shines yonder, turns away from death and evil; and also for him for whom one who knows thus chants the *udgītha*.
Thus ends the fourth section in the fourth chapter;
the fourth chapter is complete.

Now, this is the twenty-onefold *sāman*. Its *hiṅkāra* is the threefold knowledge (*trayī vidyā*). Fire, wind, and yonder sun—this is the *prastāva*. These worlds are the *ādi*, for upon these worlds everything here is supported. Faith, sacrifice, and the sacrificial fee—this is the *udgītha*. The quarters, the intermediate quarters, and space—this is the *pratihāra*. Waters, progeny, and plants—this is the *upadrava*. The moon, the stars, and the ancestors—this is the *nidhana*. This is that twenty-onefold *sāman*. He who knows this twenty-onefold *sāman* thus—for him, by this, the whole has been sung as the *udgītha*; indeed, it is from this very source.
"He who reviles one who knows thus is cut off from everything.
Thus ends the fifth section.

This very thing was the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) in the beginning, and it remains so even now. That which is this intermediate space is precisely he who blows here (the wind); for he is indeed named "Intermediate Space" (*antarikṣa*). And he is also this [wind] stretched out. Just as two leaves might be propped apart by a stick, or two wheels by an axle, even so are these two worlds propped apart by him. Within him is all this; because all this is within (*antar*) him, therefore it is called "interior" (*antara*). "Interior" (*antara*) is indeed its name, and that is the "intermediate space" (*antarikṣa*).

They speak of it as being out of sight. Just as bundles tied together hang down, even so all these worlds, being tied together, hang down from it. Of this very [Sāman], there are three *āgās*, three *āgītāni*, six *vibhūtayas*, four *pratiṣṭhās*, ten *pragās*, seven *saṃsthās*, two *stobhas*, and one *rūpa*. Those which are the three *āgās* are these very worlds. Now, those which are the three *āgītāni* are Agni, Vāyu, and that Āditya; these are the *āgītāni*. He who knows this does not fail to attain any prosperity whatsoever. 8.20

Thus ends the first section of the sixth chapter. Now, those which are the six manifestations are the seasons. 1. Now, those which are the four foundations are these very four quarters. 2. Now, those which are the ten forward-strides are these very ten vital breaths. 3. Now, those which are the seven terminuses are these very seven days and nights toward which they utter the *vaṣaṭ* call. 4. Now, those two which are the musical modulations (*stobha*) are day and night. 5. Now, that which is the single form is action itself; for by action all this is modified. 6. The gods entered into a contest over this very *Sāman*.

Prajāpati won the *hiṅkāra* by means of his *haras*; Agni, by means of his brilliance, the *prastāva*; Bṛhaspati, by means of his form, the *udgītha*; the Fathers, by means of their *svadhā*, the *pratīhāra*; and Indra, by means of his heroism, the *nidhana*. Then the other gods felt as if they had been excluded. They said to Indra, "We indeed belong to you; let us have a share in this *sāman*. He gave them the *svara*. Prajāpati said to him, "Why have you done this? You have given these gods the entire *sāman*. The *sāman* is only as much as the *svara*, or as much as the *ṛc*."

"This shall be your *svara* (tone)," he said. He replied, "Indeed, I shall take back this essence (*rasa*) from them. He said to them, "Sing unto me; let there be *svara* for me. "So be it," they said. As they sang unto him, he chanted over them and took back their essence.
Thus ends the second section of the sixth chapter.

Just as one might pour honey into a honey-vat by means of honey-veins, even so does that *sāman* pour its essence into it. Therefore, one should not sing along (*upagāyet*). The Udgātṛ is Indra; just as he takes away the essence of these [veins], so does he take away the essence of those [who sing along]. However, the sacrificer may indeed sing along at his will, for that belongs to the sacrificer; likewise, a religious student (*brahmacārin*) who has been instructed by his teacher may do so. Regarding this, they say: "One should certainly sing along; for the quarters sang along, and thus one wins co-residence (*salokatā*) with the quarters. These are those very ones...

These vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are indeed the chief ones; they are both the *udgātṛ*s and the *upagātṛ*s. These three are the *udgātṛ*s, and these four are the *upagātṛ*s. Therefore, one should appoint exactly four *upagātṛ*s. Therefore, he should touch the *upagātṛ*s, saying: "You are the quarters; do not harm my hearing. That which was its essence is this very wind that blows; that is indeed the essence. As for this, Sucitta Śailāna used to say: "Just as one would eat a morsel of honey, so should one fill oneself with this essence. That *udgātṛ* leads both himself and the sacrificer to immortality. 8.22
Thus ends the third section in the sixth chapter;
the sixth chapter is completed.

In the beginning, this was indeed only space; and even now it is that very same thing. That which is space is speech itself; therefore, from that space, speech speaks. Prajāpati pressed upon this speech; from it, thus pressed, its essence issued forth as breath, and these worlds came into being. He pressed upon these worlds; from them, thus pressed, their essence issued forth as breath, and these deities came into being: Agni, Vāyu, and that Āditya. He pressed upon these deities; from them, thus pressed, their essence...

It swelled; it became the threefold knowledge (the triple Veda). He pressed the threefold knowledge; from it, being pressed, its essence swelled, and these very *vyāhṛtis* came into being: *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*. He pressed those *vyāhṛtis*; from them, being pressed, their essence swelled, and that syllable *oṃ* came into being. He pressed that syllable; from it, being pressed, its essence swelled. Thus ends the first section of the seventh chapter.

Because it does not perish (*akṣarati*), therefore it is the Imperishable (*akṣara*); and because it does not decay (*na kṣīyate*), therefore it is indestructible (*akṣaya*). Indeed, this very Imperishable is called by the name "Akṣaya," which they speak of cryptically as "Akṣara. Now, some sing this very thing as "Om. One should not sing it in that way; for there is a danger that he might exclude himself from this essence. Or rather, it becomes as if there were two: "Om" and "O. Some indeed sing it as "O"; but that is not sung correctly, and one should not sing it in that way. One should sing it simply as "Om," for thus he includes himself with this essence.
Thus ends the second section in the seventh Anuvāka;
the seventh Anuvāka is complete.

In the beginning, this was indeed space alone; even now, it is that very same thing. That which is this space is the sun itself, for when he has risen, all this becomes manifest (ākāśate). Of him, the oceans are indeed the boundaries between the mortal and the immortal; that which is enclosed by the ocean is attained by death, while that which is beyond it is the immortal. That which is this ocean is indeed he who blows here (the wind); he is the ocean, for all beings run after him as he rushes along. Of him, heaven and earth are...

Thus [he transcends] the two shores; then, just as bronze vessels or lakes might be cast away in a river, even so this earthly ocean [is left behind]. This very sun rises from the further shore of the ocean. Rising, it ascends upon the back of the wind; it rises from the immortal itself, moves along the immortal, and is established in the immortal. Its threefold form—white, black, and the person—is not reached by death. That which is white is the form of speech, of the Ṛg-veda, and of fire, which is death. And that which is speech is the Ṛg-veda. Now...

That fire which is death is that [Agni]. Now, that which is black is the form of water, of food, of mind, and of the Yajus. Those waters are food; and that which is mind is the Yajus. Now, that which is the person is breath, that is the Sāman, that is Brahman, that is the Immortal. That which is breath is the Sāman; and that which is Brahman is the Immortal. Thus ends the first section of the eighth chapter.

Now, with reference to the self: this very eye is threefold—white, black, and the person (*puruṣa*). That which is white is the form of speech, of the *ṛc*, of fire, and of death; that which is speech, the *ṛc*, and fire—that is death. And that which is black is the form of water, of food, of the mind, and of the *yajus*; that which is water, food, and the mind—that is the *yajus*. And that which is the person is breath, that is the *sāman*, that is Brahman, that is the immortal; that which is breath, the *sāman*, and Brahman—that is the immortal.

This indeed is the ascent of Brahman; now, therefore, follows the supreme ascent. That which is the ascent is lightning itself. Now, that white form which belongs to the lightning as it flashes—that is the form of Speech, of the Ṛg-veda, of Fire, and of Death. Furthermore, that dark-blue form which belongs to the lightning as it thunders—that is the form of Water, of Food, of Mind, and of the Yajur-veda. That person who is in the lightning is Prāṇa; he is Sāman; he is Brahman; he is the Immortal. That which is Prāṇa is Sāman; and that which is Brahman is the Immortal. Thus ends the second section of the eighth lesson.

He, indeed, surrounded by immortality, sits in the midst of death, having made food his support. Now, this very person who is in the eye and he who is in the sun are the *atipuruṣa*; he who is in lightning is the *paramapuruṣa*. These, indeed, are the three persons; these are born for him. That which is in the eye is named *anurūpa* (the conforming one), for he follows after all forms. One should meditate upon him as *anurūpa*; verily, all forms follow after him. That which is in the sun is *pratirūpa* (the counterpart), for he faces toward [all things].

One should meditate upon him as "the Counter-form" (*pratirūpa*), for all forms become his counterpart. That which is in lightning is the "All-form" (*sarvarūpa*), for all forms are contained within it; one should meditate upon it as "the All-form," for all forms indeed come to be in it. These three persons, verily, are born for him who knows this thus, and also for him for whom one knowing this sings the *udgītha*.
The third section of the eighth lesson;
the eighth lesson is complete.

In the beginning, this was indeed space alone; even now it is that very same thing. That which is this space is Indra; that which is Indra is he who shines here. He is the seven-rayed bull, the most powerful. Of him, the ray consisting of speech is established in the east. That which is speech is Agni. He becomes tenfold, hundredfold, thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, hundred-thousandfold, millionfold, ten-millionfold, hundred-millionfold, billionfold, ten-billionfold, and the end of space, the imperishable lotus. He is this very one.

Its ray, having become speech, is established among all these creatures. Whoever speaks, he speaks by this very ray of his. Now, that which consists of mind is established in the south; for that which is the mind is the moon, and it becomes tenfold. This very [sun], having become the ray of mind, is established among all these creatures. Whoever thinks, he thinks by this very ray of his. Now, that which consists of sight is established in the west.

Now, that which is the eye of the sun—that becomes tenfold. It is this very ray of his which, having become the eye, is established in all these creatures; whoever sees, he sees by means of this very ray. Then there is the one consisting of hearing, established in the north. That which is the hearing—those are the quarters; it becomes tenfold. It is this very ray of his which, having become the hearing, is established in all these creatures;
whoever hears, he hears by means of this very ray. [End of the first section of the ninth anuvāka]

Now, the one consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*) is established above; that which is his breath is Vāyu, and he becomes tenfold. This very [breath], having become a ray of this [Sun], is established in all these creatures. Whoever breathes, he breathes by means of this very ray. Then, the one consisting of the vital force (*asumaya*) is established crosswise; he is indeed named Īśāna, and he becomes tenfold. This very [vital force], having become a ray of this [Sun], is established in all these creatures. Whoever...

And who is the one possessing life through the ray of this very [Self]? Now, that which consists of food is established within as the individual. That which is food is water; it becomes tenfold, hundredfold, thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, hundred-thousandfold, millionfold, ten-millionfold, hundred-millionfold, billionfold, ten-billionfold, and the end of space, the imperishable lotus. This very [Self], having become the ray of food, is established within all these creatures. Whosoever eats, he eats through the ray of this very [Self]. This is He.

"The bull with seven rays, the mighty one; this very thing is declared by a Ṛgvedic verse: 'He who, the bull with seven rays, the mighty one, released the seven rivers to flow; he who, thunderbolt-armed, struck down Rauhina as he was scaling heaven—O people, he is Indra. (7) "He who has seven rays"—for these rays of the sun are indeed seven; "the bull"—for he alone is the bull among these creatures; "the mighty one"—this is his very greatness. (8) "He released the seven rivers to flow"—for these rivers are indeed seven.

Because all this was whitened by them—because all this was whitened by them—they are called *sindhavaḥ* (the rivers). "He whose arm wields the thunderbolt shook Rauhiṇa"—for he indeed is he whose arm wields the thunderbolt and shook Rauhiṇa. "O people, he is Indra who ascended to heaven"—for he indeed is Indra.
Thus ends the second section in the ninth lesson.

"Just as paths might rise up from a mountain," so said Śāṭyāyani; "even so these rays of the sun go toward this sun from every side. He who knows this, taking hold with 'Om,' goes toward this sun from every side by means of these rays of his. This Sāman has doors on all sides and is unobstructed; yet some worship it as having doors on only one side, like a cloud-path, and thus they perceive it otherwise than it truly is. But he who knows it in this way—he alone knows this Sāman which has doors on all sides and is unobstructed.

This lightning is that [Sāman]. That which circles all around this orb is the Sāman; and that which shines forth beyond it is the essence of meritorious action. One is released toward that [essence]. This is the Sāman that is without rival. Indeed, Indra does not see any rival whatsoever. Just as Indra does not see any rival whatsoever, even so he who knows this, or for whom one knowing thus sings the Udgītha, does not see any rival whatsoever. Thus ends the third section in the ninth Anuvāka. The ninth Anuvāka is complete.

In the beginning, this was indeed only space (*ākāśa*); even now it is that very same thing. That which is this space is Indra; that which is Indra is the *sāman*. Of this *sāman*, this eastern quarter is the *hiṅkāra*; this [quarter] is the *prastāva*; this is the *ādi*; this is the *udgītha*; yonder [quarter] is the *pratihāra*; the intermediate region (*antarikṣa*) is the *upadrava*; and this [quarter] is the *nidhana*. This is the sevenfold *sāman*. He who knows this sevenfold *sāman*—whatever there is in the eastern quarter, whatever deities, humans, and animals [there may be]—[all belong to him].

Whatever food and sustenance there is, he obtains all that by means of the *hiṅkāra*. 3. Now, whatever is in the southern direction, he obtains all that by means of the *prastāva*. 4. Now, whatever is in the western direction, he obtains all that by means of the *ādi*. 5. Now, whatever is in the northern direction, he obtains all that by means of the *udgītha*. 6. Now, whatever is in yonder direction (the zenith), he obtains all that by means of the *pratihāra*. 7. Now, whatever is in the intermediate space, he obtains all that by means of the *upadrava*. 8. Now, whatever is in this direction—whatever deities, whatever humans, whatever animals, and whatever food and sustenance—he obtains all that.

Through the *nidhana*, one attains everything; indeed, for him everything becomes attained, everything conquered, and no desire whatsoever remains unfulfilled, for him who knows thus. Whatever he does in these worlds, knowing this, he does it as his own, from himself. This very thing is declared by a Ṛgvedic verse. Thus ends the first section of the tenth lesson.

"O Indra, even if there were a hundred heavens and a hundred earths for you, O Wielder of the Thunderbolt, a thousand suns could not equal you at birth, nor could the two worlds. (1) "If there were a hundred heavens, O Indra, and a hundred earths—if there were a hundred heavens and a hundred earths—this very space (*ākāśa*) is greater than them. (2) "O Wielder of the Thunderbolt, a thousand suns could not equal you"—for indeed, not even a thousand suns can equal him. (3) "Nor could the two worlds at his birth"—for indeed, these two worlds do not roar out against him when he is born. These two, indeed, are [the heaven and earth].

The two worlds (heaven and earth) are those two; this very space is greater than them, for within it these two are contained. That which is this space is indeed Indra; that which is Indra is this very one who shines there. He goes forth being released from the clouds; just as he goes forth being released from the clouds, even so does he go forth being released from all evil—he who knows this, and also he for whom one knowing thus sings the Udgītha.
Thus ends the second section of the tenth Anuvāka; the tenth Anuvāka is complete.

The *trivṛt*-sāman has four feet: Brahman is one third, Indra is one third, Prajāpati is one third, and food itself is the fourth foot. (1) Now, that which is Brahman is breath; that which is Indra is speech; that which is Prajāpati is mind; and food itself is the fourth foot. (2) Mind is the *hiṅkāra*, speech is the *prastāva*, breath is the *udgītha*, and food itself is the fourth foot. (3) One acts with speech, leads with breath, and moves with the mind; this is that which is restrained, namely the mind, by means of which—wherever...

He desires that [for himself], and he establishes both himself and the sacrificer [therein]. Now, with respect to the deities: the *hiṅkāra* is indeed the moon, the *prastāva* is Agni, the *udgītha* is Āditya, and the waters themselves are the fourth foot; for that is manifest food. These very deities come together on the night of the new moon: on the night of the new moon, the moon enters the sun, and the sun enters Agni. Because they come together (*saṃyanti*), it is called *sāman*. He is truly a knower of the *sāman*, he knows the *sāman*, who knows thus. Of these very [deities]...

Among the deities, each single deity becomes a *sāman*. This very sun is the *trivṛt* [sāman]: its rays are the first foot, the orb is the second, and the person (Puruṣa) within it is the third. The rays themselves are the *hiṅkāra*; therefore, as soon as they rise, they are extended. The orb is the *prastāva*, the person is the *udgītha*, and those waters which are within it constitute the fourth foot. In the same way, regarding the moon: its rays are the first foot, the orb is the second, and the person within it is the third. The rays themselves are the *hiṅkāra*, the orb is the *prastāva*, the person is the *udgītha*, and those waters which are within it constitute that very [fourth foot].

The fourth quarter: 10. Four others and four others—those are eight. The Gāyatrī has eight syllables; the Sāman is the Gāyatra; the Gāyatrī is indeed Brahman; he attains that Brahman. Cattle have eight hooves; therefore it is conducive to cattle. 11. 33.
Thus ends the first section in the eleventh Anuvāka.

Now, with reference to the self (*adhyātma*): this very eye is threefold and four-footed—white, black, and the person (*puruṣa*). The white part is indeed the *hiṅkāra*; the black part is the *prastāva*; the person is the *udgītha*. Those waters which are within it constitute the fourth foot. This is the course of the sun; this is the course of the moon. These are four, and these are another four; they make eight. The *gāyatrī* has eight syllables, and the *sāman* is the *gāyatra*. The *gāyatrī* is indeed Brahman, and one attains Brahman through it. Animals have eight hooves; therefore, it is beneficial for cattle. He who blows here (the wind)...

This very one is Prajāpati; that indeed is the Sāman. This deity who is the person within the eye is he who has ascended by means of the *āhuti* and *atimati*. Now, those two who are seen in the waters—the moon and the sun—are the deities of these two. Indeed, when people say "the gods of the gods," these are they; they are these who have ascended by means of the *āhuti* and *atimati*. Regarding this, Pṛthu Vainya questioned the divine Vrātyas: "By whom impelled does the wind blow? Who give the five directions their orientation?"

"Those gods who disregarded the oblations—who were they, the leaders of the waters? They replied: "One of them clothes this earth; one has encompassed the intermediate space; one bestows the sky, he who is the sustainer; and another protects all the quarters. "One of them clothes this earth"—that is Agni. "One has encompassed the intermediate space"—that is Vāyu. "One bestows the sky, he who is the sustainer"—that is Āditya. "And another protects all the quarters."
"Others protect them"—these deities indeed protect all the quarters: "the moon and the stars. These very ones, being the *sāman* itself, are truly arranged for the sake of food.
The second section in the eleventh recitation (*anuvāka*) is complete;
the eleventh recitation is finished.

Now, regarding this *sāman*, they say: "The year indeed is the *sāman*. Of that, spring is the *hiṅkāra*; therefore, in spring, animals come forth making the sound *hiṅ*. Summer is the *prastāva*; the *prastāva* is indeed undefined, and summer is undefined among the seasons. The rainy season is the *udgītha*; for it sings as it were, as it rains. Autumn is the *pratihāra*; for in autumn, indeed, the greatest number of plants ripen. Winter is the *nidhana*; for in winter, creatures become as if brought to their end.

These two join together at these two ends; following this, the year is endless. Of that [year], these two are its ends, namely winter and spring. Following this, the two ends of a village meet; following this, the two ends of a gold necklace meet; following this, one lies having drawn the outer coils around oneself. Just as the neck is completely encircled by a gold necklace on all sides, even so is the *Sāman* endless. He who knows this endless *Sāman* wins endlessness itself. Thus ends the first section of the twelfth chapter.

Now, this Sāman is in Parjanya. Its *hiṅkāra* is the east wind; that which causes the clouds to gather is the *prastāva*; that which thunders is the *udgītha*; that which flashes is the *pratihāra*; and that which rains is the *nidhana*. This is the Sāman in Parjanya. He who knows this Sāman in Parjanya becomes one for whom Parjanya rains abundantly. Now, this Sāman is in man. His *hiṅkāra* is this [breath]; his *prastāva* is this [breath]; his *udgītha* is this [breath]; his...

The *pratihāra* is this [sound], and the *nidhana* is this [sound]. This *sāman* is in the person. He who knows this *sāman* in the person indeed ascends and goes upward with offspring and cattle. Furthermore, he who knows it as facing backward (*pratyak*) wins those worlds that face backward; for him, this [breath] is the *hiṅkāra*, this is the *prastāva*, this is the *udgītha*, this is the *pratihāra*, and this is the *nidhana*; he wins those worlds that face backward. Furthermore, he who knows it as transverse wins those worlds that are transverse; for him, the hair is the *hiṅkāra* and the skin is the *prastāva*.

The flesh is the *udgītha*, the bone is the *pratihāra*, and the marrow is the *nidhana*. Of this [sāman], he sings three parts openly: the *prastāva*, the *pratihāra*, and the *nidhana*; therefore, in a person, three things are visible: the teeth and the two kinds of nails (fingernails and toenails).
Thus ends the second section in the twelfth Anuvāka.

Of these, there are three Āgās: one addressed to Agni, one to Indra, and one to the Viśvedevas. That which is soft (*mandrā*) belongs to Agni; with it the Prātaḥsavana (morning pressing) is to be chanted, for the Prātaḥsavana belongs to Agni, and this world belongs to Agni.

With that which is his own mode of singing (*svayāga*), he sings the *udgītha* for the morning pressing; he prospers in this world. Now, that which is resonant and accompanied by rhythmic beating is the mode of Indra; with that, one should sing the *udgītha* for the midday pressing. For the midday pressing belongs to Indra, and yonder world belongs to Indra. With his own mode of singing, he sings the *udgītha* for the midday pressing; he prospers in yonder world. Now, that which he sings as if swaying and as if expanding is the mode of the Viśvedevas; with that, one should sing the *udgītha* for the third pressing. For the third pressing belongs to the Viśvedevas.

This intermediate space belongs to the Vaiśvadeva; by means of his own sacrifice, he sings the *udgītha* for the third pressing and prospers in this intermediate space. Now, moreover, they say that it should be sung with only one [syllable] of the *āgā*, namely that which is the middle of his speech. For just as one sings the *udgītha* while exerting oneself with speech, that indeed is the middle of his speech. By means of that very speech, he approaches all forms of speech; he who knows thus prospers in undiluted, unified prosperity. Now, that which is the *krauñcā* [chant] belongs to Bṛhaspati. He who...

If one should desire spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), he should sing that [Sāman] as the *Udgītha*. Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman; thus he prospers in spiritual luster, and so he becomes possessed of spiritual luster. Now, Caikitāneya said: "I sing the Sāman of a single [syllable]. That Gāyatra [Sāman] should be sung without drawing breath. That [portion] up to the *Pratihāra* should be sung without drawing breath. The Gāyatra is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*); thus he prospers in the vital breath, and so he reaches a full lifespan. Thus ends the second section of the twelfth Anuvāka.

Then the Kurus approached Brahmadatta Caikitāneya as he was singing the Udgītha, saying, "O Dālbhya, sing the Sāman! Being thus approached, he sang it even more intensely. They said to him, "Why, being approached, did you sing it even more intensely? He replied, "Thinking, 'This is indeed hair (loman),' we have listened to this very thing [with our hair standing on end]. Therefore, those who have spoken ill of us, their burial grounds shall become as if covered with hair; whereas we shall continue to sing upward. Then King Jaivali [approached] Galūnasa Ārkṣākāyaṇa...

They asked him about what had been produced from the *śamūla* and the leaf: "Did you sing it with the *ṛc*, Śālāvata, or with the *sāman*? He replied, "Neither with the *ṛc*, O King, nor with the *sāman*. [The others said: "In that case, you all would have been worthy of praise, for you sang knowing this. Then, if he had said, "I sang it both with the *ṛc* and with the *sāman*," he would have said of her, "You sang it with a worn-out, useless stalk. But he said that very thing: "I sang it with the tone (*svara*) and with the *hiṅkāra*. Thus ends the third section of the twelfth chapter.

Then Satyādhivāka Caitrarathi said to Satyayajña Pauluṣiti, "O Prācīnayoga, if you, knowing the Sāman called *sāṃna*, do not perform the office of the officiating priest for me, then you shall never again desire to undergo initiation. For he had indeed been initiated many times. He replied, "He who, knowing the *sāṃna* as our glory (*śrī*), performs the office of the officiating priest, becomes truly glorious. The *sāṃna* is indeed our glory. "He who, knowing the *sāṃna* as our firm foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*), performs the office of the officiating priest..."

It rests upon speech alone; "Speech indeed is our *sāman*," [they say], for "he who, knowing our *sāman* to be gold, performs the office of the *ṛtvij*, gold goes away from his house. "Breath indeed is our *sāman*’s gold," [they say]. (4) He who, knowing the honor of the *sāman*, performs the office of the *ṛtvij* becomes honored; "The eye indeed is the honor of the *sāman*," [they say]. (5) He who, knowing the hearing of our *sāman*, performs the office of the *ṛtvij* becomes possessed of hearing;
"The ear indeed is the hearing of our *sāman*," [they say]. (6) Thus ends the fourth section in the twelfth chapter.

The twelfth section is completed: "Speech is measured in four quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them. Three, hidden in the cave, do not stir; the fourth quarter of speech is what humans speak. (1) Speech itself is the *Sāman*, for by means of speech one sings the *Sāman*. Speech itself is the *Uktha*, for by means of speech one recites the *Uktha*. Speech itself is the *Yajus*, for by means of speech the *Yajus* is followed. (2) Whatever sacred knowledge (*brahman*) is subsequent to this, all that is indeed speech. Now, as for that which is taught elsewhere as the sacred knowledge, one does not perform the priestly office (*ārlijya*) by means of it; rather, it is only by means of the aforementioned [speech] that one performs it, though in an indirect manner.
Thus ends the first section of the thirteenth chapter.

By means of this very life-breath (*asu*), the gods live, the ancestors live, humans live, animals live, the Gandharvas and Apsarases live; indeed, all this lives. Regarding this they say: "Since all this lives by means of the *asu*, what is the *asu* of the Sāman? One should reply: "The vital breath (*prāṇa*). Verily, the vital breath is indeed the *asu* of the Sāman. This same vital breath is established in speech, and speech is established in the vital breath. These two are thus established in one another. He who knows this finds a firm foundation.

This very thing is declared by the *ṛc*: "Aditi is heaven, Aditi is the mid-region; Aditi is the mother, she is the father, she is the son; all the gods are Aditi, the five peoples are Aditi; Aditi is what has been born, Aditi is what is to be born. (4) "Aditi is heaven, Aditi is the mid-region"—this one is indeed heaven, this one is the mid-region. (5) "Aditi is the mother, she is the father, she is the son"—this one is indeed the mother, this one is the father, this one is the son. (6) "All the gods are Aditi, the five peoples are Aditi"—those who were the five peoples among the gods before the Asuras, they are indeed here in that sun. (7)

"The person who is in the moon, who is in lightning, who is in the waters, and this one who is here within the eye—this indeed is that. This very one is Aditi, the born, and Aditi, the progenitor. For she indeed is the born, and she is the progenitor.
Thus ends the second section of the thirteenth Anuvāka;
the thirteenth Anuvāka is complete.

Āruṇi, the son of Vasiṣṭha, approached Caikitāneya to enter into studentship. He said to him, "Do you know, O Gautama, that deity whom we, the Caikitāneyas, worship as Sāman? Which deity do you worship? He replied, "The venerable ones, it is Sāman itself. He questioned him further: "Do you know what is in the fire? "I know it," he replied. "That which we worship as Sāman is indeed its light. "Do you know what is in the earth? "I know it," he replied. "That which we worship as Sāman is indeed its foundation."

"Do we worship it as *sāman*? "Do you know that which is in the waters? "This is indeed the peace (*śānti*) of that *sāman*, namely, that we worship it as *sāman*. "Do you know that which is in the intermediate space? "This is indeed the self (*ātman*) of that *sāman*, namely, that we worship it as *sāman*. "Do you know that which is in the wind? "This is indeed the prosperity (*śrī*) of that *sāman*, namely, that we worship it as *sāman*. "Do you know that which is in the quarters? "This is indeed the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of that *sāman*, namely, that we worship it as *sāman*. "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky?
