"This is indeed the manifestation (*vibhūti*) of that Sāman that we meditate upon as the Sāman.
Thus ends the first section of the fourteenth Anuvāka.

"Do you know that which is in the sun? "I do. "This is the radiance of that *sāman* which we meditate upon as the *sāman*. "Do you know that which is in the moon? "I do. "This is the splendor of that *sāman* which we meditate upon as the *sāman*. "Do you know that which is in the stars? "I do. "This is the wisdom of that *sāman* which we meditate upon as the *sāman*. "Do you know that which is in food? "I do. "This is the seed of that *sāman* which we meditate upon as the *sāman*. "Do you know that which is in cattle? "I do. "This is the glory..."

"What is that *sāman* of this [Sāman] which you worship as the *sāman*? "That which is in the *ṛc*. "Do you know that? "Yes. "Is it not the *stoma*? "That which we worship as the *sāman* of this *sāman*. "What is that [part] of this *sāman* which you worship as the *sāman*? "That which is in the *yajus*. "Do you know that? "Yes. "Is it not the ritual action (*karman*)? "That which we worship as the *sāman* of this *sāman*. "Then what do you worship? "The syllable (*akṣara*). "Which is that syllable? "That which, while flowing away (*kṣarat*), does not perish (*akṣīyate*). "Which is that which, while flowing away, does not perish? "Indra. "Which is that Indra? "He who, while flowing away, rejoiced."

"Of whom is it that one says, 'He delights in the eye'? "This is the deity," he said. "This person who is in the eye—this is Indra, this is Prajāpati. He is equal to the earth, equal to space, equal to heaven, equal to all beings. He shines beyond the sky; he alone is to be meditated upon as 'All this. He who knows this thus becomes radiant, possessed of a firm foundation, peaceful, self-possessed, glorious, pervasive, powerful, brilliant, full of being, wise, prolific, and famous."
It becomes possessed of praise, possessed of action, possessed of syllables, possessed of the senses, and possessed of the Sāman. This very thing is declared by a Ṛg-verse.
Thus ends the second section in the fourteenth Anuvāka.

"He became a counterpart to every form; that was his form for the sake of being seen. Indra moves in many forms through his powers of illusion (māyā), for ten hundred bay horses are yoked to him. (1) "He became a counterpart to every form": for he indeed became a counterpart to every form. (2) "That was his form for the sake of being seen": for this form of his is indeed for the sake of being seen. (3) "Indra moves in many forms through his powers of illusion": for by means of his powers of illusion, he indeed moves in these many forms. (4) "For ten hundred bay horses are yoked to him. (5)

"Ten"—these are indeed the thousand rays of the sun; they are yoked to him, and by them he carries all this. Because he carries all this with them, therefore they are called *harayaḥ* (the carriers). "He assumes form after form, Maghavan, performing his own creative powers (*māyāḥ*) around his body; when he has come from heaven three times in a moment, he who drinks out of season comes at the right time with his own mantras. "He assumes form after form, Maghavan"—for indeed, this Maghavan assumes form after form. "Performing his own creative powers around his body"—so it is said.

"For by means of illusions he thus protects his own body. (8) "When he has come from heaven three times in a moment"—for indeed, during this very moment, he goes around this earth three times on all sides, surveying these creatures. (9) "By his own mantras, drinking at the wrong seasons, yet true to the season"—for he drinks at the wrong seasons, yet he is truly one who abides in the season. (10) 44 Thus ends the third section of the fourteenth anuvāka.

Then Pṛthu Vainya questioned the divine Vrātyas: "The learned ones speak of the *uktha*, the *ṛc*, the *udgītha*, the *brahman*, the *sāman*, the *prāṇa*, the *vyāna*, the mind, the speech, the eye, the *apāna*, and the ear; they speak of these in many ways. They replied: "O Vainya, these are the ṛṣis, the makers of mantras, born of old and being born again for the protection of the Vedas. Being wise, they speak of that as the one common Person who has entered into manifold forms. Indeed, this is that deity within the threefold knowledge (*trayī-vidyā*). This...

Some reach the same goal, while others do not; for he who knows this thus truly knows that deity. This very Indra is the Udgītha. When this Indra, as the Udgītha, arrives, nothing more is perceived of the Udgātṛ or the Upagātṛs; from here upwards he rises as the *svar* (sound), and he flickers above the head. He should know: "Indra has arrived; no trace of evil shall remain here. Indeed, in him no trace of evil remains.

This is the *abhrātṛvya* (rival-free) Sāman. Indeed, Indra never beheld any rival whatsoever; and just as Indra beheld no rival whatsoever, even so he who knows this, or for whom one knowing thus sings the *udgītha*, beholds no rival whatsoever.
Thus ends the fourth section of the fourteenth Anuvāka;
the fourteenth Anuvāka is complete.

In the beginning, Prajāpati alone was this universe. He desired, "May I be many; may I procreate; may I attain abundance. He divided himself into sixteen parts: the auspicious (*bhadra*) and completion (*samāpti*), non-existence (*abhūti*) and existence (*saṃbhūti*), what has been (*bhūta*) and all (*sarva*), form (*rūpa*) and the immeasurable (*aparimita*), fortune (*śrī*) and fame (*yaśas*), name (*nāman*) and the foremost (*agra*), kinsmen (*sajātāḥ*) and milk (*payaḥ*), greatness (*mahīyā*) and essence (*rasa*). Now, that which is the auspicious is his heart; from that he created the year, and the year attends upon him.

3. Completion is his action; for by means of that action he completes [the year]. From that, he created the seasons; therefore the seasons attend upon him. 4. Manifestation is his food; that becomes fourfold. From that, he created the months, the half-months, the days and nights, and the dawns; therefore the months, the half-months, the days and nights, and the dawns attend upon him. 5. Becoming is his seed; for from seed one comes into being. 46. First section of the fifteenth anuvāka.

From that, he created the moon; the moon attends upon him from there, and therefore it is the counterpart of his semen. 1. His vital breath (prāṇa) is the past; from that, he created the wind; the wind attends upon him from there, and therefore it is his downward breath (apāna). 2. His downward breath (apāna) is everything; from that, he created cattle; cattle attend upon him from there, and therefore it is his pervasive breath (vyāna). 3. His pervasive breath (vyāna) is form; from that, he created offspring; offspring attend upon him from there, and therefore forms are perceived among these offspring. 4. The immeasurable...

The mind is his; from that he created the quarters, and the quarters attend upon him. Therefore they are unlimited, for the mind is, as it were, unlimited. 5. Prosperity is his speech; from that he created the ocean, and the ocean attends upon him. 6. Glory is his austerity; from that he created fire, and fire attends upon him. Therefore it is born as if from friction, as if from heat. 7. Name is his eye. 8. Thus ends the second section in the fifteenth chapter.

Then he created the sun; that sun stands supporting him from behind. 1. His head is the summit; that [summit] is the sky; then he created the sky; that sky stands supporting him from behind. 2. His limbs are his kinsmen, for he is born together with those limbs; then he created the trees; those trees stand supporting him from behind. 3. His hair is milk; then he created the plants; those plants stand supporting him from behind. 4. His flesh is the earth; for he grows great along with the flesh; then...

He created birds; therefore, birds attend upon him. For that reason, they are prone to fly away, just as the great pieces of flesh are prone to fly away. 5. His essence was marrow; from that he created the earth; therefore, the earth attends upon him. 6. Having thus divided himself into sixteen parts, he united with her (Sā). Because he united with her (sā), that is the origin of the name *sāman*. 7. He arose as this very golden person (*puruṣa*), the progenitor of creatures. 8. Thus ends the third section of the fifteenth anuvāka.

The gods and the Asuras contended with one another. Those gods went to Prajāpati, saying, "Let us overcome the Asuras. He said, "Indeed, neither you nor the Asuras know me. If you were to know me, then you alone would prevail and the Asuras would be defeated. They said, "Tell us that! He said, "Prajāpati is the Puruṣa; worship me as Sāman. Then indeed you will prevail and the Asuras will be defeated. They worshipped him as the Puruṣa, Prajāpati, as Sāman. Thereupon the gods prevailed and the Asuras were defeated. Whoever knows this—that Prajāpati is the Puruṣa—[attains the same].
"He worships [the breath] as 'Tissāmā'; he prospers in his own self, and his hateful rival is defeated.
Thus ends the fourth section in the fifteenth anuvāka;
the fifteenth anuvāka is completed.

The gods, having been victorious, said, "Let us make a second [partner]; let us not be alone. They said, "Let us make the Sāman itself our second; let the Sāman be our second. 1. They said to these two, Heaven and Earth, "Come together and generate this Sāman. 2. That [Heaven] was repelled by her (Earth). He said, "Indeed, much of all kinds is done upon her; people stand upon her, move about upon her, and sit upon her. Purify her, for she is indeed impure! 3. They said to Gāthā, "By you..."

They said to the *gāthā*, "Purify yourself; what would come of that? "A hundredfold [offering] would result," it replied. "So be it. They purified themselves with the *gāthā*; therefore, one presses a hundred [libations] with the *gāthā*. They said to the *kuṃbyā*, "Purify yourself; what would come of that? "A hundredfold [offering] would result," it replied. "So be it. They purified themselves with the *kuṃbyā*; therefore, one presses a hundred [libations] with the *kuṃbyā*. They said to the *nārāśaṃsī*, "Purify yourself; what would come of that? "A hundredfold [offering] would result," it replied. "So be it. They purified themselves with the *nārāśaṃsī*; therefore, one [presses] a hundred [libations] with the *nārāśaṃsī*.

They said to the Raibhī, "With you we shall purify [the Soma]. "What would come of that? he asked. "There would be a hundredfold [offering]," they replied. "So be it," he said. They purified with the Raibhī; therefore, one also presses a hundredfold with the Raibhī. This [Soma], now purified, spoke to him (Agni): "A man indeed wanders about doing all sorts of things; you, however, do not purify yourself. Thus ends the first section of the sixteenth Anuvāka.

He purified it by means of the *ailaba*. Indeed, for one who knows this, his *sāmans* become purified, his *ṛks* become purified, his *yajus* formulas become purified; what has been uttered becomes purified, and everything becomes purified. 1. They came together and generated the *sāman*. Because they came together and generated the *sāman*, that is the essence of the *sāman*'s name. 2. This *sāman* was created here, moving and swaying. It stood there, and all the gods became its possessors, each saying, "It is mine! It is mine! 3. They said, "Let us divide this. But in its division, there was no...

As they were thus dividing [the world], Prajāpati said, "Go away! This is mine; I myself shall distribute it among you. He said to Agni, "You indeed are the eldest of my sons; you choose first. He replied, "I choose the *mandra* (low-pitched) tone from the Sāman as my food. Whoever should sing this, he shall surely become an eater of food. But whoever should speak ill of one who, knowing this, sings this, he shall reach me—that is, he shall reach the gods. Then he said to Indra, "You choose next. He replied, "I choose the *ugra* (fierce) tone from the Sāman..."

"Fortune," he said. "Whoever should sing this, he shall indeed become possessed of fortune; may he not reach me, nor may he reach the gods—anyone who, knowing this, should speak ill of one who sings this. Then he said to Soma, "Choose [a boon] after me. He replied, "I choose that which is beautiful from the *sāman*; [may it be] dear. "Whoever should sing this, he shall indeed be dear to fame, dear to the eye, and dear to all; may he not reach me, nor may he reach the gods—anyone who, knowing this, should speak ill of one who sings this. Then he said to Bṛhaspati, "Choose [a boon] after me."

He said to the Krauñca [bird], "I choose the *sāman* for the sake of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). He who sings this shall indeed possess spiritual luster; he shall attain me, and he shall reach the gods—anyone who, knowing this, should speak ill of one singing this. Thus ends the second section of the sixteenth chapter.

Then he said to the All-gods (Viśve Devāḥ), "Do you choose [a portion] after me. They replied, "We choose the Vaiśvadeva [portion] of the Sāman as a means of procreation. He who sings this shall indeed be possessed of offspring; may he who, knowing this, speaks ill of one singing this, fall into misfortune among us gods. Then he said to the cattle, "Do you choose [a portion] after me. They replied, "Vāyu rules over us; he alone shall choose for us. Then Vāyu and the cattle said, "We choose the Nirukta [portion] of the Sāman, which is beneficial to cattle. He...

"He who sings this shall indeed possess cattle; he shall reach both me and Vāyu among the gods—he who, knowing thus, should speak ill of one singing this. 4. Then Prajāpati said, "I will choose after you. 5. He (Vāyu) said, "I choose the undefined Sāman, which leads to heaven. "He who sings this shall dwell in the heavenly world; he shall reach both me and the gods—he who, knowing thus, should speak ill of one singing this. 6. Then he said to Varuṇa, "You choose after [me]. 7. He (Varuṇa) said, "That which is not yours..."

"Someone might say, 'I shall avoid that which is covered. Why then do you choose the *sāman* which is dark and unfavorable to cattle? He who should sing this would become devoid of cattle; he would come upon me and he would come upon the gods who should sing this. Now, these are the eight [verses] sung and unsung. These seven *āgās* of ours are indeed sung, but this one, the *vāruṇī āgā*, is not sung. Whatever one of these seven *āgās* a man knowing thus sings, it becomes for him as if sung; he attains those desires which are contained in them. However, one should not sing this very *vāruṇī āgā*. 8–10. 52.
Thus ends the third section in the sixteenth anuvāka;
the sixteenth anuvāka is completed.

In the beginning, this universe was indeed a duality: Being (*sat*) and Non-being (*asat*). Of these two, that which was Being was the *Sāman*, the mind (*manas*), and the out-breath (*prāṇa*); and that which was Non-being was the *Ṛc*, speech (*vāk*), and the down-breath (*apāna*). Now, that which is both mind and out-breath is common; and that which is both speech and down-breath is also common. This is the common abode: the mind and the out-breath, as well as the speech and the down-breath. Therefore, a man lies on the right side of a woman. This *Ṛc* desired union with this *Sāman*. He asked her, "Who are you? She replied, "I am 'She' (*aham*). Or rather—

"I am 'I' (aham) and she is 'mine' (ama)," [he said]. That which was *sā* and *ama* became the *sāman*; that is the essence of the *sāman*. "Let us two come together," he said. "No," she replied, "you are indeed my sister; seek a mate elsewhere. She said, "Indeed, I do not find anyone with whom I might unite; let me unite with you alone. "Then purify yourself," he said, "for you are unpurified. She purified herself by means of that which the wise (*vipra*) speak. She said, "Where will this lead? "Apply your mind (*dhī*)," he replied. "Or rather, wisdom (*dhī*)," she said.

"This shall be the wisdom of these creatures, or this shall be their very life," he said; "So be it," she replied, and she restored it. Therefore, this wisdom is indeed the life of creatures. "Cleanse it! he said. She cleansed it with a *gāthā*; she cleansed it with a *kuṃbyā*; she cleansed it with a *nārāśaṃsī*; she cleansed it with ancient history (*purāṇaitihāsa*); she cleansed it with that which they do not sing after having taken up [the lute]. She said, "What will become of this? "Restore it! he said. "This shall be the wisdom of these creatures, or this shall be their very life," she said; "So be it."
He turned away from that; therefore, this speech (*dhī*) is indeed the life of creatures. "Purify it!
he said. Thus ends the first section of the seventeenth anuvāka.

She purified him with honey; therefore, a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) should not eat honey, for it is the dross of the Veda. However, he may eat it at will when it is given by his teacher. Then the *Ṛk* and the *Sāman* said, "A man indeed wanders about doing all sorts of things; you must purify him. He purified him with the *bharaṇḍakeṣṇa* [chant]. Truly, for one who knows this, his *Sāmans* become purified, his *Ṛks* become purified, his *Yajus* become purified, his recited texts become purified, and everything becomes purified. For those two, he prepared a sacrificial shed (*sadas*) for their union.

Therefore, on the night of the *upavasatha*, one should not sleep in the *sadas*. For it is here that the *Ṛc* and the *Sāman* meet in the *sadas* on the night of the *upavasatha*. Just as one who watches over a superior, so indeed is he liable to perish if he is unobserved. Now they say: "They meet in the mouth of the *udgātṛ*; therefore, one should not look at the mouth of the *udgātṛ*. But regarding this they also say: "One may look at the mouth of the *udgātṛ* at will; however, on this very night of the *upavasatha*, one should not sleep in the *sadas*."

"Indeed, on the night of the Upavasatha, these two, Ṛk and Sāman, come together in the assembly hall. As he was about to unite with her, he said: "I am the male (Ama), you are the female (Sā); you are the female, I am the male. Having become devoted to me, let us generate offspring; come, let us unite. As he united with her, he surpassed her; he said, "I do not indeed equal you. Having become the Virāj, let us generate offspring. "So be it," she replied. Having become the Virāj, the two of them generated offspring: the Hiṅkāra and the Āhāva, the Prastāva and the first [verse].

The *udgītha* and the middle [note], the *pratihāra* and the highest [note], the *nidhana* and the *vaṣaṭkāra*—thus becoming the *virāj*, they brought forth; they brought forth that which yonder shines. They pierced it. (8.54) Thus ends the second section in the seventeenth chapter.

"It has become sweet! It has become sweet!"—therefore they say, "The son of sweetness. For this reason, women do not eat honey, saying, "We are observing this vow of our sons. Then this triplet of verses took its place: this earth is the Gāyatrī, the intermediate space is the Triṣṭubh, and yonder sky is the Jagatī; such is that triplet. He burns as one placed above the Sāman; he was, as it were, unstable, as it were swaying, and he did not burn upwards. He said to the gods, "Sing out for me!"—"What would come of that? they asked.

"May I bestow prosperity upon you; may it make me firm here. "So be it," they replied. As he was singing the *udgītha*, they made him firm there, and he bestowed prosperity upon them. This is the prosperity of the gods. Then that [sun] burns facing upwards; it does not burn facing downwards. He said to the seers (*ṛṣis*), "Sing after me! "What would come of that? they asked. "I would bestow prosperity upon you; may it make me firm here. "So be it," they replied. As they were singing after him, they made him firm there, and he bestowed prosperity upon them. This is the prosperity of the seers. Then...

It burns downwards from here; it does not burn crosswise. He said to the Gandharvas and Apsarases, "Sing for me. They asked, "What would come of that? [He replied,] "I shall bestow prosperity upon you; let it support me here. They said, "So be it. As they sang for him, it supported him at this point, and he bestowed prosperity upon them. This is the prosperity of the Gandharvas and Apsarases. Therefore, it burns crosswise from there. These, indeed, are the three types of singing: the sung-for-others (sāṃ), the sung-after (anugīta), and the sung-to (āgīta). Just as we sing here, so do we sing aloud (udgāyāma).
"This is the *udgīta*; now, that which is sung according to the [textual] recitation is the *anugīta*; and 'whatever there is'—that is our *sāṃnaḥ*. For these three indeed are our *sāṃnaḥ*.
Thus ends the third section in the seventeenth anuvāka;
the seventeenth anuvāka is completed.

In the beginning, this universe was indeed a great expanse of water. One wave leaped upon another, and from that, two golden bellies came into being; these were the *Ṛk* and the *Sāman*. This *Ṛk* floated toward this *Sāman*. It asked her, "Who are you? She replied, "I am 'She' (*sā*). Then it said, "I am 'He' (*ama*). Because she is *sā* and he is *ama*, that is the essence of the *Sāman* (*sāmatva*). "Let us two unite," [the *Ṛk* said]. "No," it replied, "you are my sister; seek a mate elsewhere. She floated away.

Desiring a mate, she floated about for seventy thousand years. Regarding this, there is this verse: "In the beginning, she indeed moved about alone in the water, desiring a husband; after seventy thousand years, she gave birth. Behold! That sun over there is the beholder; it was he who was born from her, for by means of him one sees. She floated down toward him and said, "I do not find anyone with whom I may unite; let me unite with you. She, indeed—

Thus ends the first section of the eighteenth Anuvāka. That Gāyatrī purified herself with the Gāthā; the Triṣṭubh with the Nārāśaṃsī; the Jagatī with the Raibhī, [thinking], "Alas! I have cast off a terrible impurity. Therefore they are called Bhīmalāḥ. Indeed, these are thoughts (dhiyaḥ); for these thoughts have cast off impurity, therefore they are called Bhīmalāḥ. For this reason, one should not eat while those who sing are present, for they live upon impurity. Then the Ṛk spoke to the Sāman: "A man indeed wanders about doing all manner of things; do you purify him. It purified him by means of the Ūrdhvagaṇa. Verily, his Sāmans become purified and his Ṛks become purified.

The *yajus* formulas become purified, the recited verse becomes purified, and everything becomes purified for one who knows this. 3. For the sake of union, they caused the quarters to revolve around those two; as they were about to come together, they called out to one another: "I am he, you are she," and "You are she, I am he. 4. Thus, by means of speech, he surpassed her on both sides—with the *hiṅkāra* in front, with the *stobha* in the middle, and with the *nidhana* at the end. One who knows this surpasses three women of Brahmin descent who are his equals. 5. Of those two who have come together, the upward-rising vigor flowed forth.

Thus ends the second section of the eighteenth chapter. Now, as for what they say: "Who has sung forth?"—they are indeed asking, "Who has sung forth this Āditya? For they sing of him with the threefold knowledge (*trayi vidyā*), just as lute-players might cause a song to be sung. This mind is a lake filled with desires; speech is its stream. Just as one leads water from a lake to a higher level by means of a stream, even so the Udgātṛ priest, by means of speech derived from the mind, bestows the desires of the sacrificer upon whom he performs the rite. He who [approaches] the Udgātṛ...

She propitiates him with sacrificial gifts; she pursues him who does not propitiate her, and he, in turn, repels her. Now, therefore, there is both giving and receiving. That which is given is indeed smoke; it is to be given to the sacrificer by means of speech, but to oneself by means of the mind. Thus, one does not give away everything. Now, when this semen was emitted during their union, it lay there like unworked gold shimmering; so it was. All the gods were desirous of possessing it, thinking, "It is mine! "It is mine! (5–7).

They said, "It is ours. They said, "Let us fashion it. They said, "This is indeed better than ourselves; let us fashion it by means of our own selves. 8. They fashioned it by means of their own selves. Of them, Vāyu was the *hiṅkāra*, Agni the *prastāva*, Indra the *ādi*, Soma and Bṛhaspati the *udgītha*, the Aśvins the *pratihāra*, the Viśve Devas the *upadrava*, and Prajāpati himself was the *nidhana*. 9. These indeed are all the deities. This gold of his becomes praised by all the deities for one who knows thus.
He who reviles one who knows this is cut off from all these very deities.
10.58 Thus ends the third section in the eighteenth anuvāka.

Now, Brahmadatta Caikitāneya went to Abhipratārin Kākṣaseni. He requested from him the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*). Then, his domestic priest Śaunaka sat down nearby after having entered [the hall]. Without addressing him, he drank the honey-mixture. He said to him: "Knowing what, O Dālbhya, do you drink the honey-mixture without addressing us? "I enter into the essence of the Sāman," he replied. Thereupon, he questioned him right then and there: "Do you know that which is in the wind? "The *hiṅkāra* (the introductory chant)," he said.

"Is it 'sa' in this [verse]? "I know that which is in Agni. "That is its *prastāva*. "Is it 'sa' in this [verse]? "I know that which is in Indra. "That is its *ādi*. "Is it 'sa' in this [verse]? "I know that which is in Soma and Bṛhaspati. "That is its *udgītha*. "Is it 'sa' in this [verse]? "I know that which is in the Aśvins. "That is its *pratihāra*. "Is it 'sa' in this [verse]? "I know that which is in the Viśvedevas. "That is its *upadrava*. "Is it 'sa' in this [verse]? "I know that which is in Prajāpati. "That is its *nidhana*," he said. "Or rather, it is the lineage (*ārṣeya*)."

"Is this his kinship, or is this his bridge? He replied, "Homage to you, O Blessed One! You who know, accept my *madhuparka*. Then the other asked, "To which deity does one resort when entering the *sāma* called *vairāja*? To which deities do they sing the hymn? He replied, "It belongs to those very deities. This was indeed a correct answer. [The other] said, "This is its pervasion; speak further! [The first] said, "We have already paid you homage. Do not question us too far. He said, "I should indeed not have questioned you."

"Truly, you have not asked about the deity of the deity; the deities are of the nature of speech (*vāk*). Sāman has speech as its deity; of speech, the mind (*manas*) is the deity; of the mind, cattle; of cattle, plants; of plants, water. Thus, this Sāman is born from water and is established in water.
(14.59) Thus ends the fourth section in the eighteenth chapter.

The gods and the Asuras contended. Those gods sang out with the mind; the Asuras, having rushed upon them, mingled them with evil. Therefore, whatever much one meditates upon with the mind, one meditates upon both the auspicious and the inauspicious by means of it. Then they sang out with speech; they did exactly the same thing. Therefore, whatever much one speaks with speech, one speaks both the true and the false by means of it. Then they sang out with the eye; they did exactly the same thing. Therefore, whatever much one sees with the eye, one sees both the beautiful and the ugly.

With that [eye], they sang the udgītha; they did exactly so. Therefore, with that [eye], one sees much—both what is worth seeing and what is not worth seeing. With that [ear], they sang the udgītha; they did exactly so. Therefore, with that [ear], one hears much—both what is worth hearing and what is not worth hearing. With that [breath], they sang the udgītha; they did exactly so. Therefore, with that [breath], one smells much—both what is fragrant and what is foul-smelling. They sang the udgītha with that [vital breath]; then the Asuras rushed forward, thinking, "We shall do likewise. He...

Just as a clod of earth would shatter upon hitting a solid stone, even so did the Asuras perish. This vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed that solid stone. Just as a clod of earth shatters upon hitting a solid stone, even so does he perish who speaks ill of one who knows this.
Thus ends the fifth section in the eighteenth anuvāka;
the eighteenth anuvāka is complete.

Thus ends the first chapter. Prajāpati indeed conquered this world by means of the threefold Veda; that which is his conquest here, he [conquered] by that. He reflected: "If other gods should sacrifice with this Veda, they will surely win this very conquest which is mine. Come now, let me take away the essence of the threefold Veda. He took the essence of the Ṛgveda with the syllable *bhūḥ*. That became this earth. The breath that flowed from its essence became Agni, the essence of the essence. With the syllable *bhuvaḥ*, he took the essence of the Yajurveda. That became the intermediate space. The breath that flowed from its essence became Vāyu, the essence of the essence. With the syllable *svaḥ*, he took the essence of the Sāmaveda. That became yonder sky. The breath that flowed from its essence became Āditya, the essence of the essence. With the syllable *bhūrbhuvaḥ-svaḥ*, he took the essence of the Atharvāṅgirasaḥ. That became these worlds. The breath that flowed from their essence became Candramas, the essence of the essence. With the syllable *bhūḥ*, he took the essence of the Ṛgveda. That became this earth. The breath that flowed from its essence became Agni, the essence of the essence. With the syllable *svaḥ*, he took the essence of the Sāmaveda. That became yonder sky. The breath that flowed from its essence became Āditya, the essence of the essence. With the syllable *bhūrbhuvaḥ-svaḥ*, he took the essence of the Atharvāṅgirasaḥ. That became these worlds. The breath that flowed from their essence became Candramas, the essence of the essence. With the syllable *bhūḥ*, he took the essence of the Ṛgveda. That became this earth. The breath that flowed from its essence became Agni, the essence of the essence. With the syllable *bhuvaḥ*, he took the essence of the Yajurveda. That became the intermediate space. The breath that flowed from its essence became Vāyu, the essence of the essence. With the syllable *svaḥ*, he took the essence of the Sāmaveda. That became yonder sky. The breath that flowed from its essence became Āditya, the essence of the essence. With the syllable *bhūrbhu

That became this intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Its essence that breathed forth became Vāyu, the essence of the essence. 4. He took the essence of the Sāmaveda as "Svar. That became yonder sky (*dyau*). Its essence that breathed forth became Āditya, the essence of the essence. 5. Then he was unable to take the essence of even a single syllable—of this very "Om" alone. 6. That became Speech (*vāk*); its name is indeed "Om," and its essence is breath (*prāṇa*). 7. These are those eight; the Gāyatrī has eight syllables, the Sāman is Gāyatra, and the Gāyatrī is indeed Brahman; thus one attains Brahman.
"Animals have eight hooves; therefore it is beneficial for cattle.
Thus ends the first section in the first Anuvāka.

When he says "Om," that is Agni; "Vāk" (Speech) is the Earth. When he says "Om," that is Vāyu; "Vāk" is the Intermediate Space. When he says "Om," that is Āditya; "Vāk" is Heaven. When he says "Om," that is Prāṇa; "Vāk" is indeed Speech. He who, knowing this, sings the *udgītha*, takes Agni with "Om" and establishes him on the Earth; he takes Vāyu with "Om" and establishes him in the Intermediate Space; he takes Āditya with "Om" and establishes him in Heaven; he takes Prāṇa with "Om" and establishes him in Speech. This, indeed, is the *gāyatra* chant of Śailana.

"Sing 'ovā3covā3covā3 chumbhā ovā'—thus three times. Now, that [chant] is indeed as if turned away and as if not conducive to long life; it should be sung according to the course of the wind and the waters. For if the wind were to blow only away from one, it would perish. When it blows from the east, from the south, from the west, from the north, from above, and when it blows through all the directions, then it is so. Regarding this, they say: "Now this [wind] was here before, and now it blows in such a way," for when it blows creating heat and curling inward, it does so out of fear of perishing. And what...

Indeed, if the waters were to flow away only in a straight line, they would waste away; but when they go forming eddies, swirling about, and creating whirlpools, it is because they are afraid of destruction. Therefore, this [Sāman] should be sung following the path of both Vāyu and the waters.
Thus ends the second section in the first Anuvāka.

"Ovā, ovā, ovā, humbhā, ovā"—he indeed performs [the ritual] with these; by means of them, he attains his full span of life. Just as one might ascend a tree by means of climbing-steps, even so, joining together these two deities at a time, he ascends and goes toward these worlds. Death follows him as a single entity, namely hunger. Then he utters *hiṅ*; the *hiṅ* is indeed the moon, and the moon is food; by means of food they strike down hunger. Having struck down each instance of hunger with food, he is completely released from that very sun by saying "Om. This is it.

Just as there might be a hole in the sky or a gap in a chariot, so too is this a hole in the sky; it appears covered by rays. That which is above the *hiṅkāra* of the *gāyatra* is the immortal; one should place that upon oneself and also upon the sacrificer. And that other part of the *sāman*, above its *pratihāra*—just as water would mingle with water, as fire would mingle with fire, or as milk poured into milk, even so does this syllable mingle with these deities. Thus ends the third section in the first chapter.

Now, they utter this very *hiṅkāra* as "him-bhā. *Bhāḥ* is indeed glory; and that sun is *bhāḥ*. This very *nyaṅga* (limb) follows it: when [the sound] "bha" enters the generative organ of women, from that a Brāhmaṇa like a seer (*ṛṣikalpa*) is born, and a Kṣatriya who is a hero and a great archer. This very *nyaṅga* follows it: when [the sound] "bha" enters [the organ], from that a virtuous bull, a milch-cow, a draught-ox, and a stallion swift as ten [horses] are born.

This indeed follows that very limb, for it goes down with the sound "bha," as in "gardabha. Therefore, he, though being base, moves among those who are superior; therefore, from this base one, something superior is born—either a mule or a female mule. This indeed follows that very limb, for it goes down with the sound "bha," as in "kubhra. Therefore, even though he is not an Ārya, he attains the status of a king. Some indeed perform this *hiṅkāra* as "him-bhā ovā," singing it as if externally; for prosperity is indeed external, and prosperity is the *sāman*.

"Hiṅkāra! [he says]. If someone were to say of him at that point, "Verily, he has placed his prosperity outside himself; he will become worse off," then since when one dies, one is cast into the fire, [the challenger would say], "Alas, he will die soon; they will cast him into the fire. And so it would indeed happen. Therefore, one should internalize this *hiṅkāra* as "hiṃ vo" within oneself, just as it were; thus one does not place prosperity outside, and one reaches a full lifespan. The Fourth Section of the First Anuvāka.

This wicked deity stands here warding him off, saying: "Indeed, you shall go to that evil which you have committed here; for whoever is a doer of merit, he may come here. He should say: "You did not see what I did; had you not caused me to do it, you yourself would be the doer of that. She knows: "He has spoken the truth to me," for this deity is indeed Truth. She has no power over him to ward him off; she merely calls out to him with Truth. Then Ikṣvāku said: "Or rather..."

Thus ends the fifth section in the first Anuvāka. Gobala Vārṣṇa said: "Who is capable of approaching this Āditya? For from afar he shines thus; one should approach him facing downward. Having mentally brought him along that path of Sāman which lies to his east, one should place him above this very immortal [space]. Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said: "One should indeed approach him together. Who knows whether these waters on both sides [are meant], or whether it is the wind that he summons, for he then disperses his rays for him? Then Ulukya Jānaśruteya said: "Wherever this [sun]..."

"This is austerity, this is immortality; if one indeed attains this, then one turns away from death and evil. "Who knows that which is beyond the sun, and this atmosphere which is below it, being without a support? "Now, this is indeed immortality; you shall lead me to this very thing; I do not disregard this. These are the eight [syllables]; the *gāyatrī* has eight syllables, the *sāman* is *gāyatra*, and the *gāyatrī* is indeed Brahman;
he attains Brahman. Animals have eight hooves; therefore, it pertains to cattle.
Thus ends the sixth section in the first chapter.

These are the eight deities; this whole world is just this much. He makes these for him. Let him not leave room for his evil rival in these worlds; he should exclude him by means of the mind alone. This very thing is declared by a Ṛg-verse: "Speech has been measured out in four quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them. Three, hidden in secret, do not stir; the fourth quarter of speech is what humans speak. Now, those three which are hidden in secret and do not stir—these are indeed these worlds. The fourth quarter of speech is what humans [speak].

"They say"—this is indeed one quarter, for the fourth part of speech. He who knows this has performed his task with his entire speech, with all these worlds, and with everything. 5. Just as a clod of earth, having struck a stone, is shattered, even so is he shattered who speaks ill of one who knows this. 6–7. Thus ends the seventh section in the first chapter;
the first chapter is complete.

Prajāpati indeed conquered this world by means of the threefold Veda; whatever he has here conquered, that was it. He reflected: "If other gods should sacrifice with this same Veda, they will surely win this very conquest which is mine. Come now, I shall squeeze out this threefold Veda. He squeezed out this threefold Veda; while squeezing it, he was unable to squeeze out even a single syllable, namely this "Om. This, indeed, is full of sap; and for one who knows thus, the threefold knowledge becomes full of sap. He...

Having pressed this essence and set it aside, it flowed upward. As it flowed, four [beings]—Indra, Candra, Rudra, and Samudra—beheld it. Therefore, these are the most excellent among the gods, for they were the ones who beheld it. That which was this essence became heat (*tapas*). The gods looked toward this essence; they perceived it, thinking, "It has indeed become heat. Having reflected upon this triple Veda, they found within it this very syllable, *om*, as if it were pressed out.

"This very thing is indeed the essence (*sarasa*); with it he mixed him, just as one would mix parched grain with honey. They performed fervor; while they were performing fervor, their Veda swelled. By means of this fervor and that swollen Veda, they won that very victory which Prajāpati had won. All these are indeed the measure of Prajāpati: "Ayā3m, ayā3m. Therefore, for one who performs fervor, his fame becomes greater and his glory increases. He who knows this thus, by means of that very swollen Veda—

When one sacrifices or causes another to sacrifice, it is in this very same way that he causes the sacrifice with this Veda. For him who knows this, there is no affliction whatsoever; but whoever speaks ill of him, he meets with affliction. Thus ends the first section in the second chapter.

Regarding this they say: "When it is sung as 'Oṃ' or 'Oṃ', where does the *Ṛc* come into being here, and where the *Sāman*? Indeed, *Oṃ* is the *Sāman* and *Vāk* (Speech) is the *Ṛc*. *Oṃ* is the mind (*manas*) and *Vāk* is speech; *Oṃ* is the breath (*prāṇa*) and *Vāk* is indeed speech; *Oṃ* is Indra and *Vāk* is all the gods. Thus, all the gods follow after Indra alone. This very syllable *Oṃ*—by means of it, indeed, one may win over the Indra of another in a contest of recitation (*saṃsava*). By means of this very [syllable], Baka Dālbhya won over the Indra of the Ājakeśins and led him away by means of this very [syllable] *Oṃ*. These [syllables] are eight.

The Gāyatrī has eight syllables; the Sāman is the Gāyatra; the Gāyatrī is indeed Brahman, and thus one attains Brahman. Animals have eight hooves; therefore, it belongs to the animals. Its names are these: Indra, Karmā, Akṣiti, Amṛta, Vyoman, Anta, Vācas, Bahu, Bhūyas, Sarva, Sarvasmāduttara, Jyotis, Ṛta, Satya, Vijñāna, Vivācana, Aprativācya, Pūrva, Sarva, Sarvā, Vāk, and this entire world. Furthermore, as a cow she yields her milk both upward and downward. Thus ends the second section of the second Anuvāka.

She, milking the immortal nectar—which is distinct water, the earth that yields all desires, the life-breath, the eye, the ear, speech in abundance, pervaded by the mind, the tip of the heart, the auspicious food beloved by Brahmins, the rain-purifier, the fortune of cows, the highest of the earth, austerity as her body, the enclosure of Varuṇa, the excellence of Indra, consisting of a thousand syllables with ten thousand streams—overflows all these worlds. That which is "Om" is this very truth, the imperishable syllable; in it the waters are established, and in the waters, the earth.

These worlds are supported by the earth; just as leaves might be pierced by a needle, so too are these worlds pierced by this Imperishable (akṣara). This very [Imperishable], having pierced through these worlds, flows tenfold, hundredfold, thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, hundred-thousandfold, millionfold, ten-millionfold, hundred-millionfold, billionfold, ten-billionfold, hundred-billionfold, and a trillionfold; it is imperishable, the lotus, and the end of space. Just as a flood that overflows becomes greater and greater, even so does this Imperishable become greater and greater. These worlds indeed extend upwards.

These very thirteen months are thus supported. He who, knowing this, chants the *udgītha*, carries these worlds across in this very manner. By means of this syllable "Om," he places yonder sun within his mouth; for this syllable is indeed that [sun]. Everything becomes attained by him, everything is conquered; no desire whatsoever remains unfulfilled for one who knows this. Now, Pṛthu Vainya questioned the celestial *vrātyas*: "They call the pillar that supports the sky the sun, and the sun is in the intermediate space."

"Supported by the earth, the worlds rest upon the waters, bearing a great weight. Upon what, then, do the great waters rest? They replied: "The pillar that supports the sky; they say the sun is in the atmosphere. Supported by the earth, the worlds rest upon the waters, bearing a great weight. Truth, the waters rest upon. "Om"—this very syllable is truth; upon that the waters rest.
Thus ends the third section of the second chapter; the second chapter is complete.

Prajāpati created living beings; once created, they surrounded him on all sides, seeking food. He said to them, "What is your desire? They replied, "We desire food. He said, "I have indeed created only one Veda as food; that is the Sāman, and I shall bestow it upon you. They said, "Bestow it upon us. He said, "We live most abundantly upon these cattle; I shall give it to them first. He bestowed the *hiṅkāra* upon them; therefore, cattle low with the sound *hiṅ*.

The *prastāva* they move about as if desiring to know; therefore, among men, they praise, thinking, "This shall be mine, that shall be mine. The *ādi* they move about as if taking up [food] for the birds; therefore, those birds move about as if flying down while seizing [their prey]. The *udgītha* belongs to the gods as immortality; therefore, they are immortal. The *pratihāra* belongs to the wild animals of the forest; therefore, they move about as if being driven back and trembling. Thus ends the first section of the third chapter.

The *upadrava* belongs to the Gandharvas and Apsarases; therefore, they move about as if seizing the *upadrava*. The *nidhana* belongs to the Pitṛs; therefore, they conclude with the *nidhana*. Now, when he bestowed that Sāman upon them, he bestowed this very Āditya (the Sun) upon them. When he has not yet risen, that is the *hiṅkāra*; when half-risen, it is the *prastāva*; at the time of the cows being gathered (*āsaṃgava*), it is the *ādi*; at midday, it is the *udgītha*; in the afternoon, it is the *pratihāra*; when he begins to turn red at sunset, that is the *upadrava*; and once he has set, that is the *nidhana*. This is that [Sāman].

He is equal to all the worlds; because he is equal to all the worlds, therefore he is *sāman*. Indeed, he who knows thus is a knower of the *sāman*, and he truly knows the *sāman*. They said, "This is indeed far from us; place it where we may subsist upon it. He brought it toward the seasons. He made spring the *hiṅkāra*, summer the *prastāva*, the rainy season the *udgītha*, autumn the *pratihāra*, and winter the *nidhana*. He made the months and half-months the *saptamāvas*. They said, "Now this is indeed closer."
"Perform it right there where we may subsist. He then drove that rain-cloud toward [the goal]. He made the east wind itself the *hiṅkāra* (the introductory chant).
Thus ends the second section in the third lesson.

He made the clouds the *hiṅkāra*, thunder the *prastāva*, lightning the *udgītha*, rain the *pratihāra*, and the rain that causes offspring and plants to be born the *nidhana*. He performed this as the seventh [layer]. They said, "Come even closer now; perform it right there where we may subsist. He led it toward the sacrifice. He made the *yajus* formulas the *hiṅkāra*, the *ṛc* verses the *prastāva*, the *sāman* chants the *udgītha*, the *stoma* hymns the *pratihāra*, the meters the *nidhana*, and the utterances *svāhā* and *vaṣaṭ* the seventh. He performed this as the seventh [layer].

They said, "Come closer; do right here where we may subsist upon it. He led it toward a man. He made the *hiṅkāra* out of mind alone, the *prastāva* out of speech, the *udgītha* out of breath, the *pratihāra* out of sight, and the *nidhana* out of hearing; and he made semen and offspring the seventh. They said, "He has indeed done this very thing here, where we shall subsist. One should know: "I am the Sāman itself; in me are these deities. Thus ends the third section in the third chapter.

The gods are not far away; for as long as one worships the gods through the self, so long do the gods remain present for him. Now, he who knows this thus—"I am indeed the *sāman*, and in me are all these deities"—for him all these deities become present in that very way. This *sāman* is called "Devaśrut" (heard by the gods), for all the deities indeed hear one who knows this, and they cause him to perform what is virtuous and good. Sucitta Śailana used to say: "Whoever desires to perform a sacrifice, let him choose me alone."

"Therefore, the sacrifice will indeed lead him [to success]; for all the deities are satisfied along with one who, knowing this, chants the *udgītha*. Being satisfied, they will act for him in such a way that the sacrifice will lead him [to success]. Thus ends the fourth section in the third chapter;
the third chapter is completed.

The gods, indeed, desired to reach the heavenly world; yet, whether lying down, sitting, standing, or running, they did not attain it by any action whatsoever. Those gods ran to Prajāpati, saying, "We have desired the heavenly world, but whether lying down, sitting, standing, or running, we have not attained it by any action whatsoever. Instruct us so that we may reach the heavenly world. He said to them, "Proceed to the heavenly world with the Sāman, devoid of Ṛk. They [proceeded] with the Sāman, devoid of Ṛk.

"They have gone to the heavenly world" (svargaṃ lokamprāyan)—thus they sang with the *sāman*; therefore it is called *prasāma*. Therefore, when one eats food, he does so while singing aloud (*prasāmyan*). The gods, indeed, as they were going to the heavenly world, came along shaking off these bodies which are the feet of the *ṛc*s; thus they won the heavenly world. Those [bodies] remained scattered up to heaven. Then Prajāpati, having gathered together these bodies which are the feet of the *ṛc*s, worshipped them.
Because he worshipped them (*abhyarcat*), they became the *ṛc*s. Thus ends the first section of the fourth anuvāka.

This very *Ṛc* became this *Śrī*; therefore, the gods prospered. Then the Asuras seized this *Śrī* of theirs, and so it became "Asura. The gods said, "The *Śrī* that was ours, the Asuras have taken away; how indeed can we recover this *Śrī* of theirs? They said, "Let us sing the *Sāman* upon the *Ṛc* itself. They returned and sang the *Sāman* upon the *Ṛc*, and thereby they drove the Asuras out from this world. This [is done] at the midday pressing and at the third pressing.

That which he sings in the *ṛc* is a fault; by that, he repels his hateful rival from this world. And because he sings the morning libation (*prātassavana*) among the immortal deities, he goes to the heavenly world. Prajāpati indeed won this victory through the *sāman*; that victory of his was this very one, and he ascended to the heavenly world. The gods approached Prajāpati and said, "Grant this *sāman* to us as well. He replied, "So be it," and granted that *sāman* to them. This *sāman* [led] them to the heavenly world.

It did not desire to carry the world. Those gods approached Prajāpati and said, "That Sāman which you gave us—this indeed does not desire to carry our world to heaven. "Then unite it with evil," [he replied]. "What is its evil? "The Ṛc. They united it with the Ṛc. This [Sāman] stood reproaching Prajāpati, saying, "They have indeed united me with evil. He said, "Whoever shall separate himself from this, he alone shall be separated from evil. He who...

With this Ṛc, he separates [the Sāman] at the morning pressing; thus he indeed turns away from evil. (12.16) This is the second section in the fourth Anuvāka. Regarding this they say: "When 'O-vā-o-vā' is sung, where does the Ṛc come into being here, and where is the Sāman? (1) While beginning the Prastāva, he begins with eight syllables. The Gāyatrī has eight syllables; each syllable consists of three syllables, and thus they amount to twenty-four. The Gāyatrī has twenty-four syllables. (2) Having reached this Ṛc by means of the Prastāva, he remains singing it, [attaining] whatever prosperity, whatever honor, whatever heavenly world, whatever fame, and whatever food there may be. (3.17)

The third section in the fourth lesson: Prajāpati created the gods; Death, as evil, was created after them. Those gods approached Prajāpati and said, "Why did you not create us? Had you created Death as evil after us, we would not have perished. He said to them, "Gather the meters and enter them according to their proper place; then you shall be separated from Death and from evil. The Vasus gathered the Gāyatrī meter and entered it; it concealed them. The Rudras gathered the Triṣṭubh meter and entered it.

The Ādityas gathered the *jagatī* meter; they entered it, and she covered them. 6. The Viśve Devas gathered the *anuṣṭubh* meter; they entered it, and she covered them. 7. Death perceived them in this toneless *ṛc*, just as one might perceive a thread through a gem when looking at it. 8. They entered the tone (*svara*); while they were within the tone, he did not perceive them, but he followed after them by the sound of the tone. 9. They ascended this very syllable "Om"; this very syllable is the threefold knowledge (*trayī vidyā*).

When that immortal [sun] shines there, having ascended to it, they turn away from death and evil. In exactly the same way, one who knows this, having ascended to this very syllable *om*, and having reached that immortal [sun] which shines there, turns away from death and evil; and also for him for whom one who knows this sings the *udgītha*.
Thus ends the fourth section in the fourth chapter;
the fourth chapter is complete.

Now, this is the twenty-onefold *sāman*. Its *hiṅkāra* is the threefold knowledge (*vidyā*). Fire, wind, and yonder sun—these are the *prastāva*. These worlds are the *ādi*, for upon these worlds all this is established. Faith, sacrifice, and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)—this is the *udgītha*. The quarters, the intermediate quarters, and space—this is the *pratihāra*. Water, progeny, and plants—this is the *upadrava*. The moon, the stars, and the fathers—this is the *nidhana*. This is that twenty-onefold *sāman*. He who knows this twenty-onefold *sāman* thus—for him, it is as if the entire *sāman* has been sung by him; and from this very [knowledge]...
"He who reviles one who knows thus is cut off from everything.
Thus ends the fifth section.

In the beginning, this very thing was the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*); and even now it is so. Now, that which is this intermediate space is he who blows here (the wind). He indeed is named "Intermediate Space" (*antarikṣa*). And he alone is this one who is spread out (*vitata*). Just as two leaves might be propped apart by a stick, or two wheels by an axle, even so are these two worlds propped apart by him. Within him is all this; because all this is within (*antar*) him, therefore it is called "interior" (*antara*). "Interior" (*antara*) is indeed its name; that is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).

They speak of it as something beyond perception. Just as bundles tied together would hang down, even so do all the worlds hang down, tied to this [Sāman]. Of this very Sāman there are three *āgātrīs*, three sung portions (*āgītāni*), six manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*), four foundations (*pratiṣṭhāḥ*), ten preludes (*pragāḥ*), seven terminations (*saṃsthāḥ*), two musical interjections (*stobhau*), and one form (*rūpam*). Now, those three *āgātrīs* are these very worlds. Then, as for the three sung portions—Agni, Vāyu, and that Āditya (the Sun)—these are the sung portions. Indeed, he who knows this does not fail to attain any prosperity whatsoever. 8.20

Thus ends the first section of the sixth chapter. Now, those which are the six manifestations are the seasons. 1. Now, those which are the four supports are these very four quarters. 2. Now, those which are the ten forward-strides are these very ten vital breaths. 3. Now, those which are the seven terminuses are these very seven days and nights toward which they offer the *vaṣaṭ* call. 4. Now, those two which are the musical interjections (*stobha*) are day and night. 5. Now, that which is the single form is action itself; for by action all this is transformed. 6. The gods entered into a contest over this very *Sāman*.

Prajāpati won the *hiṅkāra* by means of his *haras*; Agni, by means of his brilliance, the *prastāva*; Bṛhaspati, by means of his form, the *udgītha*; the Fathers, by means of their *svadhā*, the *pratihāra*; and Indra, by means of his heroism, the *nidhana*. Then the other gods felt as if they had been excluded; they said to Indra, "We are indeed yours; let us have a share in this *sāman*. He gave them the *svara* (the tone). Prajāpati said to him, "Why have you done this? You have given them the entire *sāman*, for the *sāman* is only as much as the *svara*, or it is the *ṛc*."

"This shall become your *svara* (melodic accent)," he said. He [Soma] replied, "Indeed, I shall take back this essence (*rasa*) from them. He said to them, "Sing unto me; chant toward me with the *svara*. "So be it," they said. As they sang unto him, he chanted toward them and took back their essence.
Thus ends the second section in the sixth chapter.

Just as one might pour honey into a honey-vat by means of honey-veins, even so does that *sāman* pour its essence back into it. Therefore, one should not sing along (*upagāyet*). The Udgātṛ is Indra; just as he takes away the essence of these [veins], so does he take away the essence of those [who sing along]. However, the sacrificer may indeed sing along at will, for that belongs to the sacrificer; likewise, a religious student (*brahmacārin*) who has been instructed by his teacher may do so. Regarding this, they say: "One should certainly sing along, for the quarters sang along; thus one wins co-residence with the quarters. Those who are these...

These vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are indeed the chief ones; they are both the *udgātṛ*s and the *upagātṛ*s. These three are the *udgātṛ*s, and these four are the *upagātṛ*s. Therefore, one should appoint exactly four *upagātṛ*s. Therefore, he should touch the *upagātṛ*s, saying: "You are the quarters; do not harm my hearing. That which was its essence is this very wind that blows here; that is indeed the essence. As for this, Sucitta Śailāna used to say: "Just as one would eat a morsel of honey, so should one fill oneself with this essence. That *udgātṛ* leads both himself and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) to immortality. 8.22
Thus ends the third section in the sixth chapter;
the sixth chapter is completed.

In the beginning, this was indeed only space (*ākāśa*); and even now it is that very same thing. That which is this space is speech itself; therefore, from that space, speech speaks. Prajāpati pressed upon this speech; from its being pressed, its essence flowed forth as breath, and these worlds came into being. He pressed upon these worlds; from their being pressed, their essence flowed forth as breath, and these deities came into being: namely, Agni, Vāyu, and that Āditya. He pressed upon these deities; from their being pressed, their essence flowed forth.

From it, the threefold knowledge (the Vedas) came forth as it breathed forth. He pressed the threefold knowledge; from it, being pressed, its essence came forth as it breathed forth—these very syllables of invocation (*vyāhṛti*) became "bhūr," "bhuvaḥ," and "svar. He pressed these syllables of invocation; from them, being pressed, their essence came forth as it breathed forth—that which is this syllable "oṃ" came into being. He pressed that syllable; from it, being pressed, its essence came forth as it breathed forth. Thus ends the first section of the seventh chapter.

It is called *akṣara* because it does not perish (*a-kṣarati*); and because it does not decay (*na kṣīyate*), it is therefore imperishable (*akṣaya*). Indeed, this very syllable is by name "the Imperishable," which they call "the *Akṣara*" cryptically. Now, some chant this very thing as "Oṃ. One should not chant it in that way; for there is a danger that he might exclude himself from this essence. Or rather, it becomes as if there were two: "Oṃ" and "O. Some indeed chant it as "O"; but that is not properly chanted. One should not chant it in that way either; one should chant it simply as "Oṃ. Thus, he [unites] this with this essence.
Thus ends the second section in the seventh chapter;
the seventh chapter is completed.

In the beginning, this was indeed only space; and even now, it is that very same thing. That which is this space is the sun itself; for when he has risen, all this becomes manifest through space. Of him, the ocean is indeed the boundary between the mortal and the immortal: that part of the ocean which is enclosed is attained by death, while that which is beyond is the immortal. That which is this ocean is indeed this wind; for this is the ocean, and toward it all beings run together. Of it, heaven and earth...

Thus are the two banks; and just as there might be bronze vessels cast away in a river, or lakes, even so is this earthly ocean. This very sun rises from the further shore of the ocean. As it rises, it ascends upon the back of the wind; it rises from the immortal itself, it moves along the immortal, and it is established in the immortal. Its threefold form, which has not been reached by death, is white, black, and the person (puruṣa). That which is white is the form of speech, of the Ṛg-veda, and of fire—of death. That which is speech is the Ṛg-veda. And then...

That fire which is death is that [Agni]. Now, that which is black is the form of water, of food, of mind, and of the Yajus. Those waters are food; and that which is mind is the Yajus. Now, that which is the person is the vital breath (prāṇa), that is the Sāman, that is Brahman, that is the Immortal. That which is the vital breath is the Sāman; and that which is Brahman is the Immortal.
Thus ends the first section of the eighth chapter.

Now, with reference to the self (*adhyātma*), this very eye is threefold: white, black, and the person (*puruṣa*). That which is white is the form of speech (*vāk*), of the *ṛc*, of fire (*agni*), and of death (*mṛtyu*); that which is speech is the *ṛc*, and that which is fire is death. That which is black is the form of water (*āpas*), of food (*anna*), of mind (*manas*), and of the *yajus*; that which is water is food, and that which is mind is the *yajus*. And that which is the person is breath (*prāṇa*), that is the *sāman*, that is Brahman, that is the immortal; that which is breath is the *sāman*, and that which is Brahman is the immortal.

This indeed is the ascent of Brahman; now, therefore, follows the supreme ascent. That which is the ascent is lightning itself. Now, that white form which belongs to the lightning as it flashes—that is the form of speech, of the Ṛg-veda, of fire, and of death. Furthermore, that dark-blue form which belongs to the lightning as it thunders—that is the form of water, of food, of the mind, and of the Yajur-veda. That person who is in the lightning is breath; he is the Sāman; he is Brahman; he is the immortal. That which is breath is the Sāman; and that which is Brahman is the immortal.
Thus ends the second section in the eighth lesson.

He, indeed, being encompassed by immortality, dwells in the midst of death, having made food [for himself]. Now, this very person who is here in the eye and he who is in the sun are the *atipuruṣa* (the surpassing person); he who is in lightning is the *paramapuruṣa* (the supreme person). These, indeed, are the three persons; these are born for him. That person who is here in the eye is named *anurūpa* (the corresponding one), for he follows after all forms (*rūpa*). One should meditate upon him as *anurūpa*; then all forms follow after him. He who is in the sun is *pratirūpa* (the counterpart), for he faces toward [all things]. He who is in lightning is *pratirūpa*. One should meditate upon him as *pratirūpa*; then he becomes a counterpart to all beings. Thus, these two, *anurūpa* and *pratirūpa*, are born as a pair. Therefore, one should not eat with only one person, lest they be born as a single pair. One should eat with two people, so that they may be born as a pair. This is the rule regarding the persons. Now, concerning the *amṛtapuruṣas* (immortal persons): he who is in the fire is *amṛtapuruṣa*; he who is in the lightning is *amṛtapuruṣa*; he who is in the thundercloud is *amṛtapuruṣa*. These, indeed, are the *amṛtapuruṣas*. One should not eat with only one person, lest they be born as a single *amṛtapuruṣa*. One should eat with two people, so that they may be born as *amṛtapuruṣas*. This is the rule regarding the *amṛtapuruṣas*. Now, concerning the *sādhyapuruṣas* (persons to be attained): he who is in the wind is *sādhyapuruṣa*; he who is in the ether is *sādhyapuruṣa*; he who is in the quarters is *sādhyapuruṣa*. These, indeed, are the *sādhyapuruṣas*. One should not eat with only one person, lest they be born as a single *sādhyapuruṣa*. One should eat with two people, so that they may be born as *sādhyapuruṣas*. This is the rule regarding the *sādhyapuruṣas*. Now, concerning the *ṛtupuruṣas* (seasonal persons): he who is in the spring is *ṛtupuruṣa*; he who is in the summer is *ṛtupuruṣa*; he who is in the rainy season is *ṛtupuruṣa*; he who is in the autumn is *ṛtupuruṣa*; he who is in the winter is *ṛtupuruṣa*; he who is in the cool season is *ṛtupuruṣa*. These, indeed, are the *ṛtupuruṣas*. One should not eat with only one person, lest they be born as a single *ṛtupuruṣa*. One should eat with two people, so that they may be born as *ṛtupuruṣas*. This is the rule regarding the *ṛtupuruṣas*. Now, concerning the *pitṛpuruṣas* (ancestral persons): he who is in the past is *pitṛpuruṣa*; he who is in the future is *pitṛpuruṣa*; he who is in the present is *pitṛpuruṣa*. These, indeed, are the *pitṛpuruṣas*. One should not eat with only one person, lest they be born as a single *pitṛpuruṣa*. One should eat with two people, so that they may be born as *pitṛpuruṣas*. This is the rule regarding the *pitṛpuruṣas*. Now, concerning the *manuṣyapuruṣas* (human persons): he who is in speech is *manuṣyapuruṣa*; he who is in the mind is *manuṣyapuruṣa*; he who is in the breath is *manuṣyapuruṣa*. These, indeed, are the *manuṣyapuruṣas*. One should not eat with only one person, lest they be born as a single *manuṣyapuruṣa*. One should eat with two people, so that they may be born as *manuṣyapuruṣas*. This is the rule regarding the *manuṣyapuruṣas*. Now, concerning the *devapuruṣas* (divine persons): he who is in the Rigveda is *devapuruṣa*; he who is in the Yajurveda is *devapuruṣa*; he who is in the Sāmaveda is *devapuruṣa*. These, indeed, are the *devapuruṣas*. One should not eat with only one person, lest they be born as a single *devapuruṣa*. One should eat with two people, so that they may be born as *devapuruṣas*. This is the rule regarding the *devapuruṣas*. Now, concerning the *brahmapuruṣas* (Brahmanic persons): he who is in the *bhūr* world is *brahmapuruṣa*; he who is in the *bhuvas* world is *brahmapuruṣa*; he who is in the *svar* world is *brahmapuruṣa*. These, indeed, are the *brahmapuruṣas*. One should not eat with only one person, lest they be born as a single *brahmapuruṣa*. One should eat with two people, so that they may be born as *brahmapuruṣas*. This is the rule regarding the *brahmapuruṣas*. Now, concerning the *sarvapuruṣas* (all-encompassing persons): he who is in the earth is *sarvapuruṣa*; he who is in the atmosphere is *sarvapuruṣa*; he who is in the sky is *sarvapuruṣa*. These, indeed, are the *sarvapuruṣas*. One should not eat with only one person, lest they be born as a single *sarvapuruṣa*. One should eat with two people, so that they may be born as *sarvapuruṣas*. This is the rule regarding the *sarvapuruṣas*. Now, concerning the *sarvadevapuruṣas* (all-divine persons): he who is in the fire is *sarvadevapuruṣa*; he who is in the lightning is *sarvadevapuruṣa*; he who is in the thundercloud is *sarvadevapuruṣa*. These, indeed, are the *sarvadevapuruṣas*. One should not eat with only one person, lest they be born as a single *sarvadevapuruṣa*. One should eat with two people, so that they may be born as *sarvadevapuruṣas*. This is the rule regarding the *sarvadevapuruṣas*. Now, concerning the *sarvabhūtapuruṣas* (all-being persons): he who is in the breath is *sarvabhūtapuruṣa*; he who is in the mind is *sarvabhūtapuruṣa*; he who is in speech is *sarvabhūtapuruṣa*. These, indeed, are the *sarvabhūtapuruṣas*. One should not eat with only one person, lest they be born as a single *sarvabhūtapuruṣa*. One should eat with two people, so that they may be born as *sarvabhūtapuruṣas*. This is the rule regarding the *sarvabhūtapuruṣas*. Now, concerning the *sarvamanuṣyapuruṣas* (all-human persons): he who is in the Rigveda is *sarvamanuṣyapuruṣa*; he who is in the Yajurveda is *

"One should worship all forms as being 'corresponding to him' (tam-pratirūpa). All forms indeed become corresponding to him. That which is in lightning is of all forms, for all forms are in it; one should worship it as 'all-forms' (sarva-rūpa). All forms indeed come to be in him. These three persons, verily, are born for him who knows this thus, and also for him for whom one knowing this sings the Udgītha. The third section of the eighth lesson is completed; the eighth lesson is finished.

In the beginning, this was indeed space alone; even now, it is that very same thing. That which is this space is Indra; that which is Indra is he who shines yonder. He is the seven-rayed bull, the most powerful. His ray consisting of speech is established in the east. That which is speech is Agni. He becomes tenfold, hundredfold, thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, hundred-thousandfold, millionfold, ten-millionfold, hundred-millionfold, billionfold, ten-billionfold, and the end of the sky, the imperishable lotus. He is this very one.

Its ray, having become speech, is established among all these creatures. Whoever speaks here, he speaks by means of this very ray. Now, the one consisting of mind is established in the south. That which is the mind is the moon; it becomes tenfold. This very [sun], having become the ray of mind, is established among all these creatures. Whoever thinks here, he thinks by means of this very ray. Now, the one consisting of sight is established in the west.

Now, that which is the eye of the Sun—that becomes tenfold. It is this very ray of his which, having become the eye, is established in all these creatures. Whoever sees, he sees by means of this very ray of his. Then there is the one consisting of hearing, established in the north. That which is the hearing—that are the quarters; it becomes tenfold. It is this very ray of his which, having become the hearing, is established in all these creatures. Whoever hears, he hears by means of this very ray of his. [End of the first section of the ninth anuvāka.]

Now, the one consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*) is established above. That which is his breath is Vāyu; he becomes tenfold. This very [Vāyu], having become the ray of this [Ātman] as breath, is established in all these creatures. Whoever breathes, they breathe by means of the ray of this very [Ātman]. Next, the one consisting of the life-force (*asumaya*) is established crosswise. He is indeed named Īśāna; he becomes tenfold. This very [Īśāna], having become the ray of this [Ātman] as life-force, is established in all these creatures. Whoever...

And who is the one possessing life-breath? It is this very [Self] by its ray, the one possessing life-breath. Now, that which consists of food is established here below. That which is food is water; it becomes tenfold, hundredfold, thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, hundred-thousandfold, millionfold, ten-millionfold, hundred-millionfold, billionfold, ten-billionfold, and the end of space, the imperishable lotus. This very [Self], having become food as its ray, is established within all these creatures. Whosoever eats, he eats by this very ray of that [Self]. This is that.

"The bull with seven rays, the mighty one—this is declared by a Ṛgvedic verse: 'He who, the bull with seven rays, the mighty one, released the seven rivers to flow; he who, thunderbolt-armed, struck down Rauhina as he was scaling heaven—he, O people, is Indra. (7) "He who has seven rays"—for these are indeed the seven rays of the Sun. "The bull"—for he is indeed the bull of these creatures. "The mighty one"—this is his very greatness. (8) "He released the seven rivers to flow"—for these are indeed the seven rivers.

By them all this was made white; because by them all this was made white, therefore they are called *sindhavaḥ* (the rivers). "He who, with arm wielding the thunderbolt, shook Rauhiṇa"—for he indeed is the one who, with arm wielding the thunderbolt, shook Rauhiṇa. "O people, he who ascended to heaven, Indra"—for he indeed is Indra.
Thus ends the second section of the ninth lesson.

"Just as mountain paths rise up," so said Śāṭyāyani; "even so these rays of the sun go toward this sun from every side. He who knows this, taking hold with 'Om,' goes toward this sun from every side by means of these rays. This Sāman has doors on all sides and is unobstructed; yet some worship it as having doors on only one side, like a cloud-path, and thus they perceive it otherwise than it truly is. Now, he who knows it in this way—he alone knows this Sāman which has doors on all sides and is unobstructed.

This lightning is that [Sāman]. That which circles all around this orb is the Sāman; and that which shines forth intensely beyond it is the essence of meritorious action. One is released toward that [essence]. This is the Sāman free from rivals. Indeed, Indra saw no rival whatsoever. Just as Indra saw no rival whatsoever, even so does one who knows this see no rival whatsoever;
and likewise for him for whom one who knows thus sings the Udgītha.
Thus ends the third section in the ninth Anuvāka.

The ninth section is completed. In the beginning, this very world was space; it remains so even now. That which is this space is indeed Indra; that which is Indra is indeed the *Sāman*. Of this *Sāman*, this eastern quarter is the *Hiṅkāra*; this [south] is the *Prastāva*; this [west] is the *Ādi*; this [north] is the *Udgītha*; yonder [zenith] is the *Pratihāra*; the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) is the *Upadrava*; and this [earth] is the *Nidhana*. This is the sevenfold *Sāman*. He who knows this sevenfold *Sāman*—whatever exists in the eastern quarter, whatever deities, humans, and animals there are—[all belong to him].

Whatever food there is, all that he obtains by means of the *hiṅkāra*. 3. Then, whatever is in the southern direction, all that he obtains by means of the *prastāva*. 4. Then, whatever is in the western direction, all that he obtains by means of the *ādi*. 5. Then, whatever is in the northern direction, all that he obtains by means of the *udgītha*. 6. Then, whatever is in that [zenith] direction, all that he obtains by means of the *pratihāra*. 7. Then, whatever is in the intermediate space, all that he obtains by means of the *upadrava*. 8. Then, whatever is in this direction—whatever deities, whatever humans, whatever animals, and whatever food—all that [he obtains].

Through the *nidhana*, one attains everything; indeed, for him everything becomes attained, everything conquered. No desire whatsoever remains unfulfilled for him who knows this. Whatever he does in these worlds, being thus knowing, he does it as his own, from himself. This very thing is declared by a *ṛc* verse. Thus ends the first section of the tenth anuvāka.

"O Indra, even if there were a hundred heavens and a hundred earths for you, O Wielder of the Thunderbolt, a thousand suns could not equal you at your birth; nor could the two worlds encompass you. (1) "If there were a hundred heavens, O Indra, and a hundred earths"—if there were a hundred heavens and a hundred earths, this very space is greater than them. (2) "O Wielder of the Thunderbolt, a thousand suns could not equal you"—for indeed, not even a thousand suns could equal him. (3) "Nor could the two worlds encompass you at your birth"—for these two worlds do not encompass him who has been born. Indeed, these two are the worlds. (4)

This very space is greater than those two, for within it indeed these two exist. That which is this space is Indra; that which is Indra is he who shines yonder. He goes forth, emerging from the clouds. Just as he goes forth, emerging from the clouds, even so does he who knows this go forth, emerging from all evil; and also for him for whom one who knows thus sings the *udgītha*.
Thus ends the second section of the tenth chapter; the tenth chapter is complete.

The *Trivṛt* Sāman has four feet: Brahman is one third, Indra is one third, Prajāpati is one third, and food itself is the fourth foot. Now, that which is Brahman is breath; that which is Indra is speech; that which is Prajāpati is mind; and food itself is the fourth foot. Mind is indeed the *hiṅkāra*, speech is the *prastāva*, breath is the *udgītha*, and food itself is the fourth foot. One acts with speech, leads with breath, and moves with the mind; this is that which is restrained, namely the mind, by means of which—wherever...

He desires that; thus he establishes both himself and the sacrificer. Now, with respect to the deities: the moon is the *hiṅkāra*, Agni is the *prastāva*, the sun is the *udgītha*, and the waters are the fourth foot; for that [the waters] is manifest food. These very deities meet on the night of the new moon: on the night of the new moon, the moon enters the sun, and the sun enters Agni. Because they meet (*saṃyanti*), it is called *sāman*. He indeed knows the *sāman*, he is a knower of the *sāman*, who knows it thus. Of these very [deities],...

Among the deities, each single deity becomes a *sāman*. This very Sun is the *trivṛt* (*sāman*) with four feet: the rays, the disk, the person, and the rays themselves are the *hiṅkāra*; therefore, as soon as they rise, they are extended. The disk is the *prastāva*, the person is the *udgītha*, and those waters which are within it constitute the fourth foot. In the same way, the rays, the disk, the person, and the rays themselves are the *hiṅkāra*, the disk is the *prastāva*, the person is the *udgītha*, and those waters which are within it constitute that very [fourth foot].

The fourth quarter: 10. Four others and four others—those make eight. The *gāyatrī* has eight syllables; the *sāman* is the *gāyatra*; the *gāyatrī* is indeed Brahman, and he attains that Brahman. Animals have eight hooves; therefore, it pertains to cattle. 11. 33.
Thus ends the first section of the eleventh anuvāka.

Now, with reference to the self (*adhyātma*): this very eye is threefold and four-footed—white, black, and the person (*puruṣa*). The white is indeed the *hiṅkāra*, the black is the *prastāva*, and the person is the *udgītha*. Those waters which are within it constitute its fourth foot. This is the course of the sun; this is the course of the moon. These are four, and these are another four; they make eight. The *gāyatrī* consists of eight syllables, and the *sāman* is the *gāyatra*; the *gāyatrī* is indeed Brahman, and one attains Brahman thereby. Animals have eight hooves; thus it is beneficial for animals. That which blows here is he...

This very one is Prajāpati; that indeed is the Sāman. This deity who is this person within the eye—he is this one who has ascended by means of the *āhuti* and the *atimati*. Now, those two which are seen in the waters, the moon and the sun—they are the deities of these two. For when they say, "the gods of the gods," these are indeed they; these are the ones who have ascended by means of the *āhuti* and the *atimati*. Regarding this, Pṛthu Vainya questioned the divine Brāhmaṇas about those by whom the wind is impelled to blow, and who maintain the five directions facing together.

"Those gods who considered themselves superior to the oblations—who were they, the leaders of the waters? They replied: "One of them clothes this earth; one has pervaded the intermediate space; one bestows the sky, he who is the sustainer; and another guards all the quarters. "One of them clothes this earth"—that is Agni. "One has pervaded the intermediate space"—that is Vāyu. "One bestows the sky, he who is the sustainer"—that is Āditya. "And [he guards] all the quarters..."
"Others protect them. Indeed, these deities—the moon, the stars, and so forth—protect all the quarters. These very ones, being the *sāman* itself, are truly arranged for the sake of food.
Thus ends the second section of the eleventh recitation;
the eleventh recitation is complete.
