Now, concerning this *sāman*, they say: "The year itself is the *sāman*. Of that, spring is the *hiṅkāra*; therefore, in spring, animals come together, making the sound *hiṅ*. Summer is the *prastāva*; the *prastāva* is indeed undefined, and summer is undefined among the seasons. The rainy season is the *udgītha*; verily, the rain sings as it were. Autumn is the *pratihāra*; for in autumn, indeed, the greatest number of plants ripen. Winter is the *nidhana*; for in winter, living beings become as if brought to their end.

These two join together at these two ends; following this, the year is endless. Of that [year], these two are its ends, namely winter and spring. Following this, the two ends of a village meet; following this, the two ends of a gold necklace meet; following this, one lies having drawn up the coils of a snake. Just as the neck is completely encircled by a gold necklace on all sides, even so is the *sāman* endless. He who knows this endless *sāman* wins endlessness itself. Thus ends the first section of the twelfth lesson.

Now, this Sāman is in Parjanya. Its *hiṅkāra* is the east wind; that which causes the clouds to gather is the *prastāva*; that which thunders is the *udgītha*; that which flashes is the *pratihāra*; and that which rains is the *nidhana*. This is the Sāman in Parjanya. He who knows this Sāman in Parjanya becomes one for whom Parjanya rains abundantly. Now, this Sāman is in man. His *hiṅkāra* is this [breath], his *prastāva* is this [breath], his *udgītha* is this [breath], and his *pratihāra* is this [breath].

This is the *nidhana*. This *sāman* is in the person. He who knows this *sāman* in the person truly ascends and proceeds upward with offspring and cattle. And he who knows it as directed toward himself (*pratyak*) wins those worlds that are directed toward himself; for him, this [breath] is the *hiṅkāra*, this is the *prastāva*, this is the *udgītha*, this is the *pratihāra*, and this is the *nidhana*; he wins those worlds that are directed toward himself. And he who knows it as directed crosswise (*tiryak*) wins those worlds that are directed crosswise; for him, the hair is the *hiṅkāra* and the skin is the *prastāva*.

The flesh is the *udgītha*, the bone is the *pratihāra*, and the marrow is the *nidhana*. He sings three parts of it openly: the *prastāva*, the *pratihāra*, and the *nidhana*; therefore, of a person, three things are visible—the teeth and the two kinds of nails (those that grow upward and those that grow sideways). He conquers those worlds which are turned sideways. Moreover, he who knows this correctly conquers those worlds which are turned upright. His mind is the *hiṅkāra*, his speech is the *prastāva*, his breath is the *udgītha*, his sight is the *pratihāra*, and his hearing is the *nidhana*; he conquers those worlds which are turned upright.

Now, this Sāman is in the deities: Vāyu is its *hiṅkāra*, Agni is the *prastāva*, Āditya is the *udgītha*, Candramas is the *pratihāra*, and the quarters are the *nidhana*. This is the Sāman in the deities. He who thus knows this Sāman in the deities wins the same world as the deities themselves. Thus ends the second section of the twelfth anuvāka.

Of this [Sāman], there are these three *āgās*: one is addressed to Agni, one to Indra, and one to the Viśvedevas. That which is low-pitched (*mandrā*) belongs to Agni; with that, the *udgītha* of the morning pressing (*prātassavana*) should be sung. For the morning pressing belongs to Agni, and this world belongs to Agni; by means of its own sacrifice, he sings the *udgītha* of the morning pressing and prospers in this world. Now, that which is resonant (*ghoṣiṇī*) and accompanied by sound (*upabdimatī*) belongs to Indra; with that, the *udgītha* of the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*) should be sung. For the midday pressing belongs to Indra, and yonder world belongs to Indra; by means of its own sacrifice, he sings the *udgītha* of the midday pressing...

With that [part] he sings the *udgītha* of the morning pressing; he prospers in yonder world. Now, that which he sings while as it were shaking and as it were spreading—that belongs to the All-Gods (*vaiśvadevī*). With that he should sing the *udgītha* of the third pressing, for the third pressing belongs to the All-Gods, and this intermediate space belongs to the All-Gods. By means of his own sacrifice, he sings the *udgītha* of the third pressing; he prospers in this intermediate space. Moreover, they indeed say: "One should sing with only one [note], namely that which is the middle of his speech. Thus, that very speech with which he sings the *udgītha* while striving—that is his [speech].

This is the middle of speech; by means of this very speech, one attains all forms of speech. He who knows this prospers in undiminished, unified prosperity. Now, that [chant] which is like the cry of a curlew belongs to Bṛhaspati. He who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should chant with it; for Bṛhaspati is indeed Brahman, and thus he prospers in spiritual luster. In this way, he becomes possessed of spiritual luster. Now, Caikitāneya chants the *āgā* of only one *sāman*, namely the Gāyatra; that should be chanted without drawing breath.
That [part of the] Sāman up to the *pratihāra* should be sung without taking breath; for the Gāyatra is indeed breath. Thus one prospers with breath, and so one attains a full lifespan.
7.37. This is the second section in the twelfth chapter.

Now, while Brahmadatta Caikitāneya was singing the *udgītha*, the Kurus approached him, saying, "O Dālbhya, sing the *sāman*! As he was being urged on, he sang it even more intensely. They said to him, "Why, being urged on, did you sing it even more intensely? He replied, "Thinking, 'This is indeed hair (*loman*)'; that is exactly what we heard in response. Therefore, those who have spoken ill of us, their burial grounds shall become as if covered with hair; whereas we shall continue to sing upwards. Then King Jaivali [approached] Galūnasa Ārkṣākāyaṇa...

They asked him as he was rising from the *śamūla* grass: "Did you sing with the *ṛc*, Śālāvatya, or with the *sāman*? He replied, "Neither with the *ṛc*, O King, nor with the *sāman*. [The King said: "In that case, all of you will become objects of reproach, for you sang while knowing this [fact]. [Śālāvatya continued: "Had he said, 'I sang with both the *ṛc* and the *sāman*,' he would have said of him, 'He sang with what has been exhausted, with a worn-out stalk. But he said, 'I sang with the tone (*svara*) and with the *hiṅkāra*. Thus ends the third section of the twelfth chapter.

Then Satyādhivāka Caitrarathi said to Satyayajña Pauluṣi, "O Prācīnayoga, if you, knowing the Sāman, perform the office of the priest for me with the Sāman, then you shall never again have to undergo initiation. For he had been initiated many times. He said, "He who, knowing the splendor of the Sāman, performs the office of the priest with the Sāman, becomes truly splendid; the mind, indeed, is the splendor of the Sāman. "He who, knowing the foundation of the Sāman, performs the office of the priest with the Sāman, finds a firm foundation..."

"Speech indeed is the foundation of the Sāman," so it is said. He who, knowing the gold of the Sāman, performs the priestly office with the Sāman—gold indeed comes to his house. "Breath indeed is the gold of the Sāman. He who, knowing the honor of the Sāman, performs the priestly office with the Sāman—he indeed becomes honored. "The eye indeed is the honor of the Sāman. He who, knowing the fame of the Sāman, performs the priestly office with the Sāman—he indeed becomes famous. "The ear indeed is the fame of the Sāman. Thus ends the fourth section in the twelfth Anuvāka.

The twelfth section is completed: "Speech has four measured quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them. Three, hidden in the cave, do not stir; the fourth quarter of speech is what humans speak. (1) Speech itself is the *Sāman*, for with speech one sings the *Sāman*. Speech itself is the *Uktha*, for with speech one recites the *Uktha*. Speech itself is the *Yajus*, for with speech the *Yajus* follows. (2) Whatever is this side of the Brahman is all speech; but as for that which is taught elsewhere than the Brahman, one does not perform the priestly office by means of it, for it is done only through the indirect (the transcendent).
Thus ends the first section of the thirteenth chapter.

By means of this very *asu* (life-breath), the gods live, the ancestors live, humans live, animals live, the Gandharvas and Apsarases live; indeed, all this lives. Regarding this they say: "Since all this lives by means of the *asu*, what is the *asu* of the Sāman? One should say, "The breath (*prāṇa*). Verily, the breath is indeed the *asu* of the Sāman. This same breath is established in speech, and speech is established in the breath. These two are thus established in one another. He who knows this becomes firmly established.

This very thing is declared by the Ṛgvedic verse: "Aditi is heaven, Aditi is the intermediate space; Aditi is the mother, she is the father, she is the son; all the gods are Aditi, the five peoples are Aditi, Aditi is what is born, Aditi is what is to be born. (4) "Aditi is heaven, Aditi is the intermediate space"—she indeed is heaven, she is the intermediate space. (5) "Aditi is the mother, she is the father, she is the son"—she indeed is the mother, she is the father, she is the son. (6) "All the gods are Aditi, the five peoples are Aditi"—those gods who were formerly the five peoples among the Asuras, they are indeed here in that Āditya. (7)

"The person who is in the moon, who is in lightning, who is in the waters, and this one who is here within the eye—this indeed is that; this very one is Aditi, the born and the birth. For she indeed is the born, and she is the birth.
Thus ends the second section of the thirteenth anuvāka;
the thirteenth anuvāka is complete.

Āruṇi Vāsiṣṭha once approached Caikitāneya for the sake of studentship. He said to him, "Do you know, gentle Gautama, that deity which we, the Caikitāneyas, worship as Sāman? Which deity do you worship? He replied, "The venerable ones, it is Sāman itself. He questioned him further: "Do you know what is in the fire? "I know it," he replied. "That which we worship as Sāman is indeed its light. "Do you know what is in the earth? "I know it," he replied. "That which we worship as Sāman is indeed its foundation."

"Do we worship it as *sāman*? "Do you know that which is in the waters? "This is indeed the peace (*śānti*) of that *sāman*, namely, 'we worship it as *sāman*. "Do you know that which is in the intermediate space? "This is indeed the self (*ātman*) of that *sāman*, namely, 'we worship it as *sāman*. "Do you know that which is in the wind? "This is indeed the prosperity (*śrī*) of that *sāman*, namely, 'we worship it as *sāman*. "Do you know that which is in the quarters? "This is indeed the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of that *sāman*, namely, 'we worship it as *sāman*. "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Do you know that which is in the sky? "Yes, I know it. "What is it? "It is the truth (*satya*). "Do you know that which is beyond the truth? "Yes, I know it. "What is it? "It is the immortal (*amṛta*). "Do you know that which is beyond the immortal? "Yes, I know it. "What is it? "It is the light (*jyotis*). "Do you know that which is beyond the light? "Yes, I know it. "What is it? "It is the unmanifest (*avyakta*). "Do you know that which is beyond the unmanifest? "Yes, I know it. "What is it? "It is the fearless (*abhayam*). "Do you know that which is beyond the fearless? "No, I do not know it. "Verily, O Śākalya, you have come to the end; your heart will burst. Since you did not know that which is beyond the fearless, your head would have fallen off [if you had known]. "O Yājñavalkya, whatever reward is given to the knower of Brahman, that shall be mine. "What is that reward? "Whatever is in the world of the Kurus, including myself. "Let it be yours, O Śākalya, though you have bartered away the knowledge of Brahman. Then the seers said: "O Yājñavalkya, pray tell us, what is the extent of this Brahman? "The ether (*ākāśa*), for it is the manifestor of all forms and names; within it, all these become one. That is the Brahman, that is the immortal, that is the fearless. When one knows thus, one does not fear anything at all. Then they offered him gold, cows, and garments. He said: "These are already with me; rather, let me choose a boon from you. "Choose," they said. "Let no member of my lineage henceforth be ignorant of the *Sāman*. "So be it," they said. 1–7. 8. Then he asked them: "When people here say, 'He knows the Sāman,' what is that Sāman? "The voice, for by means of the voice one sings the *Sāman*. "Is it only that? "Yes, it is only that. "If it were only that, then a mute person would be unable to sing the *Sāman*. "Then what is it? "That which is in the waters, do you know that? "Yes, I know it. "What is it? "It is the peacefulness (*śānti*); for it is the peacefulness of that *Sāman* when we say, 'We worship it as *sāman*. "And that which is in the intermediate space, do you know that? "Yes, I know it. "What is it? "It is the self (*ātman*); for it is the self of that *sāman* when we say, 'We worship it as *sāman*. "And that which is in the wind, do you know that? "Yes, I know it. "What is it? "It is prosperity (*śrī*); for it is the prosperity of that *sāman* when we say, 'We worship it as *sāman*. "And that which is in the quarters, do you know that? "Yes, I know it. "What is it? "It is pervasion (*vyāpti*); for it is the pervasion of that *sāman* when we say, 'We worship it as *sāman*. "And that which is in the sky, do you know that? "Yes, I know it. "What is it? "It is the truth (*satya*); for it is the truth of that *sāman* when we say, 'We worship it as *sāman*. "And that which is beyond the sky, do you know that? "Yes, I know it. "What is it? "It is the immortal (*amṛta*); for it is the immortal of that *sāman* when we say, 'We worship it as *sāman*. "And that which is beyond the immortal, do you know that? "Yes, I know it. "What is it? "It is the light (*jyotis*); for it is the light of that *sāman* when we say, 'We worship it as *sāman*. "And that which is beyond the light, do you know that? "Yes, I know it. "What is it? "It is the unmanifest (*avyakta*); for it is the unmanifest of that *sāman* when we say, 'We worship it as *sāman*. "And that which is beyond the unmanifest, do you know that? "Yes, I know it. "What is it? "It is the fearless (*abhayam*); for it is the fearless of that *sāman* when we say, 'We worship it as *sāman*. "And that which is beyond the fearless, do you know that? "No, I do not know it. "Verily, O Śākalya, you have come to the end; your heart will burst. Since you did not know that which is beyond the fearless, your head would have fallen off [if you had known]. "O Yājñavalkya, whatever reward is given to the knower of Brahman, that shall be mine. "What is that reward? "Whatever is in the world of the Kurus, including myself. "Let it be yours, O Śākalya, though you have bartered away the knowledge of Brahman. 9. Then they said: "O Yājñavalkya, pray tell us, what is the extent of this Brahman? "The ether (*ākāśa*), for it is the manifestor of all forms and names; within it, all these become one. That is the Brahman, that is the immortal, that is the fearless. When one knows thus, one does not fear anything at all. 10. Then they offered him gold, cows, and garments. He said: "These are already with me; rather, let me choose a boon from you. "Choose," they said. "Let no member of my lineage henceforth be ignorant of the *Sāman*. "So be it," they said. 11. Then he asked them: "When people here say, 'He knows the Sāman,' what is that Sāman? "The voice, for by means of the voice one sings the *Sāman*. "Is it only that? "Yes, it is only that. "If it were only that, then a mute person would be unable to sing the *Sāman*. "Then what is it? "That which is in the waters, do you know that? "Yes, I know it. "What is it? "It is the peacefulness (*śānti*); for it is the peacefulness of that *sāman* when we say, 'We worship it as *sāman*. "And that which is in the intermediate space, do you know that? "Yes, I know it. "What is it? "It is the self (*ātman*); for it is the self of that *sāman* when we say, 'We worship it as *sāman*. "And that which is in the wind, do you know that? "Yes, I know it. "What is it? "It is prosperity (*śrī*); for it is the prosperity of that *sāman* when we say, 'We worship it as *sāman*. "And that which is in the quarters, do you know that? "Yes, I know it. "What is it? "It is pervasion (*vyāpti*); for it is the pervasion of that *sāman* when we say, 'We worship it as *sāman*. "And that which is in the sky, do you know that? "Yes, I know it. "What is it? "It is the truth (*satya*); for it is the truth of that *sāman* when we say, 'We worship it as *sāman*. "And that which is beyond the sky, do you
"This Sāman which we meditate upon is indeed his manifestation (vibhūti).
Thus ends the first section of the fourteenth anuvāka.

"Do you know that which is in the sun? "I do. "It is indeed the splendor (*tejas*) of that *sāman* which we meditate upon as the *sāman*. "Do you know that which is in the moon? "I do. "It is indeed the radiance (*bhās*) of that *sāman* which we meditate upon as the *sāman*. "Do you know that which is in the stars? "I do. "It is indeed wisdom (*prajñā*) of that *sāman* which we meditate upon as the *sāman*. "Do you know that which is in food? "I do. "It is indeed semen (*retas*) of that *sāman* which we meditate upon as the *sāman*. "Do you know that which is in cattle? "I do. "It is indeed glory (*yaśas*)."

"That which we meditate upon as the *sāman*—do you know what that *sāman* of his is? "In the Ṛg-veda? Do you know it? "This is the *stoma*; that which we meditate upon as the *sāman*—do you know what that *sāman* of his is? "In the Yajus? Do you know it? "This is the ritual action (*karman*); that which we meditate upon as the *sāman*—do you know what that *sāman* of his is? "Then upon what do you meditate? "Upon the syllable (*akṣara*). "Which is that syllable? "That which, though perishing, does not perish. "Which is that which, though perishing, does not perish? "Indra. "Which is this Indra? "He who delights in the imperishable (*akṣan*)."

"Of whom is it that one says, 'He delights in the eye'? "This is the deity," he said. "This person who is in the eye—this is Indra, this is Prajāpati. He is equal to the earth, equal to space, equal to heaven, equal to all beings. He shines beyond the sky; he alone is to be meditated upon as 'all this. He who knows this thus becomes radiant, possessed of a firm foundation, peaceful, self-possessed, glorious, pervasive, powerful, brilliant, full of being, wise, endowed with seed, and renowned."
It becomes possessed of praise, possessed of action, possessed of syllables, possessed of the senses, and possessed of the Sāman. This very thing is declared by a Ṛgvedic verse.
Thus ends the second section in the fourteenth Anuvāka.

"He has become the counterpart of every form; that is his form for the sake of being seen. Indra moves in many forms through his powers of illusion (*māyā*); for his bay horses, a hundred and ten, are yoked. 1. "He has become the counterpart of every form": for he has indeed become the counterpart of every form. 2. "That is his form for the sake of being seen": for this form of his is indeed for the purpose of being beheld. 3. "Indra moves in many forms through his powers of illusion": for by means of his powers of illusion, he indeed moves in these many forms. 4. "For his bay horses, a hundred and ten, are yoked."

"Ten"—these are indeed the thousand rays of the sun; they are yoked to him, and by them he carries all this. Because he carries all this by means of them, therefore they are called *harayaḥ*. "Maghavan assumes form after form, performing his own wondrous powers (*māyāḥ*) around his body, when thrice from heaven he has come in a moment according to his own mantras, drinking out of season, yet true to the cosmic order (*ṛta*). "Maghavan assumes form after form," for Maghavan indeed assumes form after form. "Performing his own wondrous powers around his body."

"For by means of illusions he thus conceals his own body. (8) "When he has come from heaven thrice in a moment"—for indeed, during this very moment, he goes three times around this earth on all sides, surveying these creatures. (9) "By his own mantras, drinking not at the seasons, yet true to the season"—for he indeed drinks not at the seasons, yet he is true to the season. (10) 44 Thus ends the third section in the fourteenth anuvāka.

Then Pṛthu Vainya questioned the divine Vrātyas: "The learned ones speak of many things—of Indra, the hymn (uktha), the verse (ṛc), the high chant (udgītha), sacred knowledge (brahman), the Sāman, the vital breath (prāṇa), the diffused breath (vyāna), the mind (manas), speech (vāk), the eye, the downward breath (apāna), and the ear. They replied: "O Vainya, these are the seers, the makers of mantras, born of old and being born again for the protection of the Vedas. Being wise, they speak of that which is the same person entered in many ways. Indeed, it is this very deity within the threefold knowledge (trayī-vidyā) that they refer to.

Some attain the same name, yet they do not all attain the same goal. Indeed, he who knows this thus truly knows that deity. This very Indra is the Udgītha. When this Indra, as the Udgītha, arrives, nothing more is perceived of the Udgātṛ or the Upagātṛs; from here alone he rises upward as the *svar* (the tone), and he flickers above the head. He should know: "Indra has arrived; no sinful blemish whatsoever shall remain here. Indeed, in him no sinful blemish whatsoever remains.

This is the *abhrātṛvya* (rival-free) Sāman. Indeed, Indra saw no rival whatsoever; and just as Indra saw no rival whatsoever, even so he who knows this, or for whom one knowing thus sings the *udgītha*, sees no rival whatsoever.
Thus ends the fourth section of the fourteenth Anuvāka;
the fourteenth Anuvāka is completed.

In the beginning, Prajāpati alone was this universe. He desired: "May I be many; may I procreate; may I attain abundance. He divided himself into sixteen parts: the auspicious (*bhadra*) and completion (*samāpti*), non-existence (*abhūti*) and existence (*sambhūti*), what has been (*bhūta*) and the whole (*sarva*), form (*rūpa*) and the immeasurable (*aparimita*), fortune (*śrī*) and glory (*yaśas*), name (*nāman*) and the foremost (*agra*), kinsmen (*sajātāḥ*) and milk (*payaḥ*), greatness (*mahīyā*) and sap (*rasa*). Now, that which is the auspicious is his heart; from it he created the year, and the year attends upon him.

Completion is his action; for by means of that action he completes [the year], and from it he created the seasons. Therefore, the seasons attend upon him. 4. Food is his manifestation; that becomes fourfold. From it he created the months, the half-months, the days and nights, and the dawns. Therefore, the months, the half-months, the days and nights, and the dawns attend upon him. 5. Semen is his generation; for from semen one is born. 6. 46. First section of the fifteenth anuvāka.

Then he created the moon; that moon attends upon him, therefore it is the counterpart of his semen. 1. His breath became the wind; that wind attends upon him. 2. His downward breath became all [beings]; those beings attend upon him. 3. His diffused breath became form; those creatures attend upon him, and therefore forms are perceived among these creatures. 4.

His mind was immeasurable; from that he created the quarters. Therefore the quarters attend upon him; therefore they are immeasurable, for the mind is, as it were, immeasurable. 5. His prosperity was speech; from that he created the ocean. Therefore the ocean attends upon him. 6. His glory was austerity; from that he created fire. Therefore fire attends upon him; therefore it is produced as if from friction, as if from heat. 7. His name was sight. 8. Thus ends the second section in the fifteenth lesson.

Then he created the sun; that sun attends upon him from behind as his head. Then he created the sky; that sky attends upon him from behind as his back. His limbs are his kinsmen, for he is born together with his limbs. Then he created the trees; those trees attend upon him from behind. His hair is milk; therefore, the plants attend upon him from behind. His flesh is the earth; for he grows great together with the flesh. Then...

He created birds; therefore, birds attend upon him. For that reason, they are prone to fly away, just as the great pieces of flesh are prone to fly away. The marrow was his essence; from that he created the earth, and the earth attends upon him. Having thus divided himself into sixteen parts, he united with her. Because he united with her (*samait*), that is the essence of the *Sāman*. This very one arose as the golden person, the progenitor of creatures. Thus ends the third section of the fifteenth chapter.

The gods and the Asuras contended with one another. Those gods went to Prajāpati, saying, "Let us overcome the Asuras. He said, "Indeed, neither you nor the Asuras know me. If you were to know me, then you alone would prevail and the Asuras would be defeated. They said, "Tell us that! He said, "Prajāpati is the Puruṣa; worship me as Sāman. Then indeed you shall prevail and the Asuras shall be defeated. They worshipped him as the Puruṣa, Prajāpati, as Sāman. Thereupon the gods prevailed and the Asuras were defeated. Whoever, knowing this thus, worships Prajāpati as the Puruṣa...
"He who worships [the breath] as 'Tissāmā' prospers in himself; his hateful rival is defeated.
Thus ends the fourth section in the fifteenth anuvāka;
the fifteenth anuvāka is completed.

The gods, having conquered, said: "Let us make a second [partner]; let us not be without a second. They said: "Let us make the *sāman* itself our second; let the *sāman* be our second. 1. They said to these two, Heaven and Earth: "Come together and generate this *sāman*. 2. That [Heaven] loathed her (Earth). He said: "Indeed, much of all kinds they do upon her—they stand upon her, move about upon her, and sit upon her. Purify her, for she is indeed impure! 3. They said to the *gāthā*: "By you..."

They said to *Punatī*, "What would come of it if we purified [the Soma] with you? "A hundredfold [reward] would come," she replied. "So be it. They purified [the Soma] with her; therefore, one presses [Soma] a hundredfold by means of *Punatī*. They said to *Kumbī*, "What would come of it if we purified [the Soma] with you? "A hundredfold [reward] would come," she replied. "So be it. They purified [the Soma] with her; therefore, one presses [Soma] a hundredfold by means of *Kumbī*. They said to *Nārāśaṃsī*, "What would come of it if we purified [the Soma] with you? "A hundredfold [reward] would come," she replied. "So be it. They purified [the Soma] with her; therefore, one presses [Soma] a hundredfold by means of *Nārāśaṃsī*.

They said to Raibhī, "With you we shall purify ourselves. He asked, "What will come of that? She replied, "A hundredfold [offering] shall be yours. "So be it," he said. They purified themselves with Raibhī; therefore, one also presses a hundred [vessels] with Raibhī. This [Soma], once purified, then said to Amu, "A man indeed wanders about doing this and that; do you purify yourself after me. Thus ends the first section of the sixteenth Anuvāka.

He purified it by means of the *ailaba* [chant]. Truly, for one who knows this, his *sāmans* become purified, his *ṛcs* become purified, his *yajūṃṣi* become purified; his recitation becomes purified, and everything becomes purified. 1. They came together and produced the *sāman*. Because they came together and produced the *sāman*, that is the essence of the name *sāman*. 2. This *sāman*, once created, rose up and stood quivering. All the gods were desirous of possessing it, saying, "It is mine! It is mine! 3. They said, "Let us divide it. But in its division, there was no...

As they were thus dividing [the Sāman], Prajāpati said: "Go away! This is mine; I myself shall distribute it among you. He said to Agni: "You indeed are the eldest of my sons; you choose first. He replied: "I choose the *mandra* (low-pitched) tone of the Sāman as food-eating. Whoever should sing this, he shall surely become an eater of food. But whoever should speak ill of one who, knowing this, sings this, he shall reach the gods on my behalf. Then he said to Indra: "You choose after me. He replied: "I choose the *ugra* (fierce) tone of the Sāman."

"Fortune," he said. "Whoever should sing this, he shall indeed become fortunate; may he not reach me, nor may he reach the gods—anyone who would speak ill of one who, knowing this, sings this. Then he said to Soma, "Choose for yourself. He replied, "I choose that which is beautiful from the Sāman; [I choose] what is dear. "Whoever should sing this, he shall indeed be dear to fame, dear to sight, and dear to all; may he not reach me, nor may he reach the gods—anyone who would speak ill of one who, knowing this, sings this. Then he said to Bṛhaspati, "Choose for yourself."

He said to the Krauñca [bird], "I choose the *sāman* of the Krauñca; may I possess spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). He who sings this shall indeed possess spiritual luster. "May he not reach me; may he who, knowing this, speaks ill of one singing this, fall among the gods. Thus ends the second section of the sixteenth chapter.

Then he said to the All-Gods (Viśvedevas), "Do you choose [a portion] after me? They replied, "We choose the Vaiśvadeva from the Sāman; it is procreative. He thought, "Whoever should sing this, he shall indeed be possessed of progeny; may he reach us gods who would speak ill of one who, knowing thus, sings this. Then he said to the cattle, "Do you choose [a portion] after me? They replied, "Vāyu rules over us; he alone shall choose for us. Then Vāyu and the cattle said, "We choose the Nirukta from the Sāman; it is conducive to cattle. He...

"He who sings this shall indeed possess cattle; he shall reach both me and Vāyu among the gods—he who, knowing thus, should speak ill of one who sings this. Then Prajāpati said, "I will choose after you. He replied, "I choose the undefined (anirukta) Sāman, which leads to heaven. "He who sings this shall indeed dwell in the heavenly world; he shall reach both me and the gods—he who, knowing thus, should speak ill of one who sings this. Then he said to Varuṇa, "You choose after us. He replied, "That which you two do not [choose]..."

"Someone might say, 'I shall avoid that which is covered,' and why would one choose the *sāman* as 'darkness' and 'unfit for cattle'? He who should sing this [verse] would indeed become devoid of cattle; he would come upon me and he would come upon the gods who should sing this. Now, these are the eight [verses] of the *sāman*, both sung and unsung. These, however, are the seven sung ones; and this very *āgā* of Varuṇa is the one unsung. Whatever one of these seven *āgās* a man knowing thus sings, it becomes for him truly sung; he attains those desires which are contained in them. However, he should not sing this very *āgā* of Varuṇa. 8–10. 52.
Thus ends the third section in the sixteenth chapter;
the sixteenth chapter is completed.

In the beginning, this universe was indeed a duality: Being (*sat*) and Non-being (*asat*). Of these two, that which was Being was the *Sāman*, the mind, and the out-breath (*prāṇa*); and that which was Non-being was the *Ṛc*, speech, and the down-breath (*apāna*). Now, as for the mind and the out-breath, they are the same; and as for speech and the down-breath, they are the same. This abode is the mind and the out-breath, and this abode is speech and the down-breath; therefore, a man lies on the right side of a woman. This *Ṛc* desired union with this *Sāman*. He asked her, "Who are you? She replied, "I am 'She' (*aham*). Or rather—

"I am 'I' (aham) and she is 'mine' (ama)," he said. That which was "she" (sā) and "mine" (ama) became the *sāman*; that is the essence of the *sāman*. "Let us two come together," she said. "No," he replied, "you are indeed my sister; seek a mate elsewhere. She said, "Indeed, I find no one with whom I may unite; I would unite only with you. "Then purify yourself," he said, "for you are unpurified. She purified herself by means of that which the inspired poets (*vipras*) speak. She said, "What will become of this? "Ponder upon it," he replied; for this is the power of meditation (*dhī*).

"Shall this become the life-force (*jīvana*) of creatures? "Yes," he replied, and so he drew it back. Therefore, this *dhī* is indeed the life-force of creatures. He said, "Purify it! She purified it with a *gāthā*; she purified it with a *kumbyā*; she purified it with a *nārāśaṃsī*; she purified it with ancient history (*purāṇaitihāsa*); she purified it with that which they do not sing after taking up [the lute]. She said, "What will this become? "Draw it back," he replied. "This is indeed *dhī*; shall this become the life-force of creatures? "Yes," he replied.
He turned it back; therefore, this intellect (*dhī*) is indeed the life-force of creatures. "Purify [it]! he said.
Thus ends the first section of the seventeenth anuvāka.

She purified him with honey; therefore, a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) should not eat honey, for it is the dross of the Veda. However, he may eat at his pleasure what is given by his teacher. Then the *Ṛk* and the *Sāman* said: "A man indeed wanders about doing all sorts of things; you must purify him. He purified him with the *bharaṇḍakeṣṇa* [chant]. Truly, for one who knows this, his *Sāmans* become purified, his *Ṛks* become purified, his *Yajus* become purified, his recited formula (*anūkta*) becomes purified, and everything becomes purified. They enclosed the *sadas* hall for those two as a couple; therefore, on the day of the fast (*upavasathīyā*), they enclose it.

One should not sleep in the assembly hall during that night; for on this very night of the fast-day (*upavasathīyā*), the *Ṛc* and the *Sāman* come together in the assembly hall. Just as one who watches over a superior is liable to be defeated if he fails to perceive him, so it is here. Furthermore, they say that the two come together in the mouth of the *Udgātṛ*; therefore, one should not look at the face of the *Udgātṛ*. However, they also say that one may indeed look at the face of the *Udgātṛ*, but on this very night of the fast-day, one should not sleep in the assembly hall; for it is on this very night of the fast-day that the *Ṛc* and the *Sāman* [come together].

"Let us unite in the assembly," he said. As he was about to unite with her, he spoke: "I am 'Ama', you are 'Sā'. You are 'Sā', I am 'Ama'. Having become devoted to me, let us produce offspring; come, let us unite. As he united with her, he surpassed her. He said, "Indeed, I do not equal you. Having become the Virāj, let us produce offspring. "So be it," she replied. Having become the Virāj, the two of them produced offspring: the *hiṅkāra* and the *āhāva*, the *prastāva* and the first [verse], the *udgītha* and the middle [verse], and the *pratihāra* and the highest [verse].

And the *nidhana* and the *vaṣaṭkāra*, having thus become the *virāj*, brought forth; they brought forth yonder one who shines there; they split it asunder. (8.54) Thus ends the second section in the seventeenth anuvāka.

"Sweetness has come forth! Sweetness has come forth!"—therefore they say, "He is the Son of Sweetness. For this reason, women do not eat honey, saying, "We are observing this vow for our sons. Then this triplet of verses took its place: this earth is the Gāyatrī, the intermediate space is the Triṣṭubh, and yonder sky is the Jagatī; such is that triplet. He shone above it, placed upon the Sāman; he was, as it were, unstable, as it were trembling, and he did not shine upward. He said to the gods, "Sing out for me!"—"What would be therefrom? they asked.

"May I bestow prosperity upon you; may it make me firm here," he said. "So be it. As they sang for him from the north, they made him firm there, and he bestowed prosperity upon them. This is the prosperity of the gods. Then that [sun] burns upwards; it does not burn downwards. He said to the seers, "Sing after me! "What would be the result of that? "I would bestow prosperity upon you; may it make me firm here. "So be it. As they sang after him, they made him firm there, and he bestowed prosperity upon them. This is the prosperity of the seers. Then...

It burns downwards from here; it does not burn crosswise. He said to the Gandharvas and Apsarases, "Sing for me. They asked, "What would come of that? [He replied,] "I shall bestow prosperity upon you; let me be established here. They said, "So be it. As they sang for him, he established himself there and bestowed prosperity upon them. This is the prosperity of the Gandharvas and Apsarases. Therefore, it burns crosswise from there. These, indeed, are the three modes of singing of the Sāman: the *udgīta* (the sung), the *anugīta* (the sung after), and the *āgīta* (the sung unto). Just as we here sing, so do we sing the *udgīta*; now...
"That which is sung as it was [originally] is the *anugīta*; and whatever else there is, that is the *āgīta* of the Sāman; for these indeed are the three [parts] of the Sāman.
Thus ends the third section in the seventeenth Anuvāka;
the seventeenth Anuvāka is complete.

In the beginning, this world was indeed a great expanse of water. One wave leaped upon another, and from that, two golden bellies came into being; they became the *Ṛk* and the *Sāman*. This *Ṛk* floated toward this *Sāman*. It asked her, "Who are you? She replied, "I am 'She' (*sā*). Then he said, "I am 'He' (*amaḥ*). Because she is *sā* and he is *ama*, that is the essence of the name *Sāman*. "Let us two come together," he said. "No," she replied, "you are my sister. Seek a mate elsewhere. She floated away.

Desiring a mate, she floated about for seventy thousand years. Regarding this, there is this verse: "In the beginning, she indeed moved about as a woman, desiring a husband in the waters; after seventy thousand years, she was born as Paśyata. Now, that Paśyata is yonder sun; it was he who was born then, for by means of him one sees. She, having floated down, spoke: "I do not find anyone with whom I may unite; let me unite only with you. She, indeed...

"Choose a second," he said. "No, indeed, you shall not lift me up today," she replied; having obtained a second, she sank down. "Choose a third," he said. "No, indeed, you two shall not lift me up," she replied; having obtained a third, she sank down. He said, "In this very place, indeed, you shall lift me up. Because he first spoke with one [verse], therefore the *sāman* belongs to a single *ṛc*. And because he set aside two, therefore they do not perform it for two verses. And because he brought them together with three, therefore the *sāman* belongs to a triplet (*tṛca*). He said to them, "Purify yourselves; you are certainly not purified. (5.6)

Thus, in the eighteenth section, the first division: That Gāyatrī purified herself with the Gāthā; the Triṣṭubh with the Nārāśaṃsī; the Jagatī with the Raibhī. "She cast off her filth," they say; therefore these thoughts are called *bhīmalā*. Indeed, these thoughts have cast off their filth; therefore they are called *bhīmalā*. Therefore, one should not eat from those who sing, for they live by means of filth. Then the Ṛc and the Sāman said: "A man indeed wanders about doing all manner of things; you must purify him. He purified him with the *ūrdhvagaṇa* hymn. Truly, his Sāmans are purified and his Ṛcs are purified.

The sacrificial formulas (*yajūṃṣi*) become purified, the recited verses (*anūktam*) become purified, and everything becomes purified for one who knows this. 3. For the sake of union, they two caused the quarters to revolve around them; as they were about to come together, they called out to each other: "I am he! You are she! and "You are she! I am he! 4. Thus, by means of speech, he surpassed her on both sides—with the *hiṅkāra* in front, with the *stobha* in the middle, and with the *nidhana* at the end. One who knows this surpasses three women of Brahmin descent who are his equals. 5. Of those two, as they were coming together, that which was the upward vital force flowed forth; these are your breaths.

Thus ends the second section of the eighteenth chapter. Now, as for what they say: "Who has sung forth?"—they are indeed asking, "Who has sung this Āditya? For they sing of him with the threefold knowledge (the Vedas), just as lute-players might cause a song to be sung. This mind is a lake filled with desires; speech is its stream. Just as they lead water from a lake to a higher level by means of a stream, even so the Udgātṛ priest, from the mind through speech, bestows the desires of the sacrificer upon him. He who [approaches] the Udgātṛ...

She propitiates him with sacrificial gifts; she follows after him who does not propitiate her, and he, in turn, repels her. Now, therefore, there is both giving and receiving. That which is given is indeed smoke; it is to be given to the sacrificer by means of speech, but to oneself by means of the mind. Thus, one does not give away everything. Now, that seed which was emitted from this union lay there, quivering like unrefined gold. All the gods were desirous of possessing it, each thinking, "It is mine! It is mine!"

They said, "Let us fashion this. They said, "This is indeed better than ourselves; let us fashion it by means of our very selves. 8. So they fashioned it by means of their very selves. Of them, Vāyu was the *hiṅkāra*, Agni the *prastāva*, Indra the *ādi*, Soma and Bṛhaspati the *udgītha*, the Aśvins the *pratihāra*, the Viśve Devas the *upadrava*, and Prajāpati himself was the *nidhana*. 9. These, indeed, are all the deities. This [gold] is fashioned from all these deities for one who knows thus, and for these [deities]...
He who reviles one who knows thus is cut off from all the deities.
10.58 Thus ends the third section in the eighteenth anuvāka.

Now, Brahmadatta Caikitāneya went to Abhipratārin Kākṣaseni. He requested from him the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*). Then, having entered his presence, Śaunaka, his domestic priest, sat down nearby. Without addressing him, he drank the honey-mixture. He said to him: "Knowing what, O Dālbhya, do you drink the honey-mixture without addressing us? He replied: "I have entered into the essence of the Sāma. He then questioned him right there: "Do you know that which is in the wind?"—"The *hiṅkāra* is its [the Sāma's]..."

“That,” he said, “is its *prastāva*. ‘Do you know that which is in Agni?’—‘That,’ he said, ‘is its *prastāva*. ‘That which is in Indra?’—‘That,’ he said, ‘is its *ādi*. ‘That which is in Soma and Bṛhaspati?’—‘That,’ he said, ‘is its *udgītha*. ‘That which is in the Aśvins?’—‘That,’ he said, ‘is its *pratihāra*. ‘That which is in the Viśvedevas?’—‘That,’ he said, ‘is its *upadrava*. ‘That which is in Prajāpati?’—‘That,’ he said, ‘is its *nidhana*. And this, he said, is its lineage (*ārṣeya*).”

"Or rather, this [Sāman] is its kinship," he said. He replied, "Homage be to you, O Blessed One; you who know, accept my *madhuparka*. Then the other asked, "To which deity does the *sāma* belong when one enters it with the *vairāja* chant? To whichever deities they praise while chanting, so he replied, "it belongs to those deities. This was indeed answered correctly. "This is its pervasion," he said. "Speak further! [The other] said, "We have already paid you homage. "Do not question me too much," he said. He replied, "I should indeed not have questioned you."

"Truly, you have not asked about the deity of the deity; the deities [are as follows]: the *sāman* has speech as its deity; of speech, the mind is the deity; of the mind, cattle are the deity; of cattle, plants are the deity; of plants, water is the deity. Thus, this *sāman* is born from water and is established in water.
(14.59) Thus ends the fourth section of the eighteenth chapter.

The gods and the Asuras contended. Those gods sang out with their mind; the Asuras, having rushed upon them, mingled them with evil. Therefore, whatever much one meditates upon with the mind, one meditates upon both the auspicious and the inauspicious by means of it. Then they sang out with speech; they did exactly the same thing. Therefore, whatever much one speaks with speech, one speaks both the true and the false by means of it. Then they sang out with the eye; they did exactly the same thing. Therefore, whatever much one sees with the eye, one sees both the beautiful and the ugly.

With this [eye] they sang the udgītha; it saw both what is visible and what is invisible. They did exactly as they had done before. Therefore, with this ear one hears much—both what is worth hearing and what is not worth hearing. With this breath (apāna) they sang the udgītha; they did exactly as they had done before. Therefore, with this breath one smells much—both what is fragrant and what is foul-smelling. With this vital breath (prāṇa) they sang the udgītha. Then the Asuras rushed forward, thinking, "We shall do likewise. He...

Just as a clod of earth would shatter upon striking a solid stone, even so did the Asuras perish. This vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed that solid stone. Just as a clod of earth shatters upon striking a solid stone, even so does he perish who speaks ill of one who knows this.
Thus ends the fifth section of the eighteenth anuvāka;
the eighteenth anuvāka is complete.

Thus ends the first chapter. Now begins the second chapter. The gods indeed had six Udgātṛ priests: Speech, Mind, Eye, Ear, Exhalation, and Inhalation. They resolved: "Let us consecrate ourselves with that Udgātṛ by which, having struck down death and having struck down evil, we may go to the heavenly world. They said, "Let us consecrate ourselves with Speech as the Udgātṛ. So they consecrated themselves with Speech as the Udgātṛ. Whatever one speaks with speech, that he sang for himself; but whatever other desires there were, those he sang for the gods. Evil was cast upon him. Whatever evil one speaks with speech, that [evil] was cast upon him.

That indeed was that evil. They said, "Verily, this one has not carried us beyond death nor beyond evil; let us consecrate ourselves with the mind as the Udgātṛ. They consecrated themselves with the mind as the Udgātṛ. Whatever he meditates upon with the mind, that he sings out for himself; but whatever other desires there are, those he wins for the gods. That evil was emitted after him; whatever evil he meditates upon with the mind, that indeed is that evil. They said, "Verily, this one has not yet carried us beyond death nor beyond evil; let us consecrate ourselves with the eye as the Udgātṛ."

8. They consecrated themselves with the eye as the Udgātṛ. Whatever one sees with the eye, that he sang as his own portion; but whatever other desires there were, those he sang for the gods. 9. Evil was created after that. Whatever evil one sees with the eye, that is that very evil. 10. They said, "Surely this one has not carried us beyond death nor beyond evil by means of the eye as the Udgātṛ. Let us consecrate ourselves with the ear as the Udgātṛ. 11. They consecrated themselves with the ear as the Udgātṛ. Whatever one hears with the ear, that he sang as his own portion; but whatever [other desires there were], those...

The desires [went] to the gods. Evil was emitted after them; whatever evil he hears with the ear, that is that very evil. They said, "Surely this one has not carried us beyond death nor beyond evil. Let us consecrate ourselves with out-breath as the Udgātṛ. They consecrated themselves with out-breath as the Udgātṛ. Whatever he breathes out with the out-breath, that he sang for himself. Then those other desires [went] to the gods. Evil was emitted after them; whatever evil odor he breathes out with the out-breath, that is that very evil.

They said, "Verily, this one has not carried us beyond death nor beyond evil by means of the breath as the Udgātṛ; let us consecrate ourselves with the breath as the Udgātṛ. 17. They consecrated themselves with the breath as the Udgātṛ. Whatever he breathes out by means of that breath, he sang that for himself; and whatever other desires there were, those he sang for the gods. 18. Evil was not created after him, for with this breath one does not speak evil, nor does one think evil, nor see evil, nor hear evil, nor breathe in an evil odor. 19. By means of that, having struck down death, having struck down evil—
Having struck down evil and indeed having struck down death, he who knows this goes to the heavenly world, which is free from evil. 20.1 Thus ends the first section in the first chapter.

That which was speech became Agni; 1. then that which was mind became the Moon; 2. then that which was sight became the Sun; 3. then that which was hearing became these quarters, as well as all the gods; 4. then that which was the out-breath became Bṛhaspati, because he is the lord (*pati*) of this great (*bṛhatī*) speech, therefore he is called Bṛhaspati; 5. then that which was the in-breath became Prajāpati. This very Udgītha, which is the in-breath, is possessed of sons and possessed of progeny.

His very voice becomes possessed of offspring for him who knows thus. 6. Now, some sing this [Sāman] directly as: "Breath! Breath! Breath! Huṃ! Bhā! Ovā! 7. Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said: "It is not right to sing this directly. Whatever one performs with speech, that alone has been accomplished by him. 8. Now, furthermore, the procreation of the Ṛk and Sāman is as follows: when he utters the *hiṅkāra*, he thereby cries out; and when he intones the *prastāva*, he thereby floats. And then...

When he takes up the *ādi*, he thereby pours out semen; then, when he sings the *udgītha*, he thereby brings the poured-out semen to development; then, when he performs the *pratihāra*, he thereby causes the developed semen to grow; then, when he utters the *upadrava*, he thereby transforms the grown semen; then, when he reaches the *nidhana*, he thereby procreates the transformed semen. This is the procreation of the *ṛc* and the *sāman*. He who thus knows this procreation of the *ṛc* and the *sāman*—the *ṛc* and the *sāman* bring him forth.
Thus ends the second section in the first chapter.

The first section is completed. This very one was here in the beginning—he who shines yonder. He, taking the brilliance, the essence, the sensory power, and the vigor of all beings, ascended upwards. He desired: "May I alone become the one syllable, sweet and soft, and win over the gods. He performed austerity; having performed austerity, he became that one syllable. The gods and the seers sought to obtain it. Then he created the Asuras, the slayers of beings, so that evil might not follow him. They sought to obtain it through speech; they ascended into speech. Of them—

He took away speech; therefore speech is taken away, for with it one speaks both truth and falsehood. They sought to appease him with the mind and ascended into the mind; he took away their mind; therefore the mind is taken away, for with it one meditates on both the auspicious and the inauspicious. They sought to appease him with the eye and ascended into the eye; he took away their eye; therefore the eye is taken away, for with it one sees both the beautiful and the ugly. Him—

They sought to overcome him with the ear; they ascended into his ear, and he took possession of their ear. Therefore, the ear is taken possession of; by means of it, one hears what is worth hearing and what is not worth hearing. (8) They sought to overcome him with the out-breath (*apāna*); they ascended into his out-breath, and he took possession of their out-breath. Therefore, the out-breath is taken possession of; for by means of it, one smells both the fragrant and the foul-smelling. (9) They sought to overcome him with the in-breath (*prāṇa*); they overcame him with the in-breath. (10) Then the Asuras, the slayers of beings, rushed forward, thinking, "We shall delude him. (11)

Thinking thus, they were destroyed just as a clod of earth would crumble upon hitting a stone; such was the destruction of the Asuras. This vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed that "stone-cutter" (aśmākhaṇa). Just as a clod of earth crumbles upon hitting a stone-cutter, even so does he crumble who speaks ill of one who knows this.
Thus ends the first section of the second anuvāka.

This very Prāṇa is the Udgītha that is self-controlled and has a radiant summit; for it brings all this under its control. He who knows this becomes self-controlled and brings his own people under his control. For this [sun] shines at the summit of this [Prāṇa], or that [Prāṇa] is at the summit of that [sun]. Śāṭyāyani describes this Udgītha as "self-controlled and having a radiant summit"; indeed, the fame of one who knows this becomes radiant. "The manifestation" (ābhūti)—so say the Kārīrādins. Verily, offspring and cattle manifest themselves in accordance with Prāṇa. He who meditates upon this as "the manifestation" [attains this].

"By this very [breath] one comes to be endowed with life-breath, offspring, and cattle," said Sātyayajñi. "It is *saṃbhūti* (coming-to-be)," said Sātyayajñaya. For it is after the breath that offspring and cattle come into being. He who meditates upon this as *saṃbhūti* comes to be endowed with life-breath, offspring, and cattle. "It is *prabhūti* (abundance)," said Śailana. For it is after the breath that offspring and cattle come forth into existence. He who meditates upon this as *prabhūti* comes forth into existence with life-breath, offspring, and cattle. "It is *bhūti* (being)," said Bhāllabina.

"Verily, offspring and cattle follow after breath. He who meditates upon this [breath] as 'prosperity' (bhūti) indeed prospers through breath, through offspring, and through cattle. "Aparodha, not to be obstructed," said Pārṣṇa Śailana; for he obstructs another, but no one obstructs him. Indeed, he who knows this obstructs his hateful rival.
Thus ends the second section of the second chapter.

"Ekavīra (the sole hero)," said Āruṇeya; for this prāṇa is indeed the sole hero. He who knows this has a single hero, a man of valor, born to him. "Ekaputra (having one son)," said Caikitāneya; for this prāṇa is indeed the one son. "He is also Dviputra (having two sons)," for there are two: prāṇa and apāna. "He is also Triputra (having three sons)," for there are three: prāṇa, apāna, and vyāna. "He is also Catuṣputra (having four sons)," for there are four: prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, and samāna. "He is also Pañcaputra (having five sons)," for there are five...

"He has six sons"—namely, Prāṇa, Apāna, Vyāna, Samāna, Avāna, and Udāna. "He has seven sons"—for there are these seven breaths in the head. "He has nine sons"—for there are seven breaths in the head and two directed downwards. "He has ten sons"—for there are seven breaths in the head, two directed downwards, and the tenth is in the navel. "He has many sons"—for all these creatures are his offspring. Indeed, it was this Udgītha that the Brahmins of old knew.
The Kāmāgāyins said: "How many sons of yours shall we sing? 12.5 Thus ends the third section in the second Anuvāka.

If he should say, "Sing for me with one," then knowing that the *udgītha* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), he should meditate on one with his mind; for the vital breath is one, and indeed one son is born to him. If he should say, "Sing for me with two," then knowing that the *udgītha* is the vital breath, he should meditate on two with his mind; for there are two, the out-breath (*apāna*) and the in-breath (*prāṇa*), and indeed two sons are born to him. If he should say, "Sing for me with three," then knowing that the *udgītha* is the vital breath, he should meditate on three with his mind; for there are three—the *prāṇa*, the *apāna*, and the diffused breath (*vyāna*)—and indeed three sons are born to him.

3. If he should say, "Sing for me four," knowing that the *udgītha* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), he should meditate on them as four in his mind; for the vital breath consists of four: *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *vyāna*, and *samāna*. Indeed, four [sons] will be born to him. 4. If he should say, "Sing for me five," knowing that the *udgītha* is the vital breath, he should meditate on them as five in his mind; for the vital breath consists of five: *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *vyāna*, *samāna*, and *avāna*. Indeed, five [sons] will be born to him. 5. If he should say, "Sing for me six," knowing that the *udgītha* is the vital breath...

The wise one, knowing that the *udgītha* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), should meditate upon it with the mind as sixfold, for the vital breath is indeed sixfold: *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *vyāna*, *samāna*, *avāna*, and *udāna*; for these six are born from him. If he should say, "Sing out for me seven," the wise one, knowing that the *udgītha* is the vital breath, should meditate upon it with the mind as sevenfold, for there are these seven vital breaths in the head; for these seven are born from him. If he should say, "Sing out for me nine," the wise one, knowing that the *udgītha* is the vital breath, should meditate upon it with the mind as ninefold: there are seven vital breaths in the head and two directed downwards, making nine.

Verily, ten are born to him. If he should say, "Sing for me ten," then knowing that the *udgītha* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), he should meditate with his mind on ten: the seven breaths in the head, two downward ones, and the tenth at the navel. Verily, ten are born to him. If he should say, "Sing for me a thousand," then knowing that the *udgītha* is the vital breath, he should meditate with his mind on a thousand. For these rays of the sun are a thousand; they are his sons. Verily, a thousand are born to him. Thus indeed is this *udgītha*.

Para, Āṭṇāra, Kakṣīvān, and Trasadasyu—these former great kings who were learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) approached Sahasraputra for instruction. They all indeed came to have a thousand sons each. Whoever knows this likewise comes to have a thousand sons.
Thus ends the fourth section in the second chapter;
the second chapter is complete.

Śaryāta Mānava performed a sacrifice on the eastern plateau. At that sacrifice, the beings sought to be assigned roles in the *udgītha* chant. The gods came from the east, saying, "Let us consecrate him with Bṛhaspati as the *udgātṛ*; let this one chant the *udgītha* for you. The fathers came from the south, saying, "Let him chant the *udgītha* for you with Bambin Ājadviṣa. The Asuras came from the west, saying, "Let him chant the *udgītha* for you with Uśanas Kāvya.

The humans came from the north, saying, "Let him chant the *udgītha* for you with Ayāsya Āṅgirasa. Then he reflected: "Come, let me ask them: 'How much does each one master? How much does each one master? How much does each one master? (1–3)

He said to Bṛhaspati, "If you were to sing the *udgītha* for me, what would come of that? He replied, "The glory would be among the gods; you would be the lord among the gods, and I would cause you to go to the heavenly world. Then he said to Aṅgirasa, "If you were to sing the *udgītha* for me, what would come of that? He replied, "The glory would be among the ancestors; you would be the lord among the ancestors, and I would cause you to go to the heavenly world. Then he said to Uśanas Kāvya, "If you were to sing the *udgītha* for me, what would come of that? He replied—

He said, "The prosperity would be among the Asuras, and the lordship among the Asuras; moreover, I would cause you to go to the heavenly world. Then he said to Ayāsya Āṅgirasa, "If you were to sing the Udgītha for me, what would come of that? He replied, "I would place the gods in the world of the gods, men in the world of men, and the ancestors in the world of the ancestors; I would push the Asuras out from this world and cause you to go to the heavenly world. Thus ends the first section of the third chapter.

He said, "Venerable sir, sing the Udgītha for me—you who are the glory of all this. Ayāsya sang the Udgītha for him; therefore, when chosen as an Udgātṛ priest, one should seek a dwelling on the north side, for that dwelling which is on the north side is indeed secure. Ayāsya Āṅgirasa, having come from the north, sang the Udgītha for Śaryāta Mānava. By means of the out-breath (prāṇa), he established the gods in the world of the gods; by the in-breath (apāna), the humans in the world of humans; by the inter-breath (vyāna), the ancestors in the world of the ancestors; and by the syllable *hiṅ*, [he established the birds].

With the thunderbolt he drove the Asuras away from this world. He said to them, "Go far away! That world is indeed named Dūra (the Far). They went to it; these are those Asuras who, having been rendered incapable of existence, were utterly destroyed. By means of the meters and through speech, he caused Śaryāta Mānava to go to the heavenly world. Those Asuras said, "Come, let us find him who has thus disposed of us. Then, as he was returning, they saw him approaching. They said, "He has indeed entered his mouth," because they had said, "He has indeed entered his mouth."

Therefore, he is Ayāsya. Indeed, his name is Ayāsya; they call him Ayāsya cryptically. 7. This Ayāsya is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*); it is the vital breath that pushed them away. 8. He who, knowing this, sings the *udgītha*, establishes the gods in the world of the gods by means of the out-breath (*prāṇa*), humans in the world of humans by means of the in-breath (*apāna*), and the ancestors in the world of the ancestors by means of the inter-breath (*vyāna*). By the very *hiṅkāra*, as a thunderbolt, he pushes away from this world the hating rival. 9. 8. Thus ends the second section of the third chapter.

He should say to him, "Go far away! and he indeed goes to that very world which the Asuras went to. (1) By means of the meters and through speech, he causes the sacrificer to go to the heavenly world. (2) These are the sacred utterances (*vyāhṛti*): *preti*, *vāk*, and *bhūr bhuvaḥ svar ud*. (3) Now, *preti* is the out-breath (*prāṇa*); it is this world; thus he causes him to partake in this world. (4) *eti* is the in-breath (*apāna*); it is yonder world; thus he causes him to partake in yonder world. (5) *Vāk* is Brahman.

This intermediate space is "Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ"—that is the threefold knowledge (*trayī vidyā*). "Ut" is yonder sun. Because he joins [the world] upward, as it were, with "Ut," and because he converges into one alone, therefore he is the "Single Hero" (*ekavīra*). Indeed, being one, he is a hero and possesses heroic power; and for him who knows this, a single son is born who is a hero and possesses heroic power. Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said: "One should worship this *Udgītha* as 'having many sons,' for these many rays of the sun are his sons; therefore, it is 'having many sons'."
"This is indeed to be meditated upon as the Udgītha"—thus ends the third section in the third chapter;
the third chapter is completed.

"The gods and the asuras were contending," they say. But in truth, it was not the gods and the asuras who contended there; rather, it was Prajāpati and Death who contended. Now, the gods were the beloved sons of that Prajāpati, and they resolved: "Let us consecrate ourselves with him as our Udgātṛ, so that, having struck down death and having struck down evil, we may go to the heavenly world. They said, "Let us consecrate ourselves with Speech as our Udgātṛ. They consecrated themselves with Speech as their Udgātṛ; Speech sang this for them—whatever one speaks here by means of speech.

Namely, that which they enjoy by means of speech—evil was emitted after it. Whatever evil one speaks with speech, that itself is that evil. They said, "Verily, this one has not carried us beyond death nor beyond evil; let us consecrate ourselves with the mind as the Udgātṛ. They consecrated themselves with the mind as the Udgātṛ. He sang out for them this mind—that which one thinks with the mind, that which one enjoys with the mind. Evil was emitted after it. Whatever evil one thinks with the mind, that itself is that evil. They said...

"Verily, this one has not carried us beyond death nor beyond evil through the *udgātṛ* of the eye; let us consecrate ourselves with the ear as the *udgātṛ*. 9. They consecrated themselves with the ear as the *udgātṛ*. For them, the eye sang forth this [world]: whatever one sees with the eye and whatever one enjoys with the eye. 10. Evil was emitted after that; whatever evil one sees with the eye, that indeed is that evil. 11. They said, "Verily, this one has not carried us beyond death nor beyond evil; let us consecrate ourselves with the ear as the *udgātṛ*. 12. They...

They consecrated themselves with the ear as the Udgātṛ. For them, the ear sang forth this [world]: whatever one hears with the ear, whatever one enjoys with the ear. 13. Evil was emitted after it; that evil which one hears with the ear—that indeed is that evil. 14. They said: "Verily, this one has not carried us beyond death, nor beyond evil. Let us consecrate ourselves with the breath as the Udgātṛ. 15. They consecrated themselves with the breath as the Udgātṛ. For them, the breath sang forth this [world]: whatever one breathes with the breath, whatever one [enjoys] with the breath...

They ate it, and evil was emitted from them. That evil which one breathes out by means of the breath—that indeed is that evil. They said, "Verily, this [breath] has not carried us beyond death nor beyond evil. Let us consecrate ourselves with this principal breath as the Udgātṛ. They consecrated themselves with this principal breath as the Udgātṛ. Death said, "This is that Udgātṛ of theirs by whom they will overcome death. For with this breath one does not speak evil, one does not think evil, nor does one do evil.
He sees no evil, he hears no evil, and he smells no evil. By this [knowledge], having struck down death and having struck down evil, he goes to the heavenly world;
indeed, he who knows thus, having struck down death and having struck down evil, goes to the heavenly world.
Thus ends the first section of the fourth chapter.

Just as one might pass by after killing and trampling [an enemy], even so did they pass beyond that death. 1. He carried speech across first; he placed it beyond death, and it became Agni. 2. Then he carried mind across; he placed it beyond death, and it became the Moon. 3. Then he carried sight across; he placed it beyond death, and it became the Sun. 4. Then he carried hearing across; he placed it beyond death, and it became these quarters, as well as the All-Gods (Viśve Devāḥ). 5.

Then he carried Prāṇa across; he deposited it beyond death, and it became Vāyu. Then he sang for himself alone the right to eat food. He is indeed Ayāsya, because he is placed in the mouth (āsya); therefore he is called Ayāsya. And because he rests (ramate) in the mouth, for that reason also he is called Ayāsya. He is indeed Aṅgirasa, because from him these limbs (aṅgāni) obtain their sap (rasa); therefore he is called Aṅgirasa. And because he is the sap of these limbs, for that reason also he is called Aṅgirasa. The gods said to him: "You have sung for yourself alone the right to eat food."

Thus ends the second section of the fourth lesson. Wherever these deities touch, indeed, no trace of evil whatsoever remains there. He should know: "No trace of evil shall remain here; all this evil these deities will utterly consume. And so it truly comes to pass. And whoever offends one who knows thus—just as one would go after having encountered these deities, so does he go; for he speaks ill of him who has sought refuge in these deities and dwells among them. Of that very person...

There is no affliction whatsoever for one who knows this; rather, it is he who speaks ill of him who suffers affliction. When he pursues him, he should approach those deities and say, "This man has pursued me; let him undergo this affliction. He indeed undergoes that affliction. As many dwellings as these vital breaths have in this world, so many dwellings do these deities have for him in yonder world. Therefore, one who knows this should neither fear the lack of a house nor the lack of a world, for these deities are his dwellings in this world.

"These deities will create houses for me in yonder world; therefore, they will bestow a world upon me. Therefore, one who knows this should neither fear the lack of a house nor the lack of a world. He should know: "These deities will create houses for me from their own abodes in this world"; and he should know: "These deities will bestow a world upon me in yonder world. Therefore, one who knows this should neither fear the lack of a house nor the lack of a world. He should know: "These deities will unite both of these for me. And so it indeed comes to pass. 9.12.12.
Thus ends the third section in the fourth Anuvāka;
the fourth Anuvāka is completed.

The gods indeed milked speech by means of the calf of Brahman; for Agni is indeed the calf of Brahman. That which is speech is Brahman itself, and that which is Agni is Death. Just as one might milk a cow after bringing her calf near so that she yields her milk, even so did the gods milk speech and all their desires. He who knows this indeed milks speech and all his desires. This very one kindles the divine speech, saying, "Speak! Speak! Speak! Whatever evil has been done here by a person, he makes it manifest, even if it was done here in secret.
If one performs [an action] thinking [it is right], he indeed makes it manifest; therefore, one should certainly not do evil.
Thus ends the first section in the fifth chapter.

This Agni, indeed, is the one among the gods who is to be served most closely. One should serve him well; for he who serves him well in this world, he (Agni) serves him well in the other world. But he who does not honor him in this world, he (Agni) does not honor him in the other world. Therefore, one should certainly serve Agni well. One should not touch him with the hands, nor with the feet, nor with a staff. When one washes oneself near him, that is touching him with the hands. And when one stretches out [one's limbs], that is touching him with the feet. If he touches him [in this way], he is liable to bring harm upon himself.
If the foundation is poorly laid, he subsequently attends to Agni well; indeed, he establishes him upon a good foundation.
Thus ends the second section of the fifth Anuvāka.

This Agni, indeed, is the greatest eater among the gods. Therefore, one should not eat that which is not given as a portion for him. For if one eats while the great eater has not eaten, the Lord (Īśvara) may afflict him; he would be eating as if it were putrid food. Moreover, when food has been announced, one should say, "Kindle your fire! Just as when food has been announced, one might say to someone, "Bring a superior person to serve [the meal]," such is that act. That which is speech is indeed the Sāman. He who meditates upon the eye as the Sāman or the ear as the Sāman does not truly accomplish anything by that. Now, he who...

"He who worships it as 'The sun is the Sāman, the moon is the Sāman'—he truly does nothing with it. But he who worships it as 'Speech is the Sāman'—he indeed knows the Sāman by way of its application (*anuṣṭhyā*), for by means of speech the office of the *ṛtvij* priest is performed. That tone which arises from speech is Agni; but speech itself is indeed speech. Thus, in this case, the Sāman becomes a single unity. He who thus knows that the Sāman becomes a single unity—in this way, indeed, this Sāman becomes a single unity—and he becomes the foremost among his own people as a single unity. Therefore, one should let only such a person as this know the Sāman."
One should not cause him to perform the office of a priest; for he alone truly knows the Sāman who knows it thus. This concludes the third section of the fifth Anuvāka.
The fifth Anuvāka is finished.
Thus ends the second Adhyāya.

Now begins the second chapter. There were indeed six Udgātṛ-priests among the gods: Speech, Mind, Sight, Hearing, Exhalation, and Inhalation. They resolved, "Let us consecrate ourselves with that Udgātṛ by which, having struck down death and having struck down evil, we may go to the heavenly world. They said, "Let us consecrate ourselves with Speech as the Udgātṛ. They consecrated themselves with Speech as the Udgātṛ. Whatever one speaks with speech, that he sang for himself; but whatever other desires there were, those he sang for the gods. Evil was cast upon her. Whatever evil one speaks with speech, that [is what was cast upon her].

That indeed was that evil. They said, "Verily, this one has not carried us beyond death nor beyond evil; let us consecrate ourselves with the mind as the Udgātṛ. They consecrated themselves with the mind as the Udgātṛ. Whatever he meditates upon with the mind, that he sings for himself; and whatever other desires there are, those he wins for the gods. That evil was released after him; whatever evil he meditates upon with the mind, that indeed is that evil. They said, "Verily, this one has not carried us beyond death nor beyond evil; let us consecrate ourselves with the eye as the Udgātṛ."

They consecrated themselves with the eye as the Udgātṛ. Whatever one sees with the eye, that he sang for himself; but whatever other desires there were, those he sang for the gods. Then evil was released after it. That which one sees as evil with the eye—that indeed is that evil. They said, "Surely this one has not carried us beyond death nor beyond evil by means of the eye as the Udgātṛ. Let us consecrate ourselves with the ear as the Udgātṛ. They consecrated themselves with the ear as the Udgātṛ. Whatever one hears with the ear, that he sang for himself; but whatever other [desires there were]...

The desires [went] to the gods. 12. Evil was created after them; whatever evil he hears with the ear, that indeed is that evil. 13. They said, "Verily, this one has not carried us beyond death nor beyond evil. Let us consecrate ourselves with the out-breath as the Udgātṛ. 14. They consecrated themselves with the out-breath as the Udgātṛ. Whatever he breathes out with the out-breath, that he sang for himself; and those other desires [went] to the gods. 15. Evil was created after them; whatever evil odor he breathes out with the out-breath, that indeed is that evil. 16.

They said, "Surely this one has not carried us beyond death nor beyond evil by means of the Prāṇa as Udgātṛ; let us consecrate ourselves with the Prāṇa as Udgātṛ. 17. They consecrated themselves with the Prāṇa as Udgātṛ. Whatever he breathes out by means of the Prāṇa, that he sang as his own portion; and whatever other desires there were, those he sang for the gods. 18. Evil was not created after him, for with this Prāṇa one does not speak evil, one does not think evil, one does not see evil, one does not hear evil, and one does not breathe in an evil odor. 19. By means of that, having struck down death, having struck down...
Having struck down evil and indeed having struck down death, he who knows this goes to the heavenly world, which is free from evil. 20.1 Thus ends the first section of the first recitation.

That which was speech became Agni; 1. then that which was mind became the Moon; 2. then that which was sight became the Sun; 3. then that which was hearing became these quarters, as well as all the gods; 4. then that which was the out-breath became Bṛhaspati—because he is the lord (*pati*) of this great (*bṛhatī*) speech, therefore he is Bṛhaspati; 5. then that which was the in-breath became Prajāpati. This very Udgītha is possessed of sons and progeny, for it is the in-breath.

His very voice becomes possessed of offspring for him who knows thus. 6. Some chant this [Sāman] directly as "Prāṇāḥ, prāṇāḥ, prāṇāḥ, hum bhā ovā. 7. Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said: "One ought not to chant this directly; for whatever one performs with speech, that alone becomes accomplished for him. 8. Now, furthermore, there is the procreation of the Ṛk and the Sāman. In that he utters the *hiṅ* sound, by that he indeed cries out; and in that he begins the *prastāva*, by that he floats forward. And then...

When he takes up the *ādi*, he thereby pours forth semen; then, when he sings the *udgītha*, he thereby brings the poured semen to fruition; then, when he performs the *pratihāra*, he thereby causes the fructified [semen] to grow; then, when he recites the *upadrava*, he thereby transforms the grown [semen]; then, when he reaches the *nidhana*, he thereby procreates the transformed semen. This is the procreation of the Ṛc and the Sāman. He who thus knows this procreation of the Ṛc and the Sāman—verily, the Ṛc and the Sāman bring him forth.
Thus ends the second section in the first Anuvāka.

The first section is completed. This very one was here in the beginning—he who shines yonder. He, taking the brilliance, the essence, the sensory power, and the vigor of all beings, ascended upwards. He desired: "May I alone become the single syllable, sweet and soft, and win over the gods. He practiced austerity; having practiced austerity, he became that single syllable. The gods and the seers sought to obtain it. Then he created the Asuras, the slayers of beings, so that evil might not follow him. They sought to obtain it through speech; they ascended into speech. Of them—

He took speech away from them; therefore speech was taken away from them, for with it they speak both truth and falsehood. They sought to appease him with the mind and ascended into the mind; he took the mind away from them; therefore the mind was taken away from them, for with it they think both what is meritorious and what is evil. They sought to appease him with the eye and ascended into the eye; he took the eye away from them; therefore the eye was taken away from them, for with it they see both what is beautiful to look upon and what is not beautiful to look upon. Him—

They sought to overcome him with the ear; they ascended into the ear, and he appropriated their ear. Therefore the ear is appropriated; by it one hears both what is worth hearing and what is not worth hearing. (8) They sought to overcome him with the out-breath (*apāna*); they ascended into the out-breath, and he appropriated their out-breath. Therefore the out-breath is appropriated; for by it one smells both what is fragrant and what is foul-smelling. (9) They sought to overcome him with the vital breath (*prāṇa*); they overcame him with the vital breath. (10) Then the Asuras, the slayers of beings, rushed forward, thinking, "We shall delude him."

Thinking thus, they were shattered just as a clod of earth would be shattered upon hitting a stone; such was the destruction of the Asuras. This vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed that "stone-breaker" (*aśmākhaṇa*). Just as a clod of earth is shattered upon hitting a stone-breaker, even so is he shattered who speaks ill of one who knows this.
Thus ends the first section of the second chapter.

This very breath is the Udgītha that is self-controlled and has a radiant summit; for it brings all this under its control.
