He who knows this becomes self-controlled and brings his own people under his control. For this [sun] shines at the summit of this [breath], or that [breath] shines at the summit of yonder [sun]. Śāṭyāyani describes this very Udgītha as "self-controlled and having a radiant summit"; indeed, he whose fame becomes radiant is he who knows thus. "The manifestation," so say the Kārīrādis; for offspring and cattle manifest themselves in accordance with the breath. He who meditates upon this as "the manifestation" [attains manifestation].

"By means of breath, one comes to be endowed with offspring and cattle," said Sātyayajñīya. "It is 'origination' (sambhūti)," said Śailana. For it is after breath that offspring and cattle originate. He who meditates upon this as 'origination' comes to be endowed with breath, offspring, and cattle. "It is 'abundance' (prabhūti)," said Śailana. For it is after breath that offspring and cattle become abundant. He who meditates upon this as 'abundance' becomes abundant indeed with breath, offspring, and cattle. "It is 'existence' (bhūti)," said Bhāllabīna. [Regarding] breath...

Or else, offspring and cattle come after him. He who meditates upon this as "becoming" (bhūti) indeed becomes [prosperous] through vital breath, progeny, and cattle. 7. Pārṣṇa Śailana said: "The unobstructed one who obstructs others. For he obstructs another, but no other obstructs him. Indeed, he who knows this obstructs his own hateful rival. 8. 4. Thus ends the second section of the second chapter.

"Ekavīra (the sole hero)," said Āruṇeya; for this breath alone is indeed the sole hero. To him who knows thus, a single hero, full of vigor, is born. "Ekaputra (the one son)," said Caikitāneya; for this breath alone is indeed the one son. "That same [breath] is 'dviputra (two sons),' for there are two: prāṇa and apāna. "That same [breath] is 'triputra (three sons),' for there are three: prāṇa, apāna, and vyāna. "That same [breath] is 'catuṣputra (four sons),' for there are four: prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, and samāna. "That same [breath] is 'pañcaputra (five sons),' for there are five..."

"He has six sons"—namely, Prāṇa, Apāna, Vyāna, Samāna, Avāna, and Udāna. "He has seven sons"—for there are these seven vital breaths (prāṇas) in the head. "He has nine sons"—for there are seven vital breaths in the head and two directed downwards. "He has ten sons"—for there are seven vital breaths in the head, two directed downwards, and the tenth is in the navel. "He has many sons"—for all these creatures are his offspring. Indeed, the Brahmins of old, knowing this Udgītha, used to [worship] it thus.
The Kāmāgāyins said: "How many sons do you have that we might sing for? 12.5 Thus ends the third section in the second anuvāka.

If he should say, "Sing for me with one," then knowing that the *udgītha* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), he should meditate on it as one with his mind; for the vital breath is one, and indeed one son is born to him. If he should say, "Sing for me with two," then knowing that the *udgītha* is the vital breath, he should meditate on it as two with his mind; for there are two, the out-breath (*apāna*) and the in-breath (*prāṇa*), and indeed two sons are born to him. If he should say, "Sing for me with three," then knowing that the *udgītha* is the vital breath, he should meditate on it as three with his mind; for there are three—the out-breath, the in-breath, and the diffused breath (*vyāna*)—and indeed three sons are born to him.

If he should say, "Sing for me four," then knowing that the *udgītha* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), he should meditate on four with his mind; for the vital breath consists of four: out-breath (*apāna*), diffused breath (*vyāna*), and level breath (*samāna*). Indeed, four sons are born to him. If he should say, "Sing for me five," then knowing that the *udgītha* is the vital breath, he should meditate on five with his mind; for the vital breath consists of five: out-breath (*apāna*), diffused breath (*vyāna*), level breath (*samāna*), and downward breath (*avāna*). Indeed, five sons are born to him. If he should say, "Sing for me six," then knowing that the *udgītha* is the vital breath...

The wise one, knowing that the *udgītha* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), should meditate on it with the mind as sixfold; for there are indeed six: the out-breath (*prāṇa*), the in-breath (*apāna*), the diffused breath (*vyāna*), the level breath (*samāna*), the downward breath (*avāna*), and the upward breath (*udāna*). Indeed, these six are produced from him. If he should say, "Seven have sung for me," the wise one, knowing that the *udgītha* is the vital breath, should meditate on it with the mind as sevenfold; for there are indeed these seven vital breaths in the head. Indeed, these seven are produced from him. If he should say, "Nine have sung for me," the wise one, knowing that the *udgītha* is the vital breath, should meditate on it with the mind as ninefold: there are seven vital breaths in the head, and two directed downwards—thus nine.

Verily, ten are born to him. If he should say, "Ten have come to me," then knowing that the *prāṇa* is the Udgītha, he should meditate on ten with his mind: the seven breaths in the head, two downward ones, and the tenth in the navel. Verily, ten are born to him. If he should say, "A thousand have come to me," then knowing that the *prāṇa* is the Udgītha, he should meditate on a thousand with his mind; for these rays of the sun are a thousand, and they are his sons. Verily, a thousand are born to him. Thus indeed is this Udgītha supreme.

Āṭṇāra, Kakṣīvān, and Trasadasyu—these ancient great kings, learned in the Vedas, approached Sahasraputra for instruction. They all indeed came to have a thousand sons each. He who knows this likewise comes to have a thousand sons.
Thus ends the fourth section in the second chapter;
the second chapter is complete.

Śaryāta Mānava performed a sacrifice on the eastern plateau; at that sacrifice, the beings sought to be included in the *udgītha*. The gods came from the east, saying, "Let us consecrate ourselves with Bṛhaspati as our *udgātṛ*"; they said, "Let this one sing the *udgītha* for you"—referring to Bamba Ājadviṣa. The ancestors came from the south, saying, "Let this one sing the *udgītha* for you"—referring to Uśanas Kāvya. The Asuras came from the west, saying, "Let this one sing the *udgītha* for you"—referring to Ayāsya Āṅgirasa. The humans came from the north, saying, "Let this one sing the *udgītha* for you. Then he reflected: "Come now, let me question them."

"How much does one master? How much does one master? How much does one master? 3. He said to Bṛhaspati, "If you were to sing the *udgītha* for me, what would come of that? 4. He replied, "There would be glory among the gods; there would be sovereignty among the gods; I would cause you to go to the heavenly world. 5. Then he said to Bambā Ājadviṣa, "If you were to sing the *udgītha* for me, what would come of that? 6. He replied, "There would be glory among the fathers; there would be sovereignty among the fathers; I would cause you to go to the heavenly world. 7. Then he said to Uśanas Kāvya, "If you were to sing the *udgītha* for me..."

"If you were to sing the *udgītha*, what would happen from that? He replied, "The glory would remain with the Asuras, and the sovereignty would remain with the Asuras; I would cause you to go to the heavenly world. Then he said to Āyāsya Āṅgirasa, "If you were to sing the *udgītha* for me, what would happen from that? He replied, "I would place the gods in the world of the gods, men in the world of men, and the ancestors in the world of the ancestors. I would drive the Asuras away from this world and cause you to go to the heavenly world. Thus ends the first section of the third chapter.

He said, "Sir, sing the Udgītha for me—you who are the glory of all this. Ayāsya sang the Udgītha for him; therefore, when chosen as an Udgātṛ priest, one should seek a dwelling on the north side, for that dwelling which is on the north is unassailable. Having come from the north, Ayāsya Āṅgirasa sang the Udgītha for Śaryāta Mānava. By means of the out-breath (prāṇa), he established the gods in the world of the gods; by means of the down-breath (apāna), he established humans in the world of humans; by means of the inter-breath (vyāna), he established the ancestors in the world of the ancestors; and by means of the *hiṅkāra* sound...

With the thunderbolt he drove the Asuras away from this world. He said to them, "Go far away! That world is indeed named Dūra (Far). They went to it; these are those Asuras who were utterly defeated beyond recovery. By means of the meters and through speech, he caused Śaryāta Mānava to go to the heavenly world. The Asuras said, "Come, let us find him who has thus disposed of us. Then they came and saw him approaching. They said, "He is indeed within his mouth," because they had said, "He is indeed within his mouth."

Therefore, he is Ayāsya. Indeed, his name is Ayāsya; they call him "Ayāsya" cryptically (parokṣam). This Prāṇa is indeed Ayāsya, for it was Prāṇa that pushed them away. He who, knowing this, sings the Udgītha, places the gods in the world of the gods by means of Prāṇa, humans in the world of humans by means of Apāna, and the ancestors in the world of the ancestors by means of Vyāna. By the Hiṅkāra itself, as a thunderbolt, he pushes away from this world the hating rival.
Thus ends the second section of the third Anuvāka.

He should say to him, "Go far away! He indeed goes to that very world which the Asuras went to. (1) By means of the meters and by speech, he causes the sacrificer to go to the heavenly world. (2) These are the sacred utterances (*vyāhṛti*): "pretya," "vāk," and "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ" followed by "ud. (3) Now, "preti" is the out-breath (*prāṇa*); it is this world; thus he causes him to partake in this world. (4) "eti" is the in-breath (*apāna*); it is yonder world; thus he causes him to partake in yonder world. (5) "Vāk" is Brahman.

This intermediate space is "Bhūr," "Bhuvaḥ," and "Svaḥ"—this is the triple knowledge (*trayī vidyā*). "Ut" is that yonder sun. Because he joins [the worlds] as it were upward with "Ut," and because he becomes one alone, therefore he is the "Single Hero" (*ekavīra*). Indeed, being one, he is a hero, a possessor of vigor; and for him who knows this, a single son is born who is a hero, a possessor of vigor. Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said: "One should worship this *Udgītha* as 'having many sons,' for these rays of the sun are his sons; therefore, it has many sons."
"This is the Udgītha; thus indeed should it be meditated upon. This is the third section in the third chapter;
the third chapter is completed.

"It is said that the gods and the asuras were contending. Indeed, it was not the gods and the asuras who contended there; rather, it was Prajāpati and Death who contended. Now, the gods were the beloved sons of that Prajāpati, and they resolved: "Let us be consecrated with him as our Udgātṛ priest, so that, having struck down death and having struck down evil, we may go to the heavenly world. They said, "Let us be consecrated with Speech as our Udgātṛ priest. They were consecrated with Speech as their Udgātṛ priest; Speech sang for them this which one speaks by means of speech.

That which they enjoy by means of speech was enveloped by evil. Whatever evil one speaks with speech, that itself is that evil. They said, "Verily, this [speech] has not carried us beyond death, nor beyond evil. Let us consecrate ourselves with the mind as the Udgātṛ. They consecrated themselves with the mind as the Udgātṛ. For them, the mind sang forth this: whatever one meditates upon with the mind, whatever one enjoys with the mind. That was enveloped by evil. Whatever evil one meditates upon with the mind, that itself is that evil. They said, "Indeed, this [mind]..."

"This one has not carried us beyond death, nor beyond evil, through the *udgātṛ* of the eye. Let us consecrate ourselves with the *udgātṛ* of the ear. 9. They consecrated themselves with the *udgātṛ* of the ear; for them, this eye sang forth—that which one sees with the eye, that which one enjoys with the eye. 10. Evil was emitted after it; whatever evil one sees with the eye, that indeed is that evil. 11. They said, "Verily, this one has not carried us beyond death, nor beyond evil. Let us consecrate ourselves with the *udgātṛ* of the ear. 12. They consecrated themselves with the *udgātṛ* of the ear.

From them, this ear was produced as that which one hears with the ear and that which one enjoys with the ear. Evil was cast off from them; whatever evil one hears with the ear, that is that very evil. They said, "Verily, this one has not carried us beyond death nor beyond evil through the Prāṇa as the Udgātṛ; let us consecrate ourselves with the Prāṇa as the Udgātṛ. They consecrated themselves with the Prāṇa as the Udgātṛ. From them, this vital breath was produced as that which one breathes with the Prāṇa and that which one enjoys with the Prāṇa. Evil was cast off from them.

Whatever evil he breathes out with that breath, that itself is the evil. They said, "Surely this one has not carried us beyond death or evil; let us consecrate ourselves with this chief breath as the Udgātṛ. They consecrated themselves with this chief breath as the Udgātṛ. Death said, "This is their Udgātṛ by whom they will overcome death. For with this breath one does not speak evil, nor does one think evil, nor does one see evil, nor does one hear evil, nor does one [commit] evil.
He breathes in the fragrance. By this, having struck down death, having struck down evil, he goes to the heavenly world;
indeed, he who knows this, having struck down death, having struck down evil, goes to the heavenly world.
Thus ends the first section of the fourth chapter.

Just as one might pass by after killing and trampling [something], even so did they pass beyond this death. 1. He carried Speech across first; he placed it beyond death, and it became Agni. 2. Then he carried Mind across; he placed it beyond death, and it became the Moon. 3. Then he carried the Eye across; he placed it beyond death, and it became the Sun. 4. Then he carried the Ear across; he placed it beyond death, and it became these quarters, and they indeed became the All-Gods (Viśve Devāḥ). 5.

Then he carried Prāṇa across; he placed him beyond death, and he became Vāyu. Then he sang for himself alone, singing for the acquisition of food. He is this very Ayāsya, for he is placed in the mouth (āsya); therefore he is Ayāsya. And because he rests (ramate) in the mouth, for that reason also he is Ayāsya. He is this very Aṅgirasa, for from him these limbs (aṅgāni) obtain their essence (rasa); therefore he is Aṅgirasa. And because he is the essence of these limbs, for that reason also he is Aṅgirasa. The gods said to him: "You have sung for yourself alone the acquisition of food."

"Grant us a share in this food; this is its state of health. "Enter him," [he said]. "Make spaces for yourself," he replied. He made these vital breaths (*prāṇa*) into spaces. Having become speech, Agni entered him; having become mind, the Moon; having become sight, the Sun; having become hearing, the Quarters; having become breath, Vāyu. This indeed is the divine assembly, the divine court, the divine congregation.

Thus ends the second section of the fourth lesson. Wherever these deities touch anything, no trace of evil whatsoever remains there. He should know: "No trace of evil shall remain here; all this evil these deities will utterly consume. And so it indeed comes to pass. Furthermore, whoever offends one who knows this goes to ruin just as if he had offended these deities themselves; for he speaks ill of one who has sought refuge in these deities and dwells among them. Of him, of this very person...

There is no affliction whatsoever for one who knows this; rather, it is he who speaks ill of him who suffers affliction. When that affliction reaches him, he should approach those deities and say, "May this person who has harmed me transfer this affliction to himself. And indeed, that affliction passes away from him. As many dwellings as these vital breaths have for him in this world, so many dwellings do those deities have for him in yonder world. Therefore, one who knows this should neither fear the lack of a house nor the lack of a world, for these deities are his dwellings in this world.

"These deities will create houses for me in yonder world; therefore, they will grant me a world. Therefore, one who knows this should not fear the lack of a house, nor the lack of a world. He should know: "These deities will create houses for me from among houses in this world, according to their own abodes. And he should know: "These deities will grant me a world in yonder world. Therefore, one who knows this should not fear the lack of a house, nor the lack of a world. He should know: "These [deities] will unite both of these for me. And so it indeed comes to pass. 9.12
Thus ends the third section in the fourth chapter;
the fourth chapter is completed.

The gods indeed milked speech by means of the calf of Brahman; for Agni is indeed the calf of Brahman. That which is speech is Brahman itself, and that which is Agni is Death. Just as one might milk a cow after bringing her calf near so that she yields her milk, even so did the gods milk all desires from that speech. He who knows this indeed milks speech and all desires. This very person kindles the divine Speech, saying, "Speak! Speak! Speak! Whatever evil has been done here by a person, he makes it manifest—even if it was done here in secret.
If one performs [an action] while thinking [it is for his own sake], he indeed makes it manifest; therefore, one should certainly not do evil.
Thus ends the first section in the fifth chapter.

This Agni, indeed, is the one among the gods who is to be served most closely. He who serves him well in this world, he serves him well in that world; but he who does not honor him in this world, he does not honor him in that world. Therefore, one should serve Agni well. One should not touch him with the hands, nor with the feet, nor with a staff. When one washes oneself near him, that is touching him with the hands; and when one stretches out [one's limbs], that is touching him with the feet. If he is touched thus, he is liable to harm him.
If he were to place it on a badly prepared [spot], he would thereby treat Agni poorly; however, by placing it on a well-prepared [spot], he indeed establishes him in a state of well-being.
5.14 Thus ends the second section in the fifth chapter.

This Agni, indeed, is the greatest eater among the gods. Therefore, one should not eat that which is not given as a portion of the sacrificial food (*vrata*). For if one eats while the great eater has not yet eaten, the lord (Agni) may seize him; he would, as it were, eat what is putrid. Furthermore, when the meal has been announced, he should say, "Kindle your fire! Just as, when a meal has been announced, one might say to someone, "Bring a superior person to the feast," such is this. This Sāman is truly speech itself. He who meditates upon the eye as the Sāman, or the ear as the Sāman, does nothing with it [it serves no purpose]. But he who...

"He who worships it as 'The Sun is the Sāman, the Moon is the Sāman' does not truly perform [the rite] by that means. 5. Now, he who worships it as 'Speech is the Sāman'—he indeed knows the Sāman thoroughly; for by means of Speech and the Sāman, the office of the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is performed. 6. The tone that arises from Speech is Agni, while Speech itself is indeed Speech; thus, in this case, the Sāman becomes a single unity. 7. He who knows that the Sāman thus becomes a single unity—he, indeed, knowing that the Sāman thus becomes a single unity, becomes preeminent among his own people as a single unity. 8. Therefore, one should have only such a person, who knows this, perform the office of the officiating priest with the Sāman."
He who knows thus indeed knows the Sāman. This concludes the third section in the fifth chapter;
the fifth chapter is completed.
Thus ends the second book.

Now begins the third chapter. There is indeed only one deity who is complete; all other deities are merely half-deities. He is this very one who blows here [the wind]. (1) He alone is the "seizers" (*graha*) of all the gods. (2) He is called *asta* by name; for they call the cups [of Soma] here behind them "the *astas*. (3) When it is said that "the sun has gone to its setting" (*astam agāt*), it means he has gone to the cups; thus he is incomplete, and he enters into him [the wind]. (4) The moon goes to its setting; thus it is incomplete, and it enters into him. (5) The stars go to their setting; thus they are incomplete, and they enter into him.

6. Agni follows after him; therefore he is incomplete; he enters into this very [Self]. 7. Day goes away and night goes away; therefore they are incomplete; they enter into this very [Self]. 8. The quarters become confused and are no longer discerned during that night; therefore they are incomplete; they enter into this very [Self]. 9. Parjanya rains and the cloud takes it up; therefore it is incomplete; it enters into this very [Self]. 10. The waters waste away, likewise the herbs, likewise the trees; therefore they are incomplete; they enter into this very [Self]. 11.

In that all this indeed enters into the wind alone, therefore the wind is the *sāman*. He who knows thus is a knower of the *sāman*; he knows the *sāman* in its entirety. Now, with respect to the self (*adhyātma*): when one sleeps, one does not speak with speech; that [speech] enters into this very breath (*prāṇa*). One does not think with the mind; that [mind] enters into this very breath. One does not see with the eye; that [eye] enters into this very breath. One does not hear with the ear; that [ear] enters into this very breath. In that all this indeed converges into the breath alone.

Therefore, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone is the *sāman*. He who knows this is a knower of the *sāman*; he truly knows the *sāman* in its entirety. Now, when people say, "Alas, it does not blow today," that [breath] remains within the person; it sits there full, perspiring. Then, while they were serving food, a Brahmin approached Śaunaka Kāpeya and Abhipratārin Kākṣaseni.
Thus ends the first section in the first chapter.
He begged of them both, but they did not grant him [alms], thinking, "Who is he? Who is he? Then he approached them with this verse:
"The one God who swallowed the four great ones—Who is He, the guardian of the world?
O Kāpeya, some do not know Him; O Abhipratārin, He has entered into many forms."

Thus [it was said]. 2. Abhipratārin said: "Enter into this very one and answer; for he has already answered on your behalf. 3. He replied to him: "He is the self of both gods and mortals, like the son of a craftsman with golden teeth. They speak of his greatness as great, that he, being himself uneaten, eats the eater. 4. "Of the Great Self there are four; God is the one"—Agni is indeed speech; he is the Great Self, the God. When he sleeps, breath swallows speech. 5. Mind is the moon; he is the Great Self, the God. He...

Where he sleeps, the Prāṇa swallows that mind; the eye is the great-souled god Āditya, and where he sleeps, the Prāṇa swallows that eye. The ear is the quarters, those great-souled gods; and where he sleeps, the Prāṇa swallows that ear. Now, as for the statement, "The one god [swallows] the four great-souled ones," this is indeed that. "Who swallows Ka?"—Ka is Prajāpati; he indeed swallows this. "The guardian of the world"—he is indeed the guardian of the world. O Kāpeya, him...

"They do not understand it as one," for indeed they do not understand this as one. (12) "Abhipratārin, it is established in many ways," for this very breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed established in many ways. (13) "The self (*ātman*) of the gods and of mortals," for this is indeed the self of the gods and of mortals. (14) "Golden-toothed, like the son of Rapas," for he is not a son; though he has the form of a son, he is not a son. (15) "They speak of his greatness as great," for they indeed speak of his greatness as great. (16) "While being uneaten, he eats him who eats," for he, being uneaten, eats him who eats. (17) 2

Thus ends the second section of the first Anuvāka. His glorious self is that which is mounted upon it, namely this Āditya. Therefore, one should not cause the Gāyatra-stotra to fail, lest one be cut off from glory. This very [breath] is the Uktha; that which breathes out in front is the head of the Uktha; that which is on the right is the right wing; that which is on the left is the left wing; and that which is behind is the tail. This vital breath (prāṇa) is the self of the Uktha. He who knows this self of the Uktha as established within his own self, he indeed [attains] in yonder world...

He becomes complete with his limbs, whole in body, and entire in that world forever—namely, whatever of a person consists of the two testicles, the penis, the ears, the nostrils, and whatever is boneless, that does not remain incomplete. Now, he who thus knows this self of the *uktha* as established within himself, he indeed becomes complete with his limbs, whole in body, and entire in that world. This is the *vaiśvāmitra-uktha*; for "all" (*viśvam*) is food, and "friend" (*mitram*) is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Viśvāmitra attained it through toil and austerity.

By means of his practice of vows, he approached the beloved abode of Indra. Indra taught him this which has come down to human beings. He sat down near it [thinking], "This *uktha* is light. There are two syllables in "light" (*jyotiḥ*), two in "breath" (*prāṇaḥ*), and two in "food" (*anna*); thus, this is established in food alone. Then Jamadagni sat down near him [thinking], "This *uktha* is life-force (*āyuḥ*). There are two syllables in "life-force" (*āyuḥ*), two in "breath" (*prāṇaḥ*), and two in "food" (*anna*); thus, this is established in food alone.

Thus ends the third section in the first Anuvāka. This very Uktha is recited as sevenfold: the Stotriya, the Anurūpa, the Dhāyyā, the Pragātha, the Sūkta, the Nivid, and the Paridhānīyā. 1. This [earth] is the Stotriya; Agni is the Anurūpa; Vāyu is the Dhāyyā; the intermediate space (antarikṣa) is the Pragātha; the sky (dyu) is the Sūkta; Āditya is the Nivid—therefore the Bahvṛcas recite the Nivid after sunrise, for the Nivid is Āditya; and the quarters (diśas) are the Paridhānīyā. This is with respect to the deities (adhidevatam). 2. Now with respect to the self (adhyātmam): the Self (ātman) itself is the Stotriya; progeny (prajā) is the Anurūpa; the vital breath (prāṇa) is the Dhāyyā; the mind (manas) is the Pragātha; and the head (śiras) is the Sūkta.

"The eye is the *nivid*, the ear is the concluding verse (*paridhānīyā*). Regarding this, some conclude with a *triṣṭubh* verse, others with an *anuṣṭubh*; however, one should indeed conclude with a *triṣṭubh*. Regarding this, some recite these sacred utterances (*vyāhṛti*) after having uttered them: "The Great One was united with the Great; the God was united with the Goddess; the Brahman was united with the Brāhmaṇī. Because they were "united" (*samadhatta*), "united," so it is said. Therefore, even now, the limbs of a person are joined together, for this *uktha* is the person himself. "The Great One with the Great... [and so on].

"He united," [it is said]. Agni is indeed the great *niyama*, and the earth is the great (*mahī*); "the god united with the goddess"—Vāyu is indeed the god, and the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) is the goddess. "The Brahman united with the Brāhmaṇī"—Āditya is indeed the Brahman, and the sky (*dyau*) is the Brāhmaṇī. Of these very deities, for each pair of deities, nine syllables are obtained; thus these worlds become *triṇava*. That is indeed the threefold (*trivṛt*); having uttered that Brahman, they recite it. And this is indeed the *stoma*; it is the *anucara*.
That which they call "the single-stoma" is this very one who blows here; he is the deity with respect to the gods, and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) with respect to the self (*adhyātman*).
His body is his follower. Just as, indeed, a string of jewels might be strung upon a gem—thus ends the fourth section in the first chapter.

In this very manner, all this is woven together: the Gandharvas and Apsarases, cattle, and human beings. Now, Muñja Sāmaśravasa set out on his journey. Śvājanin Vaiśya came before him. As he was traveling, a lump of butter fell from the intermediate space onto his chest; taking it, he ate it. Thereupon, he beheld a Stoma spread out in the intermediate space, shining greatly, and he saw its application. Having sat down for the Bahiṣpavamāna, he said, "Let me breathe forth."

"One should draw in [the breath] while performing the action, and then exhale. One should desire to see with the eyes; one should desire to hear with the ears. This mind is joined by itself. Now, when an arrow is exceedingly sharp, it does not indeed strike [its target] from that [distance]; likewise, he would not reach this [deity]. Therefore, one should exhale while thinking, "I have reached him. Just as one might lead a deer by means of a decoy, even so does he lead him by means of this deity. He acts when joined; for he is indeed joined. Thus ends the fifth section in the first chapter; the first chapter is complete.

He who knows the bestowal of the *sāman*—to him indeed is it bestowed. "I give" (*dadā*)—thus does this Agni blaze; "So be it" (*tathā*)—thus does Vāyu blow; "Hearken! (*hanta*)—thus does the Moon; "Om"—thus does the Sun. This, indeed, is the bestowal of the *sāman*. Sudakṣiṇa Kṣaimi truly discovered this bestowal of the *sāman*. One should sing this at the *ājya* chant of either the Hotṛ or the Maitrāvaruṇa: "Tā dadā3 tathā3 hantā3 hiṃ bhā ovā. To him, indeed, is it bestowed.

He, too, surpasses many others who know this acquisition of the *sāman*. Now, he who knows the *sāman* as having kin where it is without kin—wherever they do not recognize him, wherever they are angry with him, or wherever they look upon him with contempt—even there he attains preeminence, lordship, food, and the position of a domestic priest. Agni, indeed, is the *sāman* without kin; for why do they churn him from two pieces of wood, or why do they produce him by turning around? It is for preeminence, for lordship, for food, and for the position of a domestic priest.

He is born. Indeed, wherever they do not even know one who knows thus, or where they are angry, or where they look with contempt—there he attains preeminence, lordship, food, and the position of the domestic priest.
Thus ends the first section of the second Anuvāka.

One should go there oneself where they know him. Sudakṣiṇa Kṣaimi, Prācīnaśāli, and Jābāla were indeed fellow-students. They used to recite many prayers and other texts together; Prācīnaśāli and Jābāla would do so, but Sudakṣiṇa Kṣaimi would always ask only about that which was the essence of the sacrifice and well-understood. Consequently, being driven away, they wandered about reviling him, crying out, "Sudakṣiṇa Kṣaimi is a Śūdra, a bad reciter!"

Thus ends the second section of the second Anuvāka. His kinsmen were, as it were, tearful-faced, thinking, "He has gone over to one side or another. Now, whoever formerly used to engage in theological discourse (brahmavādya), they would think of him, "He has gone over to one side or another," and they would wait upon him as if he were dead. The charioteer said to him, "Venerable sir, why do you speak thus, saying that no good news has come from those two? He replied, "Yes. My teacher must go; let another [chariot] be harnessed. He mounted the chariot and drove off.

They used to wait for him, wondering, "Who is this? [Thinking,] "It is Sudakṣiṇa; surely he would not descend into this [sacrificial ground]; it must be he. Standing at the very top of the steps within the altar (antarvedi), he said, "Well now, Gṛhapati! He did not rise up after him. He said, "Do not rise after me; you are wearing a black antelope skin. The Kurus and Pañcālas understood this and said, "He indeed does not rise after him. Then his younger brother said to him, "Venerable sir, please rise after the Udgātṛ. Him—

He rose up from his seat. He said: "Truly, O Householder, a person is born thrice: first he is born from the father, then from the mother, and then from the sacrifice. Truly, he dies thrice as well. This refers to what is stated in the second Anuvāka, third Khaṇḍa: "When the father, having become semen, pours him into the womb..."

First, he dies. Indeed, the womb is like blind darkness; then he becomes either a drop of blood or a drop of water—what indeed does he become at that time? He who knows that deity whom he follows after being reborn from there, and that deity which carries him beyond death—he, as the Udgātṛ, carries himself beyond death. Now, when they initiate him for this rite, he dies a second time: they shave his hair and beard, they clip his nails, and they anoint his limbs.

He straightens his fingers; he sits wrapped and enveloped; he does not offer oblations, he does not sacrifice, and he does not approach a woman; he speaks non-human speech; indeed, at that time, he takes on the form of one who is dead. 5. He who knows that deity whom he then follows after becoming, and that deity which carries him beyond death—he, as the Udgātṛ, carries himself beyond death. 6. Now, when they place him, having departed from this world, upon the funeral pyre, that is his third death. He who knows that deity whom... [he then follows after becoming].

From there he follows after him; and that which carries him beyond death—that is the Udgātṛ who carries one beyond death. Having said this much, he mounted his chariot and drove away. His younger brother said to Jābāla as he was returning: "Sir, what kind of vulgar speech did you utter? You sought a ford with an elephant! He explained it to him: "How could I have spoken otherwise, O venerable sir? It is he who knows the carrying beyond death by means of the Sāman for the three deaths—he, the Udgātṛ, carries one beyond death. Thus ends the fourth section in the second chapter.

"Your father, indeed, O venerable one, considered him to be the Udgātṛ," he said. Now, the Prācīnaśālas knew this; however, they did not know of this man who had been chosen as their Udgātṛ. They said, "Run after Kaṇḍviya! and they ran after him. They made Kaṇḍviya the Udgātṛ and Prācīnaśāli the Brahman. Looking at him, he said, "In this way, this Brāhmaṇa has not been weary of vain talk; he does not seek us out even in the smallest degree. He indeed acted thus toward him. As for that which...

Or rather, it is the father who pours him as seed into the womb; for it is Āditya who pours him as seed into the womb. Death has power over him there. Furthermore, when the father pours him as seed into the womb, he indeed comes into being from that. For when the seed that has been poured is entered by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), then it comes into being. Moreover, when they initiate him with this [rite], it is Agni who pours him as seed into the womb. He...

Verily, he has power over death there; moreover, that *vaisarjanīyā* oblation which the Adhvaryu offers, he follows after it and becomes one with it, as do the *chandas* (metres). 7. Now, when they place him who has departed from this world upon the funeral pyre, the Moon indeed pours him out as seed into his own womb; and verily, he has power over death there for him. 8. Moreover, when they place him who has departed from this world upon the funeral pyre, he becomes one with those very waters which are used for sprinkling.

From that, it follows: the breath indeed is the waters, for the waters are the breath. Now, the Udgātṛ who knows this carries the sacrificer across Death, the Sun, by means of this syllable *om*: with *vāk* he carries him across Agni; with *hum*, Vāyu; and with *bhā*, the Moon. Indeed, by means of these deaths, the Udgātṛ—by means of this syllable *om*, by means of the breath, and by means of yonder Sun—carries both himself and the sacrificer across those very deaths. Regarding this, there is this verse: "He is the eldest among them, or indeed the youngest; he is their son, or indeed their father; he alone is one of them."

The god entered the mind; he was born first, even within the womb. (RV 10.121.1) Now, as for this verse that has been recited: "This very person who is covered within"—it is by means of this very syllable, by means of breath, and by means of yonder sun. Thus ends the fifth section in the second Anuvāka.

The second section is completed. Indeed, a person dies thrice and is born thrice. First, he dies when that which was emitted becomes a formed embryo; he then comes together with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and is born toward hope (*āśā*). Second, he dies when he undergoes consecration (*dīkṣā*); he then comes together with the meters (*chandāṃsi*) and is born toward the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Third, he dies when he actually dies; he then comes together with faith (*śraddhā*) and is born toward the world (*loka*). This threefold cycle is the *gāyatra*.

He sings with the first turn; he conquers this very world, and whatever is in this world, that he causes him to prosper through this vital breath (*prāṇa*), and he grants him that hope toward which he is born. 5. Then, with the second turn, he conquers this very intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), and whatever is in the intermediate space, that he causes him to prosper through these meters (*chandas*), and he grants him that sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) toward which he is born. 6. Then—

By means of the third [verse], he conquers this very world; and whatever there is in that world, he makes it prosper for him through this faith (śraddhā), with the same faith with which they place him into the fire, thinking, "He shall become equal to this. And he grants him this world which he is born to attain. Thus ends the first section of the third Anuvāka.

By means of these three repetitions, he indeed conquers these worlds, and he causes him to prosper with those beings whom he comes to attain. Now, therefore, concerning the *hiṅkāra* itself: Death follows him even while he is in the heavenly world with hunger. This *hiṅkāra* is indeed Śrī (Prosperity) and Prajāpati; for that which is the *hiṅkāra*, the Udgātṛ drives away death by means of that *hiṅkāra*, by means of Śrī and Prajāpati. He says, "Hum! Ma!"—that is to say, "Do not go further," as it were, toward the sacrificer. It is just as when one has been overcome by a superior.

Just as an evil person attacks, even so does Death, the Evil One, attack him. When he says "Mā," *mā* is indeed the moon; for this moon is indeed *mā-mā-saḥ* (month), therefore he says "Mā. He says it as if cryptically; and furthermore, because he says "Mā," and because he says "Mā"—these are three [meanings]—therefore one should say "Mā.
Thus ends the second section of the third lesson.

"Huṃ bhā"—this is for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); for spiritual luster, as it were, shines forth. 1. "Huṃ bo"—this is for one desiring cattle; for cattle low, as it were, with "bo. 2. "Huṃ bag"—this is for one desiring prosperity (*śrī*); for they barter for prosperity, as it were, with "bag. 3. "Huṃ bhā ovā"—this is merely a song sung to that same effect. 4. "One should sing while turning around as if toward something great," so said Nāka; "one becomes possessed of a large village and a large dwelling. That is just as if, having fixed a post, one were to go around it by this way or that way. 5. Regarding this, he (Nāka) also said:

Śāṭyāyani said: "For what purpose would one offer up a wooden post? This is merely a song; one should not pay heed to it. Thus [ends the discussion] regarding the *hiṅkāras*. Now, therefore, follows the *nidhana* itself: "Ovā"—these are two syllables. The end is indeed our *nidhana*; the end of the worlds is heaven, the summit of the radiant sun. With this syllable "Om," the Udgātṛ places that sacrificer at the end in the heavenly world. And indeed, he who climbs to the top of a tree without wings falls down from there; but—

Just as a bird that sits on the tip of a tree, or on the edge of a sword, or on the edge of a razor, does not fall from there, for it remains held fast by its two wings; even so, the Udgātṛ, having made the sacrificer’s wings [of light] with this syllable "Om," places him at the end in the heavenly world. Just as that bird sits fearless, even so he sits fearless in the heavenly world, and then he moves about. Indeed, these two syllables are the world of the gods and the world of men; and these two syllables are the sun and the moon.

The syllable *mā* is the sun, which is the world of the gods; the syllable *mā* is the moon, which is the world of men. "Om" is the sun, and "vāk" (speech) is the moon. With this syllable "Om," the Udgātṛ priest causes the sacrificer to go to the sun, the world of the gods.
Thus ends the third section in the third chapter.

When he has arrived, he asks him, "Who are you? If he does not declare himself by his name or his lineage, he says to him, "This Self of yours which has become mine—that is yours. When they have thus made him understand that Self, they draw away from him the *ṛtas* (truths) that were grasped by foot after foot; day and night seize his world. Therefore, one should declare to him: "Who am I? You are the *suvah* (heaven); you are the one who goes to heaven (*svaragāmin*). For Prajāpati is indeed "who" (*kaḥ*), and he who knows thus is indeed *suvah*. He is indeed [Prajāpati].

He goes to heaven. Then he says to him: "Who you are, that am I; who I am, that are you—come! He enters this very essence of good deeds. Whatever sacrifices men perform in this world and whatever good they do, their food rises upward and enters that moon, the world of men. Of that, this embryo, resembling a human being, comes into existence within the womb. Its food rises upward and flows toward the breasts.

When he is born, then his mother offers him her breast as food. Indeed, a man is not truly born so long as he does not sacrifice; it is through sacrifice alone that he is born, just as an egg is first hatched when it is split open. Then, the Udgātṛ who knows this causes the sacrificer to go to the world of the gods, the sun, by means of this syllable "Om. With the subsequent syllable "Vāk," he bestows upon him the moon, food, and imperishability. But for one whose Udgātṛ chants without knowing this, he does not indeed [attain these].

He causes him to go to the world of the gods and provides him with food. Just as an egg, scorched on one side, would lie without obtaining food, even so he, scorched, lies down without obtaining food. Therefore, one should cause only one who knows this to chant the *udgītha*; when called "O Udgātṛ!", one who knows this should respond. Thus ends the fifth section in the third chapter;
the third chapter is complete.

"Speech," said Indra, and he spoke this *uktha* to Viśvāmitra; that is what the Viśvāmitras worship as speech itself. Manu spoke the office of *brahman* to Vasiṣṭha; therefore they say, "The *brahman* must be one of the Vasiṣṭhas. Regarding this, they also say: "Only one who knows thus may be the *brahman*; for who indeed is worthy of being a Vasiṣṭha other than one who knows thus? Prajāpati desired to procreate. He performed austerity. He reflected: "Come now, let me create a foundation; then whatever offspring I shall produce will have this very thing as their foundation."

"Thinking, 'They will not move about without a foundation,' he generated this world, the intermediate world, and that world. Having generated these three worlds, he became exhausted. He brooded over them; from them, thus brooded upon, three pure essences (*śukra*) arose: Agni from the earth, Vāyu from the intermediate space, and Āditya from heaven. He brooded further over these pure essences; from them, thus brooded upon, three pure essences indeed arose: the *Ṛgveda* from Agni, the *Yajurveda* from Vāyu, and the *Sāmaveda* from Āditya."

From the Sun, he again heated those bright essences; from them, thus heated, three bright essences rose up: "Bhūḥ" from the Ṛgveda, "Bhuvaḥ" from the Yajurveda, and "Svaḥ" from the Sāmaveda. That indeed is the essence of the threefold knowledge. This entire world is just this much. Whoever knows this, his world becomes the same as the world of one who knows the threefold knowledge. Thus ends the first section in the fourth lesson.

This very wind that blows is indeed the sacrifice; speech and mind are its two tracks, for it moves along by means of both speech and mind. Of this sacrifice, the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, and the Udgātṛ prepare one track with speech; therefore they perform their duties with words. The Brahman alone prepares the other track with the mind; therefore he remains silent. If he were to speak while being praised or while the Śastra is being recited, he would thereby prepare that other track of his with speech as well. He...

Just as a man with one foot goes limping, or a chariot with one wheel rolls unsteadily, even so does the sacrifice go astray when it falters. Knowing this, a certain Brāhmaṇa said to another Brāhmaṇa who was sitting muttering while the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*) had been commenced: "These two have now fallen short by half of the sacrifice. Indeed, they had then fallen short by half of the sacrifice. Therefore, once the morning litany has been commenced, the *brahmán* priest should remain restrained in speech until the *vaṣaṭ*-call on the final verse of the concluding hymn (*aparidhānīyā*); for others [the other priests], [it is different].

For the sake of the non-interruption of the *stotra* and *śastra*, and for the sake of the *pavamāna* chants—just as a man with two feet does not fall into error, or as a chariot with two wheels rolling along does not fail, so now the sacrifice does not fall into error.
Thus ends the second section of the fourth chapter.

If that sacrifice should fail through a defect in the *ṛc*, they say, "Announce it to the Brahman priest"; if through a defect in the *yajus*, they say, "Announce it to the Brahman priest"; if through a defect in the *sāman*, they say, "Announce it to the Brahman priest"; and if through something unremembered, they say, "Announce to the Brahman priest, 'From where has this arisen? That Brahman priest, having gone out toward the east, should offer clarified butter into the fire with the *sruva* ladle, using these sacred utterances (*vyāhṛtis*): *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, *svaḥ*. These *vyāhṛtis* are indeed the universal expiations for all defects; just as, for example, [salt removes impurities].

One should join gold with gold, silver with silver, tin with tin, iron with iron, steel with steel, wood with wood, and leather with leather by means of glue; in this very same way, one who knows this heals all that is wrong. Regarding this they say: "They lead sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Adhvaryu, saying, 'He has offered for me,' 'He has grasped the cups for me'; to the Hotṛ, saying, 'He has recited for me,' 'He has performed the vaṣaṭ-call for me'; and to the Udgātṛ, saying, 'He has chanted for me. But what has the Brahman priest done, he who sits silently?"

"Let them lead the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the *samāvartin* together with the other officiating priests," he should say. "For he indeed possesses half of the sacrifice, since he carries half of the sacrifice. "In former times, they used to lead half of the sacrificial fees to the Brahman priest and half to the other officiating priests. Regarding this, there is this verse: "In me, I think, is all this world; in me are the worlds, in me the four quarters; in me, I think, is whatever blinks or moves; in me are all the waters and the plants. "In me, I think, is all this..."

"Everything beginning with the worlds"—in him who knows this, indeed, this entire world is dependent. (7) "In me are the worlds; in me are the four quarters"—in him who knows this, indeed, the worlds are [dependent], and in him who knows this, the four quarters are [dependent]. (8) "In me I perceive this that blinks and moves; in me are all waters and plants"—in him who knows this, indeed, this entire world is established. (9) Therefore, one should appoint only such a knower as the Brahman-priest; he alone, indeed, is the Brahman who knows thus. (10) 17. Thus ends the third section of the fourth chapter.

Alternatively, there are indeed consecratory formulas for the *stomabhāgas* themselves. (1) Now, some consecrate with the *stomabhāgas* alone; one should not do it in that way. (2) Some consecrate with the formula: "Impelled by the god Savitṛ, O Prastotṛ, seek speech for the gods! saying, "Savitṛ is the impeller of the gods; impelled by Savitṛ, we now consecrate this. One should not do it in that way either. (3) Some consecrate with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," saying, "This is indeed the threefold knowledge (*trayī vidyā*)."

"Let us consecrate this with the knowledge of the three Vedas," so they say; however, one should not do it in that way. One should simply consecrate it with "Om. Now, this is Vasiṣṭha’s consecration formula for the Ekastoma portion. With this very formula, Vasiṣṭha, desiring offspring, consecrated [the sacrifice], saying: "Impelled by the god Savitṛ, O Prastotṛ, seek speech from the gods! Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ Om! Thereupon, he indeed multiplied greatly through offspring and cattle. He himself [should perform] with that.

One should consecrate [the victim] with Vasiṣṭha’s formula for the Ekastomabhāgas; [if one does so], one is indeed multiplied manifold in offspring and cattle. However, this is the established rule: one should consecrate it with the words, "So be it. 7.18 Thus ends the fourth section in the fourth chapter.

Now, when he says, "Soma flows," or "Turn back," he grasps the thunderbolt with speech; by speech itself that thunderbolt of speech is seized, and by the truth of speech one is released from it. Therefore, one should respond with "Om" alone. The gods, by means of this triple knowledge (*trayi vidyā*), ascended straight up to the heavenly world. Fearing that humans might follow after them, they compressed the threefold Veda. While they were compressing it, they were unable to compress even a single syllable, namely this: "Om. This indeed—

Verily, the threefold knowledge (trayī vidyā) becomes full of sap for one who knows thus; it is indeed full of sap. Whatever victory he wins through that full and sap-filled threefold knowledge, and whatever prosperity he attains, he wins that victory and attains that prosperity—provided he knows this. This syllable, "Om," is indeed the foundation of the threefold knowledge. With "Om" the Hotṛ priest is established; with "Om" the Adhvaryu; with "Om" the Udgātṛ. This syllable is the triple-heaven of the Vedas; in this syllable, indeed, the officiating priests [are established].
"Having placed the sacrificer in the heavenly world, they carry him upward; therefore, one should respond with 'Om' alone.
This is the fifth section in the fourth chapter;
the fourth chapter is completed.

"You are a cave; you are a deity. Dwell near him who hates us and whom we hate. (1) "You are greatness; you are abundance; you are vastness; you are ruddy; you are the unfallen. (2) "O Earth, you are a deity; may I become great. You are prosperity; may I prosper. You are being; may I be. (3) "Those offspring of yours that have been assigned—I do not encompass them. I assign them to you. (4) "My name, my body, my foundation—these are mine in you. Do not take these away from me! Thus he spoke to this earth. (5)

"The earth greets him as he arrives, saying: 'This world is yours, O Blessed One; let this world be ours together. "What indeed have you in me? he asks. "Give that back to me," [the earth] replies. "What do you have in me? [he asks]. "My name, my body, my foundation—these are mine in you. Give those back to me," [he says]. Then this earth gives them back to him. She says to him: "Carry me away. "Toward what? "Toward Agni. He carries him toward that fire. He says to the fire: "You are the conqueror; may I be victorious. You are the winner of the world; may I win the world."

"May I conquer the world; may I eat food; may I be an eater of food"—he who knows thus becomes an eater of food. (10) "Thou art *bhūḥ*, thou art a god; may I become *bhūḥ*. Thou art prosperity (*ābhūti*); may I prosper (*ābhūyāsam*). Thou art being (*bhūti*); may I be. (11) "The offspring that have been assigned to thee—I do not encompass them. I assign them to thee. (12) "Austerity is mine, splendor is mine, food is mine, speech is mine—this [all] is mine in thee; do not take this away from me. Thus he spoke to Agni. (13) When he has returned in this very manner, Agni welcomes him: "This world is thine, O Venerable One; together [with it]. (14)

"This world is not [lost]," he said. "That which was indeed mine in you, give that back to me," he said. "What indeed is yours in me? "Austerity is mine, splendor is mine, food is mine, speech is mine;
that which is mine in you, give that back to me. Agni gives that back to him. He says to him, "Carry me forward.
Thus ends the first section in the fifth chapter.

"Whom do you fear? "Vāyu. He [the Wind] carries him toward Vāyu. He says to Vāyu: "When you were in the east, you were Indra as king; when you were in the south, you were Īśāna as king; when you were in the west, you were Varuṇa as king; when you were in the north, you were Soma as king; when you blew from above, you blew as Prajāpati. "You are a Vrātya, a singular Vrātya, unreleased. You have entered the opening of the gods. Your offspring are yours, your plants are yours, your waters are yours."

As it moves, they move after it. (1) "Thou art the earth, the god; may I become the earth. Thou art becoming; may I become. Thou art being; may I be. (2) "Those offspring which have been assigned to thee—I do not encompass them. I assign them to thee. (3) "In-breath and out-breath are mine; my sacred learning is mine. That [learning] of mine is in thee; do not take that away from me. Thus he spoke to Vāyu. (4) When he had arrived in that manner, Vāyu greeted him: "This world is thine, O venerable sir; this world is ours together. (5) "Whatever indeed is mine in thee," he said, "that indeed is mine. (6)

"Give it back to me again," he said. "What indeed is yours that is in me? "My out-breath and in-breath, my hearing—give those back to me. Vāyu gives them back to him. He says to him, "Carry me forward! "To what? "To the world of the intermediate space (antarikṣaloka). He carries him forward toward the world of the intermediate space. When he has arrived there, the world of the intermediate space welcomes him: "Welcome, venerable sir! This world is yours; let this world be ours in common. "Whatever indeed is mine that is in you, give that back to me again," he said. "What indeed is yours? [he asks].

"May it be in me"—this space is mine; that [space] of mine is in you; give that back to me. He gives that space, the intermediate world (antarikṣaloka), back to him. He says to him: "Carry me forward.
Thus ends the second section in the fifth lesson.

"To what destination? he asks. "To the quarters," they reply, and they carry him toward the quarters. When he has arrived there, the quarters greet him: "O Venerable One, this world is yours; let this world be common to us. He says, "That which indeed was mine among you, give that back to me. "What then is yours among us? they ask. "Hearing," he replies. Then the quarters give hearing back to him. He says to them, "Carry me forward. "To what destination? he asks. "To the world of day and night," they reply, and they carry him toward the world of day and night. Him—

In the same way, when day and night had returned, he greeted them, saying: "O Blessed Ones, this world is yours; let this world be ours together. (6) "What indeed is yours? they asked. "That which is mine from you two," he said. "That very thing has been given back to me," [they replied]. (7) "What then is yours from us two? he asked. "Immortality (*akṣiti*)," they said. Day and night gave that immortality back to him. (8) They said to him: "Carry us forward! (9) Thus ends the third section of the fifth chapter.

"To what [do you carry me]? "To the half-months. They carry him toward the half-months. When he has arrived there, the half-months greet him: "This world is yours, O Blessed One; let this world be common to us. "What indeed is mine among you? he says. "Give that back to me. "What then is yours among us? "These small joints; they are mine among you; join them back together for me. The half-months join those joints together for him again. He says to them: "Carry me forward. "To what? [he asks].

"Carry him for months," they said; so they carried him for months. As he thus arrived, the months greeted him, saying, "O Blessed One, this world is yours; let this world be ours together. He said, "That which was indeed mine among you, give that back to me. They asked, "What was it that was yours among us? [He replied,] "These thick joints; those were mine among you; join them back to me. The months joined those [joints] of his back together again.
He said to them, "Carry me forward! Thus ends the fourth section of the fifth chapter.

"To what do you carry me? "To the seasons," they replied. As he arrived, the seasons greeted him: "Welcome, O Blessed One! This world is yours; let this world be ours together. "What indeed is yours among us? he asked. "Give that back to me," he said. "What do you have among us? [they asked]. "These superior joints; those are mine among you. Reunite them with me," he said. The seasons reunite those for him once more. He said to them, "Carry me forth. "To what? "To the year," he replied. As he arrived...

They carry him forth for a year. When he has returned in that same manner, the Year greets him: "O Venerable One, this world is yours; let this world be ours in common. "What indeed do you have in me? [the Year asks]. "Give that back to me," [he replies]. "What indeed do you have in me? [the Year asks]. "This is my Self (ātman); give that to me in you; give it back to me," [he says]. The Year gives that Self back to him. He says to it: "Carry me forth! Thus ends the fifth section in the fifth chapter.

"Whither? "To the divine Gandharvas. He carries him toward the divine Gandharvas. When he has arrived there, the divine Gandharvas welcome him, saying, "Welcome, O Blessed One! This world is yours; this world is ours in common. "What indeed is mine among you? he asks. "Give that back to me," they reply. "What do you have among us? "Fragrance is mine, joy is mine, and delight is mine. Give those back to me. Then the divine Gandharvas give them back to him. He says to them: "Lead me forth..."

"Carry me away! he says. "To what? "To the Apsarases," he replies. The Apsarases carry him away. When he has arrived there, the Apsarases greet him: "Welcome, O venerable one! This world is yours; let this world be shared by us. "What indeed do you have among yourselves? they ask. "Give that back to me," he replies. "What do you have among us? they ask. "My laughter, my play, my union—give those back to me," he says. The Apsarases give those back to him. He says to them, "Carry me away. Thus ends the sixth section of the fifth chapter.

"To what [do you wish to go]? "To heaven," he says. They carry him toward heaven. Heaven greets him as he arrives in that very manner, saying, "O Venerable One, this world is yours; let this world be ours together. "What indeed is it that is in me? he asks. "That indeed, give back to me," he replies. "What indeed is it that is in you? "Satisfaction," she says. For she is indeed satisfied once and for all; thus, heaven gives satisfaction back to him. He says to her, "Carry me forth. "To what? "To the gods," he says. They carry him toward the gods. The gods [greet] him as he arrives in that very manner.

"The world here rejoices, saying: 'O Blessed One, this world is yours; let it be ours as well. "Whatever indeed you have among us," he said, "give that back to me. "What do you have among us? they asked. "Immortality. Then the gods give immortality back to him. He said to them: "Carry me forward!
Thus ends the seventh section of the fifth chapter.

"What do you fear? "The sun. They lead him toward that sun. He says to the sun: "Thou art pervasive in the east; thou art united in the west. Thou art united; thou art favorable to men. The seer who is wrathful against the wrathful slays evil. He becomes one whose evil has been struck away, he who knows thee thus. (1) "Thou art the earth; may I become the earth. Thou art prosperity; may I become prosperous. Thou art being; may I become. (2) "The offspring that have been assigned to thee—I do not encompass them. I assign them to thee. (3) "Vigor for me! Strength for me! (4)

"The eye is mine; that [eye] of mine is in you; do not take that away from me," he said to the sun. When he had returned in that very manner, the sun greeted him: "This world is yours, O venerable one; this world is ours together. "That which indeed is in you, give that back to me," he said. "What indeed is in me? [the sun asked]. "Vitality, strength, and the eye—those are mine; they are in you; give them back to me. The sun gave those back to him. He said to him, "Carry me forward. "Toward what? "Toward the moon. He [carried him] toward the moon.

He carries [the oblation] for a month; he is Candra (the Moon). "The path of truth does not abandon you; the path of immortality does not abandon you. (10) "Being born, you become ever new. O Brāhmaṇa named Bhara, you worship me. Therefore, both gods and men bring food to you as a true one. He who knows you thus becomes an eater of food. (11) "Bhūḥ! You are a god; may I become. You are prosperity; may I prosper. You are being; may I be. (12) "The offspring that have been assigned to you—I am not yours. (13)

"I know them; I point them out to you. "My mind, my semen, my offspring, and my renewed being—those are mine; do not take them away from me," he said to the moon. The moon welcomed him as he approached in that very manner, saying, "This world is yours, O Venerable One; let this world be shared by us both. "What indeed have you in me? [the moon asked]. "That which is mine, give that back to me," he replied. "And what indeed is yours in me? [the moon asked]. "My mind, my semen, my offspring, and my renewed being—those are mine; those are in you; do not take them away from me," he said.
"Give it back to me," he says; then the Moon gives it back to him. He says to him, "Carry me.
Thus ends the eighth section in the fifth chapter.

"To what [world]? "To the world of Brahman. He carries him toward the sun. He says to the sun, "Carry me forward. "To what? "To the world of Brahman. He carries him toward the moon. In this way, he moves along with these two deities. This is the end; there is no further carrying beyond this. Whatever worlds we have mentioned here as being in front, all those are attained by him, they are conquered, and for one who knows thus, there is freedom of movement in all of them. If he should so desire—

Furthermore, thinking "May I be born here again," in whichever family he might desire to be born—whether in a Brāhmaṇa family or in a royal family—in that very one he is born. He goes forth, ascending again to this world, knowing it. Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said: "This world is indeed widely scattered and manifold. For the sake of this [world], people either speak or exert themselves. Who would cast this away and come back again? One should remain right here.
Thus ends the ninth section of the fifth chapter.

The fifth section is completed. Uccaiḥśravas Kaupayeya was a king of the Kauravyas. Keśī Dārbhya, a king of the Pañcālas, was his sister’s son. They lived together as mutual favorites. 1. That Uccaiḥśravas Kaupayeya departed from this world. When he had passed away, Keśī Dārbhya went out hunting in the forest, desiring to remove his unpleasantness [by forgetting him]. 2. As he was thus wandering about, pursuing deer, he came upon Uccaiḥśravas Kaupayeya in the midst of it. 3. He said to him, "I am arrogant."

"Do not be conceited, thinking 'I know myself,'" he said. "Do you know who I am? I am that very one whom you think me to be. Then [Nārada] said, "And as for what they say, sir: 'He who manifests himself, others enter his world'—how was it possible for you to manifest yourself to me? "Om," he replied. "When I had found the guardian of that world, then I manifested myself to you, thinking: 'I shall remove what is displeasing to him, and I shall instruct him. "So be it, sir," Nārada said. "May I now embrace you?"

As one might pass through smoke, wind, space, the flame of a fire, or water, so indeed does he pass through him; he does not perceive him as something to be embraced. 7.29 Thus ends the first section in the sixth chapter.

He said, "That form which you had before—that is indeed your form; however, I do not perceive it for the sake of embracing you. "Yes," he replied, "there was a Brahmin who, knowing the *sāman*, sang the *udgītha* for me. He struck down my bodies with his bodiless self. For it is said that when one who knows the *sāman* sings the *udgītha* for someone, he causes them to go to the same world as the deities. "Pataṅga Prājāpatya," he said, "was the beloved son of Prajāpati. He taught this *sāman* to him, and by means of it—"

"The seers sang it forth," he said, "for these seers have shaken off their bodies. "No," Prajāpati replied, "the gods sang it forth; these gods above have shaken off their bodies. He instructed him in that Sāman; having instructed him, he said: "Whoever knows this Sāman, let him indeed sing the Udgītha for you. Having been thus instructed, he returned and wandered about among the Brahmins of the Kurus and Pañcālas, questioning them. Thus ends the second section of the sixth chapter.

"I am about to perform the twelve-day sacrifice with the *vyūḍha-chandas* arrangement. Whoever among you knows that *sāman* which I know—he shall be my *udgātṛ*. Examine yourselves. 1. Not one of those who were examining themselves could give him a satisfactory answer. 2. Wandering in that very state, he ran up to one lying on a mat in a cemetery or in a forest; as he was fleeing, the other abandoned him. 3. He said to him, "Who are you? "I am a Brāhmaṇa, Prātṛda Bhālla," he replied. 4. "What then..."

"Do you know that Sāman? "I do," he said. "I am about to perform the twelve-day sacrifice with its meters arranged in a specific order (*vyūḍha-chandas*). If you know that Sāman which I know, then you alone shall chant the *udgītha* for me; consider it well. As he was considering it, he replied to him exactly as before. He said to him, "This man here shall chant the *udgītha* for me. Then the Brahmins of the Kurus and Pañcālas, being envious, said to him: "While these members of our own family are present, he will chant the *udgītha*? How can he be capable of this? "He is indeed capable."
"Indeed, she said to me, 'She is sufficient for me, she is enough for me'; it was she alone who sang the *ujjaga* for him.
Therefore, they cause it to be proclaimed: 'He has sung the *ālāla*.
6.3.10. This is the third section in the sixth chapter.

Regarding this, the followers of Sātyakī say: "Whatever deity we worship, we assign only one form to that deity—a single form in a cow, a single form in a horse, a single form in an elephant, a single form in a human, and a single form in all beings; for this entire world is the form of that very deity. But this is merely one form, namely breath (*prāṇa*). For as long as one breathes with breath, so long does one possess form. That is what constitutes form. However, when the breath departs, one becomes like a useless log of wood.

No form whatsoever remains; its inner self is austerity (*tapas*). Therefore, for one who practices austerity, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) becomes hotter. The inner self of austerity is fire; it is explicitly defined, and therefore it burns. Now, with respect to the deities: this very deity is he who blows here (the wind). Within him are these waters; that is food. He is to be meditated upon as non-arid (*arūkṣa*). Because there are waters within him, he is non-arid. His inner self is austerity; therefore, as he blows, he blows hotter while shining forth. The inner self of austerity is...

Lightning is its *nirukta* (etymological manifestation); therefore, it too burns. These four *sāmans* are indeed breath, speech, mind, and tone. This very breath acts through speech, having the mind as its guide; its offspring are the tones. He who knows this becomes possessed of offspring. Thus ends the fourth section in the sixth chapter.

That which is Vāyu is indeed Prāṇa; that which is Agni is indeed Vāc; that which is the Moon is indeed Manas; and that which is Āditya is indeed Svara. Therefore, they say of this Āditya: "He goes as Svara. Now, he who worships those deities which are there above the gods—these are indeed of distant forms, difficult to reach, as if hard to attain—who knows whether he will reach them or not? But he who worships them with reference to the self (*adhyātma*) becomes one whose god is near (*antideva*). For these [deities] seem to decay from here; or rather, it is his [who worships them thus].

These [channels] waste away along with the life-breath (*prāṇa*) when the body decays; who indeed knows whether they reach [the heart] or not? But he who knows these two kinds [of channels] as becoming one—that one truly knows the *anuṣṭubh*, that one knows the *sāman*, that one knows the Self, that one knows Brahman. Regarding this they say: "From a span (*prādeśa*) below, these become one; for from there this breath (*prāṇa*), being celestial, moves higher and higher. But some say: "From four finger-breadths below, these become one; for from there..."

"Truly, this breath, being celestial, moves higher and higher. This is the turning-point of Brahman. He who knows this turning-point of Brahman—toward him turn back offspring and cattle; he reaches a full span of life. He who, knowing thus, having breathed out with the out-breath and breathed in with the in-breath, brings these two classes of deities into his own self by means of the mind and places them in his mouth—for him everything becomes attained, everything conquered. No desire whatsoever remains unfulfilled for him who knows thus. Thus ends the fifth section of the sixth chapter.

This is that pair: speech and breath are a pair, and the *Ṛk* and the *Sāman* are a pair; indeed, a pair is fourfold and productive. When he says, "The Soma is being purified," or "Turn back," they then utter the *hiṅ* sound together with speech, mind, breath, and tone; thus, by the *hiṅ* sound, a pair is formed. Together with speech, mind, breath, and tone, they reach the *nidhana*; thus, by the *nidhana*, a pair is formed. That is sevenfold; it is for us seven times.

The Udgātṛ brings forth both himself and the sacrificer from the body. For as the seed of one is, so does he become; whether it be the seed of a man, he becomes a man; if that of a cow, a cow; if that of a horse, a horse; if that of a wild animal, a wild animal—whatever the seed is, that indeed he becomes. Just as gold, when cast into the fire, becomes more and more beautiful, even so [he becomes] more and more beautiful.
He who knows this becomes himself more auspicious. This very thing is stated in a Rigvedic verse.
Thus ends the sixth section in the sixth chapter.

"The wise behold the Bird anointed by the magic power (*māyā*) of the Asura with their heart and mind; within the ocean the seers discern him; the ordainers seek his station in the rays. (RV 1.164.21) 1. "The Bird anointed": the Bird is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*), for he moves as if flying among these limbs; they call him the "Bird" because he looks down upon the chariot. 2. "By the magic power of the Asura": the mind (*manas*) is the Asura, for it delights (*ramate*) among the senses (*asu*); he is anointed by its magic power. 3. "The wise behold with the heart and mind": [they behold] with the heart alone.

Thus ends the seventh section of the sixth lesson. "The winged one (pataṅga) bears speech with his mind; the Gandharva spoke it within the womb; the seers guard that shining, celestial wisdom at the place of Eternal Order. "The winged one bears speech with his mind": the winged one is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa); he bears this speech with his mind. "The Gandharva spoke it within the womb": the Gandharva is indeed the vital breath, and the person (puruṣa) is the womb; he speaks this speech within the person. "That shining, celestial wisdom": [this refers to] the inspired thought (manīṣā).

"For this inspired thought (manīṣā) goes to heaven, which the sages (kavayaḥ) guard at the place of Truth (ṛta). Now, Truth is the mind; the sages are those who know thus. This very syllable "Om" is Truth. By means of that, when they investigate the Ṛg-veda, the Yajur-veda, and the Sāma-veda, they thereby guard it. Thus ends the eighth section of the sixth chapter.

"I saw the herdsman, never resting, moving hither and thither along his paths; clothing himself in convergent and divergent rays, he revolves repeatedly within the worlds. (1) "I saw the herdsman, never resting"—the herdsman is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*), for he protects all this world without ever resting. (2) "Moving hither and thither along his paths"—for those which are these vital breaths here and those rays yonder, by means of these he moves both hither and thither along his paths. (3) He clothes himself in convergent...

"Clad in those moving in all directions"—for he indeed clothes himself in these offspring, both those moving together and those moving apart. "He revolves within the worlds"—for he indeed revolves within these worlds. This very Indra is the Udgītha. When this Indra, as the Udgītha, approaches, nothing more is perceived of either the Udgātṛ or the Upagātṛs; from here alone he rises upward as the *svar* (the light/celestial), and he flickers above the head. He should know: "Indra has arrived; no trace of evil shall remain here."

In that [Sāman], not a single trace of evil remains. This is the *Abhrātṛvya* Sāman; indeed, Indra does not see any rival. Just as Indra does not see any rival, so too he who knows this, or for whom one knowing this sings the *udgītha*, does not see any rival.
Thus ends the ninth section of the sixth chapter;
the sixth chapter is complete.

Brahman created Prajāpati; he created him without eyes and without a mouth. As he lay there without eyes and without a mouth, Brahman entered him—the Puruṣya. Verily, Brahman is breath; it was breath that entered him. He arose as the progenitor of creatures, and the Rākṣasas pursued him. He protected himself by singing this very Sāman. Because he protected himself while singing, that is the "Gāyatra" nature of the Gāyatra. He who knows this is protected and is released from all evil. [Sing] unto him... for us.

They approached with the verse, "Sing forth, O men," which is worthy of being heard. Because they sang, "Sing forth, O men, for him," it became the *gāyatra*; therefore, this very [verse] should be used as the introductory hymn (*pratipad*). They sang sixteen syllables to the *pavamāna* [laud]: "O Indra, come toward the god; huṃ bhā kṣātā. The Brahman consists of sixteen parts (*kalā*); thus, the Brahman entered him part by part. This *gāyatra* consists of twenty-four syllables: the *prastāva* has eight syllables and the sung portion (*gīta*) has sixteen syllables; these amount to twenty-four.

Twenty-four half-months make a year; the year is the *sāman*. Those *ṛc*s, by means of their body (*śarīra*), followed death. That which has a body is reached by death; now, that which is bodiless is immortal. By means of its bodilessness, that *sāman* shook off the bodies. Thus ends the first section of the seventh chapter.

"Ovā3c ovā3c ovā3chum bhā ovā"—thus he sang sixteen syllables. For man consists of sixteen parts; by each part, he shook off his bodily constituents. He is this one whose evil has been struck away and whose body has been shaken off. While singing "tad ekam," he cast aside the covering; while singing "vṛṣā," he cast it aside. "Ā" means "he has covered"; "vāk" (speech) is that Brahman, that is this intermediate space, which is this wind that blows. "Hum" is the moon; "bhā" is the sun. Indeed, they say of this very syllable, "it shines" (*bhāti*), because of its creative power (*kratu*). Of this very [syllable], indeed...

This they call the cloud of this imperishable sacrifice; 4. this they call the whirlwind of this imperishable sacrifice; 5. this they call the bright radiance of this imperishable sacrifice; 6. this they call the bull of this imperishable sacrifice; 7. this they call the *darbha* grass of this imperishable sacrifice; 8. this they call that which shines of this imperishable sacrifice; 9. this they call the union of this imperishable sacrifice.
They say, "It comes into being. Whatever there is of "bhā" and "bhā," that is this couple, the Gāyatra. He who knows this is procreated through a couple.
Thus ends the second section in the seventh chapter.

This is that immortal Gāyatra; by means of this, indeed, Prajāpati attained immortality—by this the gods, by this the seers. Prajāpati told this Brahman to Parameṣṭhin Prājāpatya; Parameṣṭhin Prājāpatya told it to the god Savitṛ; the god Savitṛ told it to Agni; Agni told it to Indra; Indra told it to Kāśyapa; Kāśyapa told it to Ṛśyaśṛṅga Kāśyapa; Ṛśyaśṛṅga Kāśyapa told it to Devataras Śyāvasāyana Kāśyapa; Devataras Śyāvasāyana Kāśyapa [told it to his disciples].

From Kāśyapa Śruṣa Vāhneya, [it was received] by Kāśyapa Śruṣa Vāhneya; from Indra Daivāpa Śaunaka, [it was received] by Indra Daivāpa Śaunaka; from Dṛti Aindra, [it was received] by Dṛti Aindra; from Tiśa Śaunaka, [it was received] by Tiśa Śaunaka; from Puluṣa Prācīnayogya, [it was received] by Puluṣa Prācīnayogya; from Satyayajña Pauluṣi Prācīnayogya, [it was received] by Satyayajña Pauluṣi Prācīnayogya; from Somaśuṣma Sātyayajñi Prācīnayogya, [it was received] by Somaśuṣma Sātyayajñi Prācīnayogya.

Prācīnayogya [received it] from Hṛtsvāśaya Āllakeya; Hṛtsvāśaya Āllakeya from King Māhāvṛṣa; King Māhāvṛṣa from Janaśruta Kāṇḍviya; Janaśruta Kāṇḍviya from Sāyaka Jānaśruteya Kāṇḍviya; Sāyaka Jānaśruteya Kāṇḍviya from Nagarin Jānaśruteya Kāṇḍviya; Nagarin Jānaśruteya Kāṇḍviya from Śaṅga Śāṭyāyani Ātreya; Śaṅga Śāṭyāyani Ātreya from Rāma Krātujāteya Vaiyāghrapadya; Rāma Krātujāteya Vaiyāghrapadya [received it]. 2.40.

Thus ends the third section of the seventh chapter: [The lineage] from Śaṅkha Bābhravya to Śaṅkha Bābhravya; from Śaṅkha Bābhravya to Dakṣa Kātyāyani Ātreya; from Dakṣa Kātyāyani Ātreya to Kaṃsa Vāraki; from Kaṃsa Vāraki to Proṣṭhapāda Vārakya; from Proṣṭhapāda Vārakya to Kaṃsa Vārakya; from Kaṃsa Vārakya to Jayanta Vārakya; from Jayanta Vārakya to Kubera Vārakya; from Kubera Vārakya to Jayanta Vārakya; from Jayanta Vārakya to Janaśruta Vārakya; [and] from Janaśruta Vārakya to Janaśruta.
