Vārakya received it from Sudatta Pārāśarya; Sudatta Pārāśarya from Āṣāḍha Uttara Pārāśarya; Āṣāḍha Uttara Pārāśarya from Vipaścit Śakunimitra Pārāśarya; Vipaścit Śakunimitra Pārāśarya from Jayanta Pārāśarya; Jayanta Pārāśarya [received it] from Pārāśarya. 1.41 Thus ends the fourth section in the seventh lesson.

To Śyāmajayanta Lauhitya; Śyāmajayanta Lauhitya [gave it] to Palligupta Lauhitya; Palligupta Lauhitya [gave it] to Satyaśravas Lauhitya; Satyaśravas Lauhitya [gave it] to Kṛṣṇadhṛti Sātyaki; Kṛṣṇadhṛti Sātyaki [gave it] to Śyāmasujayanta Lauhitya; Śyāmasujayanta Lauhitya [gave it] to Kṛṣṇadatta Lauhitya; Kṛṣṇadatta Lauhitya [gave it] to Mitrabhūti Lauhitya; Mitrabhūti Lauhitya [gave it] to Śyāmajayanta Lauhitya.

Śyāmajayanta Lauhitya to Triveda Kṛṣṇarāta Lauhitya; Triveda Kṛṣṇarāta Lauhitya to Yaśasvin Jayanta Lauhitya; Yaśasvin Jayanta Lauhitya to Jayaka Lauhitya; Jayaka Lauhitya to Kṛṣṇarāta Lauhitya; Kṛṣṇarāta Lauhitya to Dakṣajayanta Lauhitya; Dakṣajayanta Lauhitya to Vipaścit Dṛḍhajayanta Lauhitya; Vipaścit Dṛḍhajayanta Lauhitya to Vaipaścita.

To Dārḍhajayanti, the son of Dṛḍhajayanta; to Lauhitya, the son of Vipaścit. To Dārḍhajayanti, the son of Dṛḍhajayanta; to Lauhitya, the son of Vipaścit; to Gupta, the son of Lauhitya. 1. This indeed is the immortal Gāyatra; and as for those other songs that have been sung—whatever they may be, whatever they may be.
2. 42. Thus ends the fifth section in the seventh chapter.
The seventh section is completed;
thus ends the third chapter.
Now begins the third chapter.

Verily, there is only one complete deity; all others are merely half-deities. This very one who blows here [the wind] is indeed the cups (grahas) of all the gods. He is called "Asta" by name; for they call the cups hereafter "asta. When the sun has gone to its setting (astam), it is as if it has gone to the cups (grahān); therefore, it is not whole, and it enters into this very one. The moon goes to its setting (astam); therefore, it is not whole, and it enters into this very one. The stars go to their setting (astam); therefore, they are not whole, and they enter into this very one.

Agni follows after him; therefore he is incomplete, and he enters into this very [breath]. Day follows it, and night follows it; therefore they two are incomplete, and they both enter into this very one. The quarters become confused and are no longer discerned during that night; therefore they are incomplete, and they enter into this very one. Parjanya rains and the cloud takes it up; therefore it is incomplete, and it enters into this very one. The waters waste away, likewise the herbs, and likewise the trees; therefore they are incomplete, and they all enter into this very one. Now, all this—

One attains the wind itself; therefore, the wind alone is *sāman*. 12. He who knows this is a knower of the *sāman*; he who knows thus knows the *sāman* in its entirety. 13. Now, with respect to the self (*adhyātma*): when one sleeps, one does not speak with speech; that [speech] indeed attains the vital breath (*prāṇa*). 14. One does not think with the mind; that [mind] indeed attains the vital breath. 15. One does not see with the eye; that [eye] indeed attains the vital breath. 16. One does not hear with the ear; that [ear] indeed attains the vital breath. 17. Since all this attains the vital breath, therefore the vital breath alone is *sāman*.

18. He indeed is a knower of the Sāman; he knows the Sāman in its entirety who knows it thus. 19. Now, when people say, "Alas, there is no wind today," it is this [breath] that rests within the person; being full, it remains perspiring. 20. Then, while they were serving food, a Brahmin approached Śaunaka Kāpeya and Abhipratārin Kākṣaseni. Thus ends the first section in the first chapter.

He begged of them both, but they did not grant it, thinking, "Who is he? Who is he? Then he approached them with this verse: "The one God among the four great ones—who has swallowed him, the guardian of the world? O Kāpeya, some do not know him; O Abhipratārin, he is entered into many forms. Abhipratārin said, "Enter into this man and answer; or rather, let him answer after having been addressed by you. He then replied to him: "He is the self of the gods and of mortals, like the son of the golden-toothed Rapa."

"They say his greatness is great, for he, being himself un-eaten, eats the eater" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.6). "The four of the Great Self are one God" (ibid. 1.4.11). Agni is speech; he is the Great Self, the God. When he sleeps, the breath swallows speech. 5. The moon is the mind; he is the Great Self, the God. When he sleeps, the breath swallows the mind. 6. The sun is the eye; he is the Great Self, the God. When he sleeps, the breath swallows the eye. 7. The quarters are the ear; they are the Great Selves, the Gods. When he sleeps...

The vital breath swallows that ear. That which is expressed by "the one god [swallows] the four of the Great Self"—this indeed is that. "Who swallows him? Prajāpati is indeed "Who"; he has swallowed this. "The guardian of the world"—he is truly the guardian of the world. "O Kāpeya, they do not know him as 'the one'"—for they do not know him as the one. "O Abhipratārin, he is established in many ways"—for he is indeed established in many ways, namely as the vital breath. "The self of the gods and of mortals"—for he is indeed the self.

"Of gods and of mortals" (14). "He with golden teeth, like the son of Rapas"—for he is not a son; though he has the form of a son, he is not a son (15). "They speak of his greatness as great"—for they indeed speak of his greatness as great (16). "While being uneaten, he eats him who does not eat"—for he, while being uneaten, eats him who does not eat (17). 2. Thus ends the second section in the first chapter.

His glorious self is this very sun that has risen; therefore, one should not desire to inhale during the Gāyatra-stotra, lest he be cut off from glory. This very [sun] is the Uktha: when it breathes out in front, that is the head of the Uktha; what is on the right is the right wing; what is on the left is the left wing; and what is behind is the tail. This vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed the self of the Uktha. He who knows this self of the Uktha as established within his own self, he [truly exists] in yonder world.

He indeed comes into being in that world with his limbs, his body, and everything complete—namely, whatever belongs to a person: the two testicles, the penis, the ears, the nostrils, and whatever is boneless; nothing fails to come into being. Now, he who thus knows this self of the *uktha* as established within himself—he indeed comes into being in that world with his limbs, his body, and everything complete. This is the *vaiśvāmitra-uktha*; "all" (*viśva*) is food, and "friend" (*mitra*) is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Viśvāmitra attained it through toil, austerity, and the observance of vows, [and so did] Indra.

He went to his beloved abode. He then proclaimed to him that which has come down to human beings. He sat down near it, thinking, "This light is the Uktha. There are two syllables in "light" (*jyotiḥ*), two in "breath" (*prāṇaḥ*), and two in "food" (*anna*); thus, this [Uktha] is established upon food alone. Then Jamadagni sat down near him, saying, "Life-span (*āyuḥ*) is the Uktha. There are two syllables in "life-span," two in "breath," and two in "food"; thus, this [Uktha] is established upon food alone. Then Vasiṣṭha...

"The cow sat down with this *uktha*," he said; that is indeed food, for the cow is food. 13 Regarding this, they ask: "If the human body belongs to this vital breath (*prāṇa*), then by what means do the other vital breaths possess bodies? 14 He should reply: "That which one speaks with speech—that is the body of speech. That which one thinks with the mind—that is the body of the mind. That which one sees with the eye—that is the body of the eye. That which one hears with the ear—that is the body of the ear. In this way, the other vital breaths possess bodies. 15 Thus ends the third section in the first chapter.

This sevenfold *uktha* is recited: the *stotriya*, the *anurūpa*, the *dhāyyā*, the *pragātha*, the *sūkta*, the *nivit*, and the *paridhānīyā*. This [earth] is the *stotriya*; Agni is the *anurūpa*; Vāyu is the *dhāyyā*; the intermediate space is the *pragātha*; the sky is the *sūkta*; Āditya is the *nivit*—therefore the Bahvṛcas recite the *nivit* after sunrise, for the *nivit* is Āditya; and the quarters are the *paridhānīyā*. This is with respect to the deities (*adhidevatam*). Now with respect to the self (*adhyātmam*): the Self (*ātman*) is the *stotriya*; progeny is the *anurūpa*; the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the *dhāyyā*; the mind (*manas*) is the *pragātha*; and the head is the *sūkta*.

The eye is the *nivid*, the ear is the concluding verse (*paridhānīyā*). Regarding this, some conclude with a *triṣṭubh* verse, others with an *anuṣṭubh* verse; however, one should indeed conclude with a *triṣṭubh*. Regarding this, some recite these sacred utterances (*vyāhṛti*) after having uttered them: "The Great One was united with the Great; the God was united with the Goddess; the Brahman was united with the Brāhmaṇī. As for why they say "he united, he united," it is because the limbs of a person are now joined together; for man is this *uktha*. "The Great One with the Great... [and so on].

"Samadhātta" (he placed together). "Agni indeed is the great one; the earth is the great one. "The god with the goddess he placed together"—Vāyu indeed is the god, the intermediate space is the goddess. "Brahman with the Brāhmaṇī he placed together"—Āditya indeed is the Brahman, the sky is the Brāhmaṇī. Of these very deities, for each pair of deities, nine syllables are obtained; thus these worlds become "three-nines" (triṇava). That is indeed the threefold Brahman; having uttered that Brahman, they recite. This indeed is the Stoma; it is the *anucara* (the following verse).
That which they call "the single-stoma" is this very wind that blows; this is the deity with respect to the gods, and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) with respect to the self.
His body is his follower. Just as, indeed, a string of jewels might be strung upon a gem.
Thus ends the fourth section in the first chapter.

In this very way, all this is woven together within it: the Gandharvas and Apsarases, cattle, and human beings. Now, Muñja Sāmaśravasa set out on his journey; Śvājani Vaiśya went along with him. As he was traveling, a lump of fresh butter fell from the intermediate space onto his chest. Taking it, he ate it. Then, indeed, he beheld a Stoma spread out in the intermediate space, appearing very beautiful; he saw its application: "Having sat down for the Bahiṣpavamāna, let one breathe out and in repeatedly."

"One should draw [the breath] in deeply, hold it, and then exhale. One should desire to see with the eyes; one should desire to hear with the ears. This [mind] is joined by oneself. Now, when an arrow is exceedingly sharp, it does not indeed strike [its target] from that [distance]. Likewise, this [breath] would not reach him [the deity]; therefore, one should exhale while thinking "pa. Just as one might lead a deer by means of a decoy, even so does one lead this [deity] by means of this deity. He acts when he is yoked; for he indeed is yoked. Thus ends the fifth section in the first chapter; the first chapter is complete.

He who knows the bestowal of the Sāman—for him it is indeed bestowed. "Dadā" (Give!)—thus does this Agni blaze; "Tathā" (So be it)—thus does Vāyu blow; "Hanta" (Come!)—thus does Candra; "Om"—thus does Āditya. This, indeed, is the bestowal of the Sāman. Sudakṣiṇa Kṣaimi truly knew this bestowal of the Sāman. One should sing this in the *ājya* chant of either the Hotṛ or the Maitrāvaruṇa: "Dadā3! Tathā3! Hantā3! Himbhā! Ovā! For to him it is indeed bestowed.

He, too, surpasses many others who rise above them—he who thus knows this bestowal of the *sāman*. And he who knows the *sāman* as having kin where it is without kin—wherever they do not recognize him, wherever they are angry with him, or wherever they look down upon him—even there he attains preeminence, lordship, food, and the office of the domestic priest. Agni, indeed, is the *sāman* without kin; for why do they churn him from the two fire-sticks, or why do they churn him after turning around? He is born for preeminence, for lordship, for food, and for the office of the domestic priest.

Wherever they do not recognize one who knows thus, or where they become angry, or where they look upon him with contempt—even there he attains preeminence, lordship, food, and the position of a priest. 8.6 Thus ends the first section in the second Anuvāka.

One should go of one's own accord to where they know him to be. Sudakṣiṇa Kṣaimi, Prācīnaśāli, and Jābāla were fellow students. They used to recite many prayers and other texts together; among them were Prācīnaśāli and Jābāla. Now, whenever Sudakṣiṇa Kṣaimi encountered anything beautiful or well-known regarding the sacrifice, he would invariably ask about it. But those others, being driven away, wandered about crying out; they cried out against Sudakṣiṇa Kṣaimi, saying, "He is a Śūdra, a bad reciter!"

Thus ends the second section of the second lesson. His kinsmen were, as it were, tearful-faced, thinking, "He has approached one of the two [extremes]. Now, whoever formerly engaged in theological discourse (brahmavādya), they used to think of him, "He has approached one of the two," and they used to worship him as if he were the Immortal itself. The charioteer said to him: "Sir, why do you speak thus, saying that no good comes from those two? He replied, "Yes; my teacher must be gone, or else something else is being driven. He mounted his chariot and drove off.

They used to wait for him, wondering, "Who is this? [Thinking], "It is Sudakṣiṇa; surely he would not descend here," they concluded, "It must be he. As he was standing on the steps at the edge of the sacrificial altar (antarvedi), he said, "O householder, have you understood? He did not rise to greet him. He said, "Do not fail to rise to me; you are wearing the black antelope skin. The Kurus and Pañcālas knew this, and they said, "He indeed does not rise to greet him. Then his younger brother said to him, "Sir, please rise to the Udgātṛ. Him—

He rose up from his seat. He said: "Truly, O Householder, a person is born thrice. First he is born from the father; then from the mother; then from the sacrifice. Indeed, he dies thrice. As for the statement, "When the father pours him as seed into the womb"—this was in the third section of the second Anuvāka.

First, he dies. Indeed, the womb is like blind darkness; at that time, he becomes either a drop of blood or a drop of water—for what indeed does he become then? He who knows that deity from whom he subsequently arises and that which carries him beyond death—he, as the Udgātṛ, carries himself beyond death. Now, when they initiate him for this [sacrifice], he dies a second time: they shave his hair and beard, they clip his nails, they anoint his limbs, and they straighten his fingers.

He sits withdrawn and enveloped; he does not offer oblations, he does not sacrifice, and he does not approach a woman. He speaks non-human speech; indeed, at that time he takes on the form of one who is dead. 4. He who knows that deity whom he follows from there, and that deity which carries him beyond death—he, as the Udgātṛ priest, carries himself beyond death. 5. Now, when they place him, having departed from this world, upon the funeral pyre, he dies for the third time. 6. He who knows that deity whom he follows from there...

"And he who carries him across that death—he, as the Udgātṛ, carries one across death. Having said this much, he mounted his chariot and drove off. Then his younger brother said to Jābāla, "Who are you, O Śūdra? Who spoke these words? You have sought a ford with an elephant! He then confessed to him: "How did you speak, venerable sir? [Jābāla replied: "He who knows the carrying across by means of the Sāman for the three deaths—he, as the Udgātṛ, carries one across death.
Thus ends the fourth section in the second Anuvāka.

"Your father, indeed, O venerable sir, considered him to be the Udgātṛ," he said. "The Prācīnaśālas knew this, for he was the one chosen as their Udgātṛ; however, they did not know him. They said, "Run after Kāṇḍvīya! and they ran after him. They made Kāṇḍvīya the Udgātṛ and Prācīnaśāli the Brahman. Looking at him, he said, "In this way, this Brāhmaṇa has not grown weary of empty talk; he does not seek the Sāman in its subtle form. He indeed surpassed him with that. As for what happened then...

Or rather, it is the father who pours him out as seed into the womb; for it is Āditya who pours him out as seed into the womb. Death has power over him at that point. Moreover, when the father pours him out as seed into the womb, he indeed comes into being from that. For when the seed that has been poured is entered by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), then it comes into being. Furthermore, when they initiate him with this rite, Agni indeed pours him out as seed into the womb; and he alone is his [master].

In that regard, he is subject to death there. Now, when the Adhvaryu offers this Vaisarjanīya oblation, it is from that very [oblation] that he comes into being again, as well as the *chandas* meters. 7. And when they place him, who has departed from this world, upon the funeral pyre, then the Moon indeed pours him out as seed into his womb; and he is indeed subject to death there. 8. Furthermore, when they place him, who has departed from this world, upon the funeral pyre, then those waters which are used for sprinkling—he [becomes] those very waters.

From that, he comes forth into breath alone; for water is indeed breath. Now, the Udgātṛ who knows this carries the sacrificer across Death, the Sun, by means of this syllable "Om": with "Vāk" (Speech) he carries him across Agni; with "Hum" he carries him across Vāyu; and with "Bhāḥ" he carries him across the Moon. By means of these very deaths, through the Sāman, the Udgātṛ carries both himself and the sacrificer across—by means of the syllable "Om," by means of breath, and by means of yonder Sun. Regarding this, there is this verse: "He is the eldest among them, or indeed the youngest; he is their son, or indeed their father; he is the one God."

"Having entered the mind, he was born in the beginning; he is indeed within the womb. (RV 4.27.1) Now, as for this verse being recited: it refers to this very person who is covered within, by means of this very syllable, by means of breath, and by means of that very Āditya.
Thus ends the fifth section in the second Anuvāka.

The second section is completed. Indeed, a person dies thrice and is born thrice. He dies for the first time when his seed is emitted and becomes an embryo; he then comes into being through the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and is born from hope (*āśā*). Then he dies for the second time when he undergoes consecration (*dīkṣā*); he then comes into being through the meters (*chandas*) and is born from the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Then he dies for the third time when he actually dies; he then comes into being through faith (*śraddhā*) and is born from the world (*loka*). Therefore, he sings this threefold *gāyatra* chant; of that—

By the first turning, he conquers this very world; whatever is in this world, that he makes prosperous for him by means of this vital breath (*prāṇa*) which he attains, and he grants him this hope which he is born to fulfill. Then, by the second turning, he conquers this very intermediate space (*antarikṣa*); whatever is in the intermediate space, that he makes prosperous for him by means of these meters (*chandas*) which he attains, and he grants him this sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) which he is born to receive. Then, by the third turning, he conquers yonder world; whatever is there...

And in that other world, he causes him to prosper through this very faith with which they place him into the fire, thinking, "He will come into being at the appointed time. And he grants him that world which he is born to attain.
Thus ends the first section of the third chapter.

By means of these three repetitions, he indeed conquers these worlds and endows him with those beings into which he enters. Now, therefore, concerning the *hiṅkāra*: Death follows him even while he is in the heavenly world with hunger. This *hiṅkāra* is indeed prosperity and Prajāpati within the Sāman; by means of that *hiṅkāra*, as prosperity and as Prajāpati, the Udgātṛ drives away death. He says, "Hum! Mā!"—this is not merely a measure, but rather it signifies, "Do not go where the sacrificer is. It is just as one who has been successfully assisted by a superior.

Just as an evil person attacks [another], even so does Death, the Evil One, attack him. When he says "Mā" (Do not), it means "O Moon," for this moon is indeed "Mā-māsa" (Month). Therefore he says "Mā. He says "Bhā" as if in secret; and furthermore, because he says "Mā," and because he says "Mā," these are three syllables. Therefore, one should say "Mā. Thus ends the second section of the third chapter.

"Humbhā"—this is for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), for spiritual luster, as it were, resounds. "Humbo"—this is for one desiring cattle; cattle, indeed, low "bo. "Humbag"—this is for one desiring prosperity (*śrī*); they call out for prosperity "bag. "Humbhā ovā"—this is merely a song sung in accompaniment. "One should sing while turning around as if toward something great," so said Nāka. "A great village and a great settlement come to be," he said. "It is just as if one were to drive a wedge into a stump and then go around it by this way or that way; such is that [performance]. Regarding this, moreover, he said:

Śāṭyāyani said: "For what purpose should one offer up a wooden post? This is merely a song; one should not pay heed to it. Thus far concerning the *hiṅkāra*s. Now, therefore, as for the *nidhana*: "Ovā"—these are two syllables. The *nidhana* is indeed the end of the *sāman*; the end of the worlds is heaven; the end is the summit of the radiant sun (*bradhna*). The Udgātṛ places that sacrificer, by means of this syllable "Om" at the end, in the heavenly world. For truly, he who climbs to the top of a tree without wings falls down from there; but—

Just as a bird that sits on the tip of a tree, or on the edge of a sword, or on the edge of a razor, does not fall from there—because it remains held fast by its two wings—even so the Udgātṛ, having made the sacrificer’s wings the heavenly world by means of this syllable "Om," places him at the end in the heavenly world. Just as the bird sits fearless, even so he sits fearless in the heavenly world; then he moves about. These two syllables are indeed the world of the gods and the world of men; and these two syllables are the sun and the moon.

The *mā* is the sun, for it is the world of the gods; the *candramas* (moon) is the world of men. "Om" is the sun, and "vāk" (speech) is the moon. 12. Thus, with this syllable "Om," the Udgātṛ priest causes the sacrificer to go to the sun, the world of the gods. 13. Thus ends the third section in the third chapter.

When he has arrived, he asks him, "Who are you? He replies with his name or his lineage. He says to him, "This Self of mine which has become yours—this is that [Self] of yours. When they have thus attained that Self, the Seasons, having seized it by means of the sacrificial formulas (*ṛc*), pull it away from the noble station. Day and Night seize his world. Therefore, one should answer him with this: "Who am I? You are *suvah* (the good path). You are *svargya* (leading to heaven); go to heaven. For Prajāpati is indeed "Who" (*kaḥ*), and for one who knows thus, he is indeed *suvah*. He is indeed [Prajāpati].

He goes to heaven. Then he says to him: "Who you are, that am I; who I am, that are you. Come! He enters this very essence of good deeds. Whatever sacrifices men perform in this world and whatever good they do, their food rises upward; it enters that moon, which is the world of men. Within its belly, there arises this human-like embryo. Its food rises upward toward the breasts. When he is born, then for him—

The mother gives her breast, which provides food. Indeed, a man is as if unborn so long as he does not sacrifice; it is by means of the sacrifice that he is born, just as an egg is when first hatched. Then, the Udgātṛ who knows this causes the sacrificer to go to the world of the gods, the sun, by means of this syllable "Om. With the subsequent syllable "Vāk," he bestows upon him the moon, food, and imperishability. Now, if one who does not know this performs the Udgītha for him, he certainly does not cause him to go to the world of the gods, nor...

He causes him to prosper with food. Just as an egg, scorched and unable to obtain food, would lie there scorched and unable to obtain food, even so does he lie scorched and unable to obtain food. Therefore, one should indeed cause only one who knows this to chant the *udgītha*; when called "O Udgātṛ," such a knower should respond here on earth.
Thus ends the fifth section in the third chapter;
the third chapter is complete.

"Speech"—this, indeed, Indra told Viśvāmitra as the *uktha*; therefore, the Viśvāmitras worship speech alone as such. 1. Manu, indeed, told Vasiṣṭha the office of the *brahman* priest; therefore they say, "The *brahman* priest must be a descendant of Vasiṣṭha. 2. But regarding this they also say: "Only one who knows thus may be the *brahman* priest; for who is worthy of being a *vasiṣṭha* unless he knows thus? 3. Prajāpati desired to procreate. He performed austerity. He reflected: "Come now, let me create a foundation; then whatever offspring I shall produce will have this very thing as their foundation."

"Thinking, 'They will not burn while moving without a foundation,' he generated this world, the intermediate world, and that world. Having generated these three worlds, he exerted himself over them. He brooded over them, and from them, thus brooded upon, three pure essences (*śukra*) arose: fire from the earth, wind from the intermediate space, and the sun from the sky. He brooded further over these pure essences, and from them, thus brooded upon, three more pure essences arose: the *Ṛgveda* from fire, the *Yajurveda* from wind, and the *Sāmaveda* from the sun."

From the Āditya [he drew them]. He heated these bright essences again; from them, thus heated, three bright essences rose up: "Bhūḥ" from the Ṛgveda, "Bhuvaḥ" from the Yajurveda, and "Svaḥ" from the Sāmaveda. That indeed is the same. This is indeed the bright essence of the threefold knowledge (trayī vidyā); this whole world is only so much. Verily, whatever world belongs to one who knows the threefold knowledge, that world becomes his who knows this. Thus ends the first section in the fourth lesson.

This very wind that blows is indeed the sacrifice; speech and mind are its two tracks, for it moves along by means of both speech and mind. Of this sacrifice, the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, and the Udgātṛ prepare one track with speech; therefore they perform their duties with words. The Brahman alone prepares the other track with the mind; therefore he remains silent. If he were to speak while being praised or while the Śastra is being recited, he would thereby prepare that other track of his with speech as well. He...

Just as a man goes with one foot faltering, or a chariot rolls with a single wheel, even so does the sacrifice go faltering at that time. A Brāhmaṇa who knew this once said to a Brahmán priest who was sitting and murmuring after the morning recitation (*prātaranuvāka*) had been commenced: "These two have now left half of the sacrifice behind. Indeed, they then left half of the sacrifice behind. Therefore, when the morning recitation has been commenced, the Brahmán priest should remain restrained in speech until the *vaṣaṭ*-call on the concluding verse (*aparidhānīyā*) for the others.

The *pavamāna* chants are for the sake of ensuring that the *stotra*s and *śastra*s do not come to a halt. Just as a man with two feet does not fall into error, or as a chariot with two wheels continues rolling, even so the sacrifice at this time does not fall into error.
Thus ends the second section of the fourth chapter.

"If the sacrifice should fail through the *ṛc*, they say, 'Announce it to the Brahman'; if it should fail through the *yajus*, they say, 'Announce it to the Brahman'; if it should fail through the *sāman*, they say, 'Announce it to the Brahman'; and if it should fail from something unremembered, they say, 'Announce to the Brahman: "From where has this arisen? Then that Brahman, having gone out toward the east, should offer clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle into the *āgnīdhra* fire using these *vyāhṛtis*: "Bhūr! Bhuvaḥ! Svaḥ! These *vyāhṛtis* are indeed the universal expiations (*sarvaprāyaścitta*). It is just as if, for example, with salt...

One should join gold with gold, silver with silver, tin with tin, iron with iron, steel with steel, wood with wood, and leather with leather by means of glue; in this very same way, one who knows this heals everything. Regarding this they say: "They lead sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Adhvaryu, saying, 'He has sacrificed for me,' 'He has grasped the cups for me'; to the Hotṛ, saying, 'He has recited for me,' 'He has performed the vaṣaṭ-call for me'; and to the Udgātṛ, saying, 'He has chanted for me. But what has the Brahman priest done, he who sits silently?"

"Let them lead the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) with the other priests equally," he [the sacrificer] should say. He should reply: "He indeed possesses half of the sacrifice, for he carries half of the sacrifice. "In former times, they used to lead half of the sacrificial fees to the Brahman priest and half to the other priests. Regarding this, there is this verse: "In me I believe all these worlds originate; in me the worlds, in me the four quarters; in me I believe whatever blinks and whatever moves; in me are all the waters and the plants. "In me I believe all these worlds originate."

"Everything"—indeed, this entire world is dependent upon one who knows thus. "In me are the worlds; in me are the four quarters"—in one who knows thus, indeed, the worlds are truly established, and in one who knows thus, the four quarters are truly established. "In me I believe all this that moves, even the twinkling of an eye; in me are the waters and all the plants"—in one who knows thus, indeed, this entire world is established. Therefore, one should appoint only such a person as the Brahman priest; he alone, indeed, is the true Brahman priest who knows thus. Thus ends the third section of the fourth chapter.

Alternatively, these are the consecratory formulas for the *stomabhāgas* themselves. Regarding this, some consecrate with the *stomabhāgas* alone; one should not do so. Some consecrate with the formula: "Impelled by the god Savitṛ, O Prastotṛ, utter speech to the gods," saying, "Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; impelled by Savitṛ, we now consecrate this. One should not do so either. Some consecrate with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," saying, "This is indeed the threefold knowledge (*trayī vidyā*)."

"Let us consecrate this with the knowledge of the three Vedas," so they say; however, one should not do it in that way. One should simply consecrate it with "Om. Now, this is Vasiṣṭha’s consecration formula for the *ekastoma* (single-stoma) portion. With this very formula, Vasiṣṭha, desiring offspring, consecrated himself: "Impelled by the god Savitṛ, O Prastotṛ, seek speech from the gods! Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ Om! Thereupon, he indeed multiplied greatly through offspring and cattle. He [should act] in the same way with that.

One should consecrate [the sacrificer] with Vasiṣṭha’s formula for the Ekastomabhāgas; [for it is said,] "He is indeed multiplied with offspring and cattle. However, this is the settled rule: one should consecrate him with the words, "So be it" (iti). 7.18 Thus ends the fourth section in the fourth chapter.

Now, when he says, "Soma is being purified," or "Turn back," he wields the thunderbolt of speech; by speech itself that thunderbolt of speech is grasped, and by the truth of speech one is released from it. Therefore, one should respond with "Om" alone. By means of this threefold knowledge, the gods ascended straight up to the heavenly world. Fearing that humans might follow after them, they compressed the three Vedas. While they were compressing it, they were unable to compress even a single syllable, namely this "Om. This indeed—

Verily, the threefold knowledge (*trayī vidyā*) becomes full of sap for one who knows thus; it is indeed full of sap. Whatever victory he wins and whatever prosperity he attains through that full and sap-filled threefold knowledge, that victory he wins and that prosperity he attains—whosoever knows this. This syllable, "Om," is indeed the foundation of the threefold knowledge. With "Om," the Hotṛ priest is established; with "Om," the Adhvaryu; with "Om," the Udgātṛ. This syllable is the triple-heaven of the Vedas; in this syllable, indeed, the officiating priests [are established].
"Having placed the sacrificer in the heavenly world, they carry him upward; therefore, one should respond with 'Om' alone.
Thus ends the fifth section of the fourth chapter;
the fourth chapter is completed.

"You are a cave; you are a deity; you are a dwelling-place. Envelop him who hates us and whom we hate. (1) You are greatness; you are abundance; you are vastness; you are the ruddy one; you are the unfallen one. (2) You are the god of becoming; may I become. You are prosperity; may I prosper. You are being; may I be. (3) Those offspring of yours that have been assigned—I do not encompass them. I assign them to you. (4) My name, my body, my foundation—these are mine; let them not be taken away from me in you. Thus he spoke to this earth. (5)

"The earth welcomes him as he arrives, saying: 'O Blessed One, this world is yours; let this world be ours together. "What indeed have you in me? [he asks. "Give back to me that which was indeed in me," [the other replies. "What do you have in me? [he asks. "My name, my body, and my foundation—give those back to me in me," [the other replies. Then this earth gives these back to him. He says to her: "Carry me forward. "Toward what? "Toward Agni. He carries him forward toward that Agni. He says to Agni: "You are victorious; may I be victorious. You are the conqueror of the world; may I be the conqueror of the world."

"May I conquer the world; may I eat food; may I be an eater of food—he who knows thus becomes so. (10) "You are the arising god; may I arise. You are prosperity; may I prosper. You are being; may I be. (11) "The offspring that have been assigned to you—I do not master them. I assign them to you. (12) "Austerity is mine, splendor is mine, food is mine, speech is mine—this [all] is mine in you; do not take this away from me," he said to Agni. (13) Agni welcomes him when he has returned in this very manner: "This world is yours, O venerable one; let this be ours together. (14)
"World! [he says]. "That which indeed was mine in you, give that back to me," he said. "What indeed is yours in me? "Austerity is mine, splendor is mine, food is mine, speech is mine;
that which is mine in you, give that back to me. Agni gives that back to him. He says to him, "Carry me forward.
Thus ends the first section in the fifth chapter.

"Whom do you fear? "Vāyu. He then drives toward Vāyu. He says to Vāyu: "When you were in the east, you were Indra as king; when you were in the south, you were Īśāna as king; when you were in the west, you were Varuṇa as king; when you were in the north, you were Soma as king; when you blew from above, you blew as Prajāpati. You are a Vrātya, a singular Vrātya, unreleased; you have entered the mouth of the gods. Your offspring, your plants, and your waters follow after you as you move."

4. "Sambhūḥ art thou, O Deva; may I become sambhūḥ. Ābhūḥ art thou; may I become ābhūḥ. Sambhūtiḥ art thou; may I become sambhūtiḥ. 5. "Those offspring which have been assigned to thee—I do not master them. I assign them to thee. 6. He said to Vāyu: "Out-breath and in-breath are mine; hearing is mine; that [hearing] of mine is in thee; do not take that away from me. 7. When he had come back in this manner, Vāyu greeted him: "This world is thine, O Blessed One; let this world be ours in common. 8. "Whatever indeed is in thee," [Naciketas] said, "give that back to me. 9. "What indeed is in me? [Vāyu asked.]

"May my out-breath and in-breath be restored to me; may my hearing be restored to me; that which is mine, restore it to me. Vāyu restores that to him. He says to him, "Carry me forward. "Toward what? "Toward the world of the intermediate space (antarikṣaloka). He carries him forward toward that world of the intermediate space. When he has arrived there, the world of the intermediate space welcomes him: "O venerable sir, this is your world; let this world be common to us both. "That which was indeed mine in you," he says, "restore that indeed to me. "What then is yours in me? "This space (ākāśa) here is mine in you."
"Give that back to me," he says; then the intermediate space, the world of the atmosphere, gives it back to him. He says to it: "Carry me forward.
Thus ends the second section in the fifth lesson.

"To what do you direct me? he asks. They carry him toward the quarters. When he has arrived there, the quarters greet him: "O Venerable One, this world is yours; let this world be ours together. "What indeed have you given to me among yourselves? he says. "Give that back to me," they reply. "What then have you [given] to us? he asks. "The sense of hearing," they say. Then the quarters give the sense of hearing back to him. He says to them, "Carry me forward. "To what? he asks. "To the world of day and night," they say. They carry him toward the world of day and night. Him—

In the same way, when day and night returned, he greeted them, saying: "O Blessed Ones, this world of yours is ours as well. They said, "That which was indeed ours, [you took]; he replied, "That very thing has been given back to me. They asked, "What then is ours from us two? He said, "Immortality. Day and night gave that immortality back to him. He said to them, "Carry me forward.
Thus ends the third section of the fifth chapter.

"To where? "To the half-months. They carry him toward the half-months. When he has arrived there, the half-months greet him: "Welcome, O Venerable One! This world is yours; this world is ours in common. "What indeed is mine among you? he asks. "Give that back to me," they reply. "What then is yours among us? he asks. "These small joints; those are yours among us; join them back for me," they say. The half-months join those [joints] back for him. He says to them, "Carry me forward. "To where? he asks.

"Carry me for the months," he said; "the months carry him forth for those months. The months welcome him as he arrives, saying, "O Blessed One, this world is yours; let this world be ours together. "Whatever indeed you have taken from me," he said, "give that back to me. "What indeed have you taken from us? [they replied]. "These thick joints; they were in you; join them back to me.
The months join those [joints] back to him again. He says to them, "Carry me forward!
Thus ends the fourth section in the fifth chapter.

"Whither? "To the seasons. They carry him toward the seasons. When he has arrived there, the seasons welcome him: "This world is yours, O venerable one; let this world be common to us. "What indeed do you have that is in me? Give that back to me," he says. "What indeed is yours in us? "These superior joints; they are in you; restore them to me. The seasons restore those [joints] to him. He says to them, "Carry me forward. "Whither? "To the year. They carry him toward the year.

They carry him forth for a year. When he has returned in that very manner, the Year greets him: "O Venerable One, this world is yours; let this world be ours in common. "What indeed do you have in me? [the Year asks]. "Give that back to me," [he replies]. "What indeed do you have in me? [the Year asks]. "This Self (ātman) is mine; give that to me," [he replies]. The Year gives that Self back to him. He says to it: "Carry me forth. Thus ends the fifth section in the fifth chapter.

"To what [world] do you wish to go? "To the divine Gandharvas. He is carried toward the divine Gandharvas. When he has arrived there, the divine Gandharvas greet him: "Welcome, O Blessed One! This world is yours; let this world be shared by us together. He says: "Whatever indeed is mine among you, that give back to me. They say: "What do you have among us? "Fragrance is mine, joy is mine, and delight is mine. That which is mine among you, give that back to me. Then the divine Gandharvas give it back to him. He says to them: "Lead me forth..."

"Carry me away! he says. "To what? "To the Apsarases. They carry him toward the Apsarases. When he has arrived there, the Apsarases welcome him, saying: "O venerable sir, this world is yours; let this world be ours together. He says: "Give back to me that which was indeed mine among you. They say: "What is it that was yours among us? "My laughter, my play, my union—give those back to me. Then the Apsarases give them back to him. He says to them: "Carry me away! Thus ends the sixth section of the fifth chapter.

"To what [do you carry me]? "To heaven. They carry him toward heaven. When he has arrived there, Heaven greets him: "O Venerable One, this world is yours; let this world be ours in common. "What indeed have I given to you? he asks. "Give that back to me again," [Heaven] replies. "What indeed have you received from me? "Satisfaction," [Heaven] says. For she is as if satisfied once and for all; thus Heaven gives satisfaction to him again. He says to her, "Carry me forward. "To what? "To the gods. He carries him toward the gods. When he has arrived there, the gods—

"The world here, O Blessed One, welcomes you; let this world be ours together," [he said]. "That which is indeed yours among us, give that back to me," he replied. "What do you have among us? "Immortality. Then the gods gave immortality back to him. He said to them, "Carry me forward!
Thus ends the seventh section of the fifth chapter.

"What do you fear? "The Āditya. They lead him toward that Āditya. He says to the Āditya: "Vibhū [the Pervasive] art thou in front; Sampat [the Attainment] art thou behind. Thou art Samyaṅ [the Perfect]; thou art the one who makes men straight. The seer (Ṛṣi) art thou; thou slayest evil. He who knows thee thus becomes one whose evil is struck away. 2. Thou art the god Sambhū [the Prosperous]; may I become prosperous. Thou art Ābhūti [the Manifestation]; may I manifest myself. Thou art Bhūti [the Being]; may I become. 3. "Those offspring of thine which have been assigned to me—I do not know them. I assign them to thee. 4. "Ojas [vital power] for me! Bala [strength] for me!"

"My eye is yours; do not take that away from me," he said to the Sun. When he had returned in that very manner, the Sun greeted him: "This world is yours, O Venerable One; let this world be ours together. "That which you said was in you, give that back to me," [the guest] said. "What indeed is in me? [the Sun asked]. "Vitality, strength, and my eye—give those back to me," [the guest replied]. The Sun gave those back to him. He said to him, "Carry me forward. "Toward what? "Toward the Moon. Toward that Moon...

The Moon carries [the oblation] for a month; he is called Candra (the Shining One). The path of Truth does not abandon you; the path of Immortality does not abandon you. Being born again and again, you become ever new. O Brāhmaṇa named Bhara, you worship me; therefore, both gods and humans bring food to you as a true one. He who knows this becomes an eater of food. You are a god who has come into being; may I also come into being. You are prosperity; may I prosper. You are the source of being; may I be. Those offspring which have been assigned to you—I do not desire them from you.

"I know them; I give them back to you. "My mind, my semen, my offspring, my rebirth—this which is mine, that is in you; do not take it away from me," he said to the moon. The moon welcomed him as he approached in that very manner, saying, "This world is yours, O venerable one; let this world be common to us both. "That which you say is in you, give that back to me," [the other said]. "What indeed is yours in me? "My mind, my semen, my offspring, my rebirth—this which is mine, that is in you; give that back to me."
Then the Moon gives it back to him. He says to him, "Carry me forward.
Thus ends the eighth section in the fifth chapter.

"To what [world]? "To the world of Brahman. He carries him toward that sun. He says to the sun, "Carry me forward. "To what [world]? "To the world of Brahman. He carries him toward that moon. In this way, he moves along with these two deities. This is the end; there is no further carrying beyond this. Whatever worlds we have mentioned here as being in front, they are all attained by him, they are conquered, and for one who knows thus, there is freedom of movement in all of them. If he should so desire—

Furthermore, thinking "May I be born here again," in whichever family he may desire to be born—whether in a Brāhmaṇa family or in a royal family—in that very one he is born. Knowing this world once more and ascending it, he goes forth. Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said: "This world is indeed widely dispersed and manifold. For the sake of this [world], people either speak or exert themselves. Who would cast this away to come back here again? One should remain right here.
Thus ends the ninth section of the fifth chapter.

The fifth section is completed. Uccaiḥśravas Kaupayeya was a king of the Kauravyas; Keśin Dārbhya, a king of the Pañcālas, was his sister’s son. They lived as dear friends to one another. That Uccaiḥśravas Kaupayeya departed from this world. When he had passed away, Keśin Dārbhya went hunting in the forest, desiring to remove the unpleasantness [of his absence]. As he was thus wandering about, pursuing deer, he came upon Uccaiḥśravas Kaupayeya in the midst of it. He said to him, "I am arrogant."

"Do not be arrogant, thinking 'I know myself,'" he said. "Do you know who I am, whom you think I am? Then [the other] said, "As for what they say, sir, that 'another comes to his world,' how was it possible for you to appear to me? He replied, "Indeed, when I had found the guardian of that world, then I appeared to you. And I shall remove what is unpleasant for him, and I shall instruct him. "So be it, sir," he said. "May I then embrace you?"
As one might pass through smoke, wind, space, the flame of a fire, or water, even so he passes through him; indeed, he does not perceive him as something to be embraced.
Thus ends the first section of the sixth chapter.

He said, "That form which you had before—that is indeed your form; however, I do not perceive it for the sake of embracing you. He replied, "Om! A Brāhmaṇa, knowing the Sāman, sang the Udgītha for me with the Sāman. He shook off my bodies with the bodiless Sāman. Indeed, he who, knowing the Sāman, sings the Udgītha with the Sāman, causes one to attain the same world as the deities. "Pataṅga Prājāpatya," he said, "was the beloved son of Prajāpati. He told this Sāman to him, and by means of it—"

"Prajāpati said, 'With this very Sāman, he sang the Udgītha for the Ṛṣis; these Ṛṣis were "those whose bodies had been shaken off. 'With this very Sāman,' he said, 'he sang the Udgītha for the gods; these gods were "those above, whose bodies had been shaken off. He instructed him in that [Sāman], and having instructed him, he said: "Whoever knows this Sāman, let him indeed sing the Udgītha for you. Having been thus instructed, he returned and wandered about among the Brahmins of the Kurus and Pañcālas, questioning them. Thus ends the second section of the sixth chapter.

"I am about to perform the twelve-day sacrifice with the *vyūḍha-chandas* arrangement. Whoever among you knows that *sāman* which I know—that very person shall chant the *udgītha* for me. Examine yourselves! 1. Not one of those who were examining themselves could give him a satisfactory answer. 2. Wandering on in that very manner, he approached a man lying turned over on his back in a cemetery or a forest; as he was running toward him, the man let him go. 3. He said to him, "Who are you? "I am a Brāhmaṇa, Prātṛda Bhālla," he replied. 4. "What do you know? he asked.

"‘Sāman! [the other] said. ‘Om,’ he replied. ‘I am about to perform the twelve-day sacrifice with the *vyūḍhacchandas* arrangement. If you know that *sāman* which I know, then you alone shall chant the *udgītha* for me; consider it well. As he was considering it, he immediately recognized it. He said to him, ‘This man here will chant the *udgītha*. The Brahmins of the Kurus and Pañcālas, being envious of him, said, ‘While these [other] kinsmen are present, this man will chant the *udgītha*; how is he capable of this? ‘He is indeed capable of it for me,’ he used to say. And because he was capable, he chanted the *udgītha* for him with full capability.”
"Therefore, they cause him to announce, 'O Āgnīdhra, let the Udgātṛ take his seat!
Thus ends the third section in the sixth chapter.

Regarding this, the followers of Sātyakī say: "Whatever deity we worship, we assign but one form to that deity—a cow as its vehicle, an elephant as its vehicle, a man as its vehicle; even among all beings, everything is but the form of that very deity. But this is only one form, namely breath (*prāṇa*). For as long as one breathes with breath, so long does one possess form; one possesses that very form. But when breath departs, one becomes like a useless log of wood.

No form whatsoever remains; its inner self is austerity (*tapas*). Therefore, for one who practices austerity, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) becomes hotter. The inner self of austerity is fire (*agni*); it is explicitly defined (*nirukta*), and therefore it burns. Now, with respect to the deities: this very deity who blows here is she. Within him are the waters; that is food. He is to be meditated upon as non-arid (*arūkṣa*). Because there are waters within him, he is non-arid. His inner self is austerity; therefore, he blows hotter as he scorches. The inner self of austerity is...

Lightning is its *nirukta* (etymological explanation); therefore, it too burns. These, indeed, are the four *sāmans*: breath (*prāṇa*), speech (*vāk*), mind (*manas*), and tone (*svara*). This very breath acts by means of speech, having the mind as its guide. His offspring are his tone; he becomes possessed of offspring who knows this.
Thus ends the fourth section in the sixth chapter.

That which is Vāyu is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa); that which is Agni is indeed speech (vāk); that which is the Moon is indeed the mind (manas); and that which is Āditya is indeed the voice (svara). Therefore, they say of this Āditya, "He goes as a voice" (*svar eti*). Now, whoever worships those deities which are the deities above (the celestial sphere)—for these are of difficult form, as if hard to reach—who knows whether he will reach them or not? But he who worships them with reference to the self (*adhyātma*) becomes one whose god is near (*antideva*). For these [deities] are, as it were, wasting away from here. Or rather, of him...

These [channels] waste away along with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) when the body decays. Who indeed knows whether they reach [the heart] or not? But he who knows these two kinds [of channels] as becoming one—that one truly knows the *anuṣṭubh*, that one knows the *sāman*, that one knows the self (*ātman*), and that one knows Brahman. Regarding this they say: "From a span (*prādeśa*) from here these become one; for from there this vital breath moves upward, sounding. But some say: "From four finger-breadths from here these become one. From there...

"Indeed, this vital breath (*prāṇa*), being celestial, moves ever upwards. This is the turning-point (*āvarta*) of Brahman. He who knows this turning-point of Brahman—toward him offspring and cattle turn; he reaches a full lifespan. He who, knowing this, having breathed out with the out-breath (*apāna*) and breathed in with the in-breath (*prāṇa*), brings these two classes of deities into his own self by means of the mind and places them in his mouth—for him everything becomes attained, everything is conquered. No desire whatsoever remains unfulfilled for him who knows thus. Thus ends the fifth section of the sixth chapter.

This pair consists of speech and breath; the *Ṛk* and the *Sāman* are a pair. Indeed, a pair is a fourfold procreative union. When he says, "The Soma is being purified," or "Turn back," they then utter the *hiṅ* sound together with speech, mind, breath, and tone. By that *hiṅ* sound, a pair is formed. Together with speech, mind, breath, and tone, they reach the *nidhana*. By that *nidhana*, a pair is formed. Thus, this sevenfold *Sāman* is performed by the Udgātṛ seven times upon himself.

Thus ends the sixth section of the sixth lesson. "The wise behold with their heart and mind the Bird anointed by the magic power (*māyā*) of the Asura; within the ocean the seers perceive him; the ordainers seek his station among the rays of light. (RV 1.164.21) 1. "The Bird anointed": the Bird is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*), for he moves as if flying through these limbs; they call him "the Bird" (*pataṅga*). 2. "By the magic power of the Asura": the mind is the Asura, for it delights (*ramate*) among the senses (*asu*); he is anointed by its magic power. 3. "The wise behold with their heart and mind": [they behold] by means of the heart alone.

"For these seers behold that which the mind perceives; within the ocean, the sages discern it"—the ocean is indeed the Person (*puruṣa*), and those who know thus are the sages; they discern this speech within the Person. "The wise seek the station of the rays"—for these deities, namely Agni, Vāyu, Āditya, Candra, and Mā, are like rays. Indeed, there is no station for these deities; by a station, one follows after death again. Thus ends the seventh section of the sixth lesson. "The winged one (pataṅga) bears speech with his mind; the Gandharva spoke it within the womb; the seers guard that shining, celestial wisdom at the station of Eternal Order (ṛta). 1. "The winged one bears speech with his mind": the winged one is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa); he bears this speech with his mind. 2. "The Gandharva spoke it within the womb": the Gandharva is indeed the vital breath, and the person (puruṣa) is the womb; he speaks this speech within the person. 3. "That shining, celestial wisdom": [the word] *svaryā* means...
"This is that wisdom: 'The sages guard speech at the station of Ṛta. Mind is indeed Ṛta; the sages are those who know thus. The syllable *oṃ* is this very Ṛta.
By means of it, when they investigate the *Ṛgveda*, the *Yajurveda*, and the *Sāmaveda*, they guard it.
Thus ends the eighth section of the sixth chapter.

"I saw the herdsman, never resting, moving hither and thither along his paths; he, clothing himself in converging and diverging rays, revolves repeatedly within the worlds. (1) "I saw the herdsman, never resting"—the herdsman is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*), for it protects all this world without ever resting. (2) "Moving hither and thither along his paths"—for those which are these vital breaths here and those rays yonder, by means of them this [breath] moves hither and thither along its paths. (3) "He, clothing himself in converging..."

"Clad in those turned in all directions"—for he indeed clothes himself in offspring that are both turned together and turned in all directions. "He revolves within the worlds"—for he indeed revolves within these worlds. This very Indra is the Udgītha. When this Indra, as the Udgītha, approaches, nothing more is perceived of either the Udgātṛ or the Upagātṛs; from here upwards he rises as the *svar* (the tone), and he flickers above the head. He should know: "Indra has arrived; no trace of evil shall remain here."

In that [Sāman], not a single trace of evil remains. This is the *abhrātṛvya* (rival-free) Sāman; indeed, Indra saw no rival whatsoever. Just as Indra saw no rival whatsoever, even so he who knows this, or for whom one knowing thus sings the *udgītha*, sees no rival whatsoever.
Thus ends the ninth section in the sixth chapter;
the sixth chapter is complete.

Prajāpati created Brahmā; he created him without eyes and without a mouth. While he lay there without eyes and without a mouth, Brahmā entered him. For Brahmā is indeed breath; it was breath that entered him. He stood up as the progenitor of creatures, and the Rākṣasas pursued him. He protected himself by singing this very Sāman; because he protected himself while singing, that is the origin of the name *Gāyatra* for the Gāyatra. Whoever knows this is protected and is liberated from all evil. Sing to him... [upāsmai]... [the Sāman].

With the verse "Sing forth, O men," they sang the approach with a most beautiful sound. Because [they sang] "Sing forth, O men, for him," it became the Gāyatra; therefore, this very [verse] should be used as the introductory chant (*pratipad*). They sang sixteen syllables to the *pavamāna* [laud]: "O Indra, come hither to the god, huṃ bhā kṣātā. For Brahman consists of sixteen parts (*kalā*); thus, part by part, Brahman entered him. This Gāyatra consists of twenty-four syllables: the *prastāva* has eight syllables and the sung portion (*gīta*) has sixteen syllables; thus they amount to twenty-four.

Twenty-four half-months make a year; the year is the *Sāman*. Those *Ṛc*s follow death by means of their body—that which has a body is reached by death. Now, that which is bodiless is immortal. With that bodiless *Sāman*, he shook off his bodies. Thus ends the first section of the seventh chapter.

"Ovā3co-vā3co-vā3-chumbhā ovā"—thus he sang sixteen syllables. For man consists of sixteen parts; part by part he shook off his bodies. He is this one whose evil has been struck away, whose bodies have been shaken off. Singing "tadek-kriyā-vṛti-udāsaṅga," [the word] "udāsa" means "having risen up"; "ā" means "having returned. "Vāk" (Speech) is that Brahman, that is this intermediate space, and this is the wind that blows. "Hum" is the moon; "bhā" is the sun. Indeed, they call this world the "shining" (*bhāti*) of the power (*kratu*) of this Imperishable. Of this indeed... *(Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)*

They call this the "cloud" of this imperishable sacrifice (kratu). 4. They call this the "kubhra" of this imperishable sacrifice. 5. They call this the "shubhra" of this imperishable sacrifice. 6. They call this the "bull" of this imperishable sacrifice. 7. They call this the "darbha" of this imperishable sacrifice. 8. They call this the "one that shines" of this imperishable sacrifice. 9. Of this very imperishable sacrifice...
They say it arises from the *kratu* (sacrificial will). Whatever there is as "bhā3" and "bhā3," that is this couple, the Gāyatra. He who knows thus is procreated through the couple.
Thus ends the second section in the seventh chapter.

This is that immortal *gāyatra* [sāman]. By means of this, indeed, Prajāpati attained immortality; by this, the gods; by this, the seers. Prajāpati told this *brahman* to Parameṣṭhin Prājāpatya; Parameṣṭhin Prājāpatya told it to the god Savitṛ; the god Savitṛ told it to Agni; Agni told it to Indra; Indra told it to Kāśyapa; Kāśyapa told it to Ṛśyaśṛṅga Kāśyapa; Ṛśyaśṛṅga Kāśyapa told it to Devataras Śyāvasāyana Kāśyapa; Devataras Śyāvasāyana Kāśyapa [told it to his disciples].

From Kāśyapa Śruṣa Vāhneya, [it was received] by Kāśyapa Śruṣa Vāhneya; from Indra Daivāpa Śaunaka, [it was received] by Indra Daivāpa Śaunaka; from Dṛti Aindra, [it was received] by Dṛti Aindra; from Tiśa Śaunaka, [it was received] by Tiśa Śaunaka; from Puluṣa Prācīnayogya, [it was received] by Puluṣa Prācīnayogya; from Satyayajña Pauluṣi Prācīnayogya, [it was received] by Satyayajña Pauluṣi Prācīnayogya; from Somaśuṣma Sātyayajñi Prācīnayogya, [it was received] by Somaśuṣma Sātyayajñi Prācīnayogya.

Prācīnayogya [received it] from Hṛtsvāśaya Āllakeya; Hṛtsvāśaya Āllakeya from King Māhāvṛṣa; King Māhāvṛṣa from Janaśruta Kāṇḍviya; Janaśruta Kāṇḍviya from Sāyaka Jānaśruteya Kāṇḍviya; Sāyaka Jānaśruteya Kāṇḍviya from Nagarin Jānaśruteya Kāṇḍviya; Nagarin Jānaśruteya Kāṇḍviya from Śaṅga Śāṭyāyani Ātreya; Śaṅga Śāṭyāyani Ātreya from Rāma Krātujāteya Vaiyāghrapadya; Rāma Krātujāteya Vaiyāghrapadya. 2.40.

Thus ends the third section of the seventh lesson: [The lineage is] Śaṅkha Bābhravya from Śaṅkha Bābhravya; Dakṣa Kātyāyani Ātreya from Dakṣa Kātyāyani Ātreya; Kaṃsa Vāraki from Kaṃsa Vāraki; Proṣṭhapāda Vārakya from Proṣṭhapāda Vārakya; Kaṃsa Vārakya from Kaṃsa Vārakya; Jayanta Vārakya from Jayanta Vārakya; Kubera Vārakya from Kubera Vārakya; Jayanta Vārakya from Jayanta Vārakya; Janaśruta Vārakya from Janaśruta Vārakya.

Vārakya received it from Sudatta Pārāśarya; Sudatta Pārāśarya from Aṣāḍha Uttara Pārāśarya; Aṣāḍha Uttara Pārāśarya from Vipaścit Śakunimitra Pārāśarya; Vipaścit Śakunimitra Pārāśarya from Jayanta Pārāśarya; Jayanta Pārāśarya [received it] from Pārāśarya. 1.41 Thus ends the fourth section in the seventh chapter.

To Śyāmajayanta Lauhitya; Śyāmajayanta Lauhitya [gave it] to Palligupta Lauhitya; Palligupta Lauhitya to Satyaśravas Lauhitya; Satyaśravas Lauhitya to Kṛṣṇadhṛti Sātyaki; Kṛṣṇadhṛti Sātyaki to Śyāmasujayanta Lauhitya; Śyāmasujayanta Lauhitya to Kṛṣṇadatta Lauhitya; Kṛṣṇadatta Lauhitya to Mitrabhūti Lauhitya; Mitrabhūti Lauhitya to Śyāmajayanta Lauhitya.

Śyāmajayanta Lauhitya to Triveda Kṛṣṇarāta Lauhitya; Triveda Kṛṣṇarāta Lauhitya to Yaśasvin Jayanta Lauhitya; Yaśasvin Jayanta Lauhitya to Jayaka Lauhitya; Jayaka Lauhitya to Kṛṣṇarāta Lauhitya; Kṛṣṇarāta Lauhitya to Dakṣajayanta Lauhitya; Dakṣajayanta Lauhitya to Vipaścit Dṛḍhajayanta Lauhitya; Vipaścit Dṛḍhajayanta Lauhitya to Vaipaścita.

To Dārḍhajayanti, the son of Dṛḍhajayanta; to Lauhitya, the son of Vipaścit; from Dārḍhajayanti, the son of Dṛḍhajayanta, to Lauhitya, the son of Vipaścit; to Gupta, the son of Lauhitya. This indeed is the immortal Gāyatra; as for those other songs that are sung, they are merely optional, they are merely optional. Thus ends the fifth section in the seventh chapter.
The seventh section (anuvāka) is completed;
thus ends the third chapter.
Now begins the fourth chapter.

White-horsed, beautiful to behold, you are green-blue, touching the green; O you who are awakened by the same [thought], do not harm me! You do not know me; run away! (1) When you, descending, approach the sleeping man who is ignorant, may Varuṇa shield me with an armor made of stone. (2) When you, descending, approach the sleeping man who is ignorant, may Varuṇa shield me with an armor made of iron. (3) When you, descending, approach the sleeping man who is ignorant, [shield me] with an armor made of bronze. (4)

May Varuṇa shield me within with his armor when you, O Abhyavacaraṇa, approach the sleeping man who is unaware; may Varuṇa shield me within with armor made of silver. May Varuṇa shield me within with armor made of gold when you, O Abhyavacaraṇa, approach the sleeping man who is unaware. Life is your mother, thought is your father; homage to you, O Āviśoṣaṇa! You are the Seizer by name, the All-Living; to you, for all days, be homage! Homage to Tāṃrāyas, homage to Varuṇa, homage to him who seeks to strike us down!
O King Yakṣman, do not harm me; O Yakṣman, O King, do not harm me. Through the agreement of those two, may I attain a full span of life. 8.1 The first Anuvāka is completed.

The sacrifice is indeed man. Those twenty-four years of his constitute the morning pressing (*prātassavana*). The *gāyatrī* has twenty-four syllables, and the morning pressing belongs to the *gāyatra* [chant]. These are the Vasus; the Vasus are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), for the vital breaths gather all this wealth (*vasu*) here. If, at that time, some affliction or calamity should befall him, he should say: "O Vasus, who are the vital breaths, continue this morning pressing of mine with the midday pressing. Thus he becomes free from disease. Now, as for those...

Forty-four years constitute that midday pressing; the *triṣṭubh* has forty-four syllables, and the midday pressing belongs to the *triṣṭubh*. That [pressing] belongs to the Rudras. The Rudras are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), for it is the vital breaths that make all this weep (*rud*). If, at that time, some affliction or calamity should befall him, he should say: "The Rudras are the vital breaths; may this midday pressing of mine be extended by means of the third pressing. He will surely become free from disease. Now, as for those forty-eight [years]...

The rainy season is his third *savana*; the *jagatī* consists of forty-eight syllables, and the third *savana* belongs to the *jagatī*. (8) Those [deities] belong to the Ādityas; the Ādityas are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), for the vital breaths take up all this. (9) If, at that time, some affliction or calamity should befall him, he should say: "O vital breaths, O Ādityas, extend this third *savana* of mine along with my life-force! Thus, he indeed becomes free from disease. (10) Knowing this, the Brahmin Mahidāsa Aitareya once said when he was afflicted: "What is this affliction that afflicts you?"

He who thinks, "May I not be sent away by this affliction," lived for sixteen hundred years; he lives for sixteen hundred years, and breath does not desert him before his full span of life, who knows thus.
The second section (anuvāka) is completed.

The threefold life-span of Kaśyapa, the threefold life-span of Jamadagni—the three flowers of immortality, the three life-spans—you have bestowed upon me. O life-giving Soma, enter us as one who brings peace, being auspicious to our bodies. Those fires which have entered the earth, dwelling within the soil—of them you are the highest; impel us toward long life. 3.3.1–3.3.3.
The third section is completed.

You are the calf of the forest, possessing all names, protecting all; you are the ripened essence of the waters, the messenger of Varuṇa, whose name is "Invisibility. 1 Just as you, being immortal, are hidden from mortals, so do you hide us from those who seek to harm us. You are the invisibility against thieves. 2 The fourth section is completed.

At dawn you become Savitṛ; as you are about to rise, Viṣṇu; as you rise, Puruṣa; once risen, Bṛhaspati; as you move forward, Maghavan Indra; at midday, Vaikuṇṭha; in the afternoon, Bhaga; as you turn red, the fierce deity; at sunset, you become Yama. 1. During the eating [of food], you are King Soma; during the night, the King of the Ancestors; in sleep, you enter into men, and with milk, into cattle. 2. At the end of the night, you become Bhava; in the latter part of the night, Aṅgiras; at the time of the Agnihotra, Bhṛgu. 3. Of him, this very solar orb is the udder; these two are his teats.
"From speech and from breath, milk for me: study, celibacy, offspring, cattle, the heavenly world, and association with kinsmen. These blessings I desire:
Bhūr, Bhuvas, Svar! When it has risen, I place that pure radiance within my self.
The fifth section is completed.

King Bhageratha, the descendant of Ikṣvāku, was about to perform the Kāmapra sacrifice. Then the Brahmins of the Kurus and Pañcālas said, "This King Bhageratha, the descendant of Ikṣvāku, is about to perform the Kāmapra sacrifice; let us go there and speak with him. They went to him, and when they had arrived, he paid them honors. Then he approached them with his hair and beard shaved, his nails clipped, anointed with ghee, and carrying a staff and sandals. He spoke to them as follows:

"Venerable Brahmins," he said, "which of you knows this: how it is that when the *śrāvaṇa* and *pratyāśrāvaṇa* have been performed, one goes to the gods? Then he said: "Which of you knows this: how it is that from one who knows [this], there arise a skilled *udgātṛ*, a skilled *hotṛ*, a skilled *adhvaryu*, and one who is well-versed in what is human? Then he said: "Which of you knows this: why the meters (*chandas*) are employed, and how all of them, once chanted together, come to coincide? Then he said: "Which of you knows this: how it is with the two final syllables of the *gāyatrī*..."
"Go back again to the sacrifice," he said. Then he asked: "Which of you knows how the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās), once accepted, do not cause harm?
Sixth Anuvāka, First Khaṇḍa.

He asked him these five questions. Now, among those Kurupañcālas, there was Baka Dālbhya, who was well-versed in sacred tradition (*anūcāna*). He said: "Regarding the call and the response (*āśrāvitapratyāśrāvita*), it is said that they go to the gods. Indeed, O King, in the eastern direction the call and the response go to the gods; therefore, standing facing the east, one makes the call, and standing facing the east, one responds. Then he said: "Regarding the statement, 'When one is born as a good *udgātṛ*, a good *hotṛ*, a good *adhvaryu*, or one who possesses true human knowledge'—what indeed is the human [element]?"

"He knows prosperity," he said, "for him there arises a skilled Udgātṛ, a skilled Hotṛ, a skilled Adhvaryu, and one who possesses excellent human knowledge. "O King, the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) indeed constitute the prosperity of a man," [the other] replied. Then he said: "As for the fact that the meters (*chandāṃsi*) are employed, and how all of them, when fully chanted, converge upon one another—O King, all the meters when fully chanted converge upon the Gāyatrī. Then he said: "How is it that at the two final syllables of the Gāyatrī, the sacrifice returns again?"

"By means of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, O King, the *gāyatrī* indeed returns again to the sacrifice through its last syllable," he said. Then he said, "Just as sacrificial gifts, once accepted, do not cause harm.
Sixth Anuvāka, Second Khaṇḍa.

"Whoever knows the mouth of the Gāyatrī," he said, "the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) received do not harm him. 1. "O King, Agni indeed is the mouth of the Gāyatrī; therefore, whatever one places into the fire, it becomes greater by that very act and truly increases. In the same way, a Brahmin who knows this and accepts gifts becomes greater and truly increases. 2. He said, "This Brahmin is indeed a learned scholar (anūcāna); I am coming to you with this sacrifice. 3. "I shall sing the Udgītha for you in such a manner," [he replied].

He said, "Just as one who has become a sole ruler (*ekarāj*) shall go to the heavenly world. For him, he sang out with this *gāyatra* *udgītha*. He indeed became a sole ruler and went to the heavenly world. By means of this very same [singing], whoever knows thus becomes a sole ruler and goes to the heavenly world. (5) "Oṃ vā"—these are two syllables; "Oṃ vā" in the fourth [verse]; "Oṃ vā" in the sixth; "Huṃ bhā" and "Oṃ vāk" in the eighth. (6) By means of this very same [singing], Pratīdarśa sang out against his fearful and unruly [opponent]. (7) He said to him: "What did you [sing]? (8)

"I shall sing," he said. "Bring me my two divine horses, the bay steeds," [the other] replied. "So be it," [the former] said. He sang them for him, and they came to him. This, indeed, is the Udgītha of desires: *saṃpada oṃ vā3caoṃ vā3caoṃ vā3chuṃ bhā oṃ vāk*. He who knows this thus becomes possessed of limbs, possessed of a body, and immortal; and so too does he for whom one who knows this sings the Udgītha. Sixth Anuvāka, Third Khaṇḍa.

The sixth section is completed. Man is indeed the sacrifice; man is the *udgītha*. Now, these are the very deaths: fire, wind, the sun, and the moon. They bind man with the fetters of death as soon as he is born: fire binds his speech, wind his breath, the sun his sight, and the moon his hearing. Regarding this, they say: "Is there an *udgātṛ* who, for the sake of the sacrificer, releases him from the fetters of death beyond his vital breaths? Thus, for one who knows this, when [the priest] chants the *prastāva*, that which is in his speech...

The noose of death is released from him alone. 4. Now, for whomsoever one who knows thus sings the *udgītha*, the noose of death that is in his breath (*prāṇa*) is released from him alone. 5. Now, for whomsoever one who knows thus performs the *pratihāra*, the noose of death that is in his sight (*cakṣus*) is released from him alone. 6. Now, for whomsoever one who knows thus approaches the *nidhana*, the noose of death that is in his hearing (*śrotra*) is released from him alone. 7. Thus indeed does the *udgātṛ* who knows thus release the nooses of death from the breaths of the sacrificer. 8. Regarding this, they say:
Or rather, it is the Udgātṛ who, having released from the sacrificer’s vital breaths the nooses of death, then rescues him—along with his limbs, his body, and his whole being—from all death.
(9) The first section of the seventh chapter.

Thus, when one who knows this utters the *hiṅ* sound, he thereby releases from him that bond of death which is in his hair. 1. Then, when one who knows this performs the *prastāva*, he thereby releases from him that bond of death which is in his skin. 2. Then, when one who knows this takes up the *ādi*, he thereby releases from him that bond of death which is in his flesh. 3. Then, when one who knows this sings the *udgītha*, he thereby releases from him that bond of death which is in his sinews. 4. Then, when one who knows this...

The wise one performs the *pratihāra* [chant]; from whatever noose of death is upon his limbs, from that very thing he delivers him. 5. Then, for whomever the wise one performs the *upadrava*, from whatever noose of death is upon his bones, from that very thing he delivers him. 6. Then, for whomever the wise one approaches with the *nidhana*, from whatever noose of death is upon his marrow, from that very thing he delivers him. 7. Thus indeed does the Udgātṛ who knows this, having released the nooses of death from the sacrificer’s vital breaths, deliver him—along with his limbs, along with his body—from all death. 8.

Regarding this, they say: "The Udgātṛ is he who, having released the bonds of death from the vital breaths of the sacrificer, then places him—along with his limbs, his body, and having touched all of death—in the heavenly world in seven ways. Now, as he rises, he becomes Indra Vaimṛdha; when risen, he is Savitṛ; at the time of the gathering of cattle (saṃgava), he is Mitra; at midday, he is Indra Vaikuṇṭha; as he turns back, he is the fierce god Śarva; as he moves toward the redness (of twilight), he is Prajāpati; and when set, he is Saṃveśa. Therefore, for whomsoever one who knows thus utters the *hiṅ* sound...

Thus, for one who exerts himself [in this way], there is the heavenly world; in that very world he establishes him. 11. Now, for whomsoever an officiant knowing thus chants the *prastāva*, in whatever heavenly world of his belongs to the risen [sun], in that very world he establishes him. 12. Now, for whomsoever an officiant knowing thus takes up the *ādi*, in whatever heavenly world of his belongs to the time of the gathering of cattle (*saṃgava*), in that very world he establishes him. 13. Now, for whomsoever an officiant knowing thus sings the *udgītha*, in whatever heavenly world of his belongs to midday, in that very world he establishes him. 14. Now, for whomsoever an officiant knowing thus performs the *pratihāra*...

In that very world which is his heavenly realm in the afternoon, he places him. (15) Now, for whomsoever an Udgātṛ who knows thus approaches with the *upadrava*, in that very world which is his heavenly realm at sunset, he places him. (16) Now, for whomsoever an Udgātṛ who knows thus performs the *nidhana*, in that very world which is his heavenly realm when the sun has set, he places him. (17) Thus indeed does the Udgātṛ who knows thus, having released the bonds of death from the vital breaths of the sacrificer, and having touched him along with his limbs and body, place him sevenfold in the heavenly world. (18) 10
The second section in the seventh chapter;
the seventh chapter is completed.

There are indeed six deities that are self-existent: Agni, Vāyu, that Āditya (the Sun), Prāṇa, Anna (Food), and Vāk (Speech). They disputed for preeminence, each saying, "I am the best! I am the best! Worship me as the glory! They could not agree upon one another’s preeminence. They said, "We shall certainly not submit to one another’s preeminence; let us all speak together so that we may all be preeminent. They spoke to Agni, "How are you the best? He replied, "I [am the mouth] of the gods..."

"I am the mouth of other creatures; through me the oblations are offered. I transform myself into the food of the gods and the food of human beings. (5) If I were not to exist, the gods would be mouthless, and so would other creatures. No oblations would be offered; neither the food of the gods nor that of human beings would be prepared. (6) From that, all this would perish, and nothing at all would remain. (7) "It is exactly so," they said. "If you were not to exist, nothing at all would remain here. (8) Then...

They said to Vāyu, "How are you the best? He replied, "I am the breath (*prāṇa*) of the gods; I am [the breath] of other creatures as well. Because when I depart from them, they float away. If I were not to exist, then all this would perish, and nothing at all would remain. They said, "It is even so. If you were not to exist, nothing at all would remain here. *The First Section of the Eighth Anuvāka.*

Then they said to Āditya, "How are you the best? He replied, "When I rise, it becomes day; when I set, it becomes night. By me as the eye, all actions are performed. If I were not to exist, there would be neither day nor night, and no actions would be performed. From that, this entire universe would perish, and nothing at all would remain. They said, "It is even so; if you were not to exist, nothing at all would remain here. Then they spoke to Prāṇa: "How are you..."

"You are the best," [they said]. He replied: "Becoming breath, fire blazes; becoming breath, the wind experiences the ether; becoming breath, the sun rises. From breath comes food; from breath comes speech. "If I were not to exist, then all this would perish, and nothing at all would remain," he said. "So it is indeed," they replied. "If you were not to exist, nothing at all here would remain. Then they said to food: "How are you the best? He replied: "In me..."

"Fire blazes by resting in me; the wind prevails through space by resting in me; the sun rises by resting in me; even my breath and my speech exist because of me. "If I were not to exist, then all this would perish, and nothing at all would remain. "So be it," they said. "Indeed, nothing at all would remain if you were not to exist. Then they spoke to Speech: "How are you the best? She replied: "By me alone is this known; by me is that [known]."

"If I were not to exist, this sound would not be perceived. Consequently, all this would perish, and nothing at all would remain here. "It is exactly so," they said. "If you were not to exist, nothing at all would remain here.
Section 2, Eighth Anuvāka.
