They said, "Indeed, all these deities are but one by one; if not even one of all these deities were to remain, then this entire universe would perish, and nothing at all would be left. Come, let us come together and become that which is the best among us. 1. They gathered together in this *prāṇa* (breath) as the syllable *oṃ* and in speech as the syllable *a*. Because they gathered together (*samāyan*), that is the essence of the *sāman*. 2. They said, "Those of ours which are mortal, not free from evil, and imperishable..."

"Having extracted those [syllables] from the immortal, sinless, pure, and imperishable [elements], let us sing the Gāyatra chant upon the fire, the wind, the sun, the breath, the food, and the speech; thereby, having struck down death and having struck down evil, may we go to the heavenly world. 3. "Ā"—this is the immortal, sinless, pure, and imperishable syllable of fire; "gni"—this is its mortal, non-immortal, and non-sinless syllable. 4. "Vā"—this is the immortal, sinless, pure, and imperishable syllable of wind; "yu"—this is its mortal, non-immortal, and non-sinless syllable. 5. "Ā"—this is the immortal, sinless, pure, and imperishable syllable of the sun; "di"—this is its mortal, non-immortal, and non-sinless syllable.

*Eti* is the immortal of the sun, free from evil, pure, and imperishable; *tya* is its mortal part, not free from evil, and perishable. *Pra* is the immortal of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), free from evil, pure, and imperishable; *ṇa* is its mortal part, not free from evil, and perishable. *Eti* is the immortal of food, free from evil, pure, and imperishable; *na* is its mortal part, not free from evil, and perishable. *Va* is the immortal of speech, free from evil, pure, and imperishable; *gi* is its mortal part, not free from evil, and perishable. These are those [syllables].

Having extracted from the mortal syllables those that are not free from evil, they sang the *gāyatra* chant upon the immortal, evil-free, pure syllables—namely, in fire, wind, the sun, breath, food, and speech. By this, having struck down death and having struck down evil, they went to the heavenly world. (10) He who knows this, having struck down death and having struck down evil, goes to the heavenly world.
(11) Eighth Anuvāka, Third Khaṇḍa.

They said to Brahman, "Establishing ourselves in you, let us lift this up. Brahman said to them, "By means of the breath of the mouth, you shall attain me through the breath of the mouth. They, with this breath—the *oṃ*—aiming at the syllable *ka*, [producing] the syllable *bha* from the *hiṅkāra*, and sounding forth speech after the syllable *o* with the syllable *o*, sang the *gāyatra* chant with both breaths: *ovā3 covā3 covā3 chuṃ bhā vo vā*. Just as one with two feet stands firmly, even so does one stand in the heavenly world.

They established themselves; he who knows thus establishes himself in the heavenly world. And indeed, he who departs from this world knowing this becomes breath itself and enters into Vāyu. From Vāyu he passes into the clouds, from the clouds into rain, and by means of rain he pervades this world. The seers once performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*). Again and again, with various and numerous introductory verses (*pratipad*), they could not at all find the door to the heavenly world. Then, through toil, austerity, and the observance of vows, they [reached] Indra.

They were in distress. They said to him: "We indeed desired the heavenly world, but though we have approached it again and again with many various approaches, we have not found the door to the heavenly world. Teach us so that, having recognized the door to the heavenly world, we may go to the heavenly world unharmed, having reached the completion of the year. He said to them: "Who among you is the oldest?
Fifth Section of the Fourth Chapter in the Eighth Anuvāka.

"I am Agastya," he said. "Come, indeed," he [the other] replied. "I shall tell you that which, knowing it, the wise, having recognized the door of the heavenly world, go unhurt to the successful completion of the year and reach the heavenly world. To him he spoke this secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of the Gāyatra-udgītha—concerning fire, wind, the sun, breath, food, and speech. Then, indeed, they recognized the door of the heavenly world and, going unhurt to the successful completion of the year, reached it.
They went to the heavenly world. In this very same way, one who knows thus, having discerned the door of the heavenly world, reaches the end of the year unharmed and goes to the heavenly world.
Fifth section of the eighth lesson;
the eighth lesson is completed.

Thus, indeed, Indra taught this Upaniṣad—the immortal Udgītha of the Gāyatra—to Agastya; Agastya to Iṣa Śyāvāśvi; Iṣa Śyāvāśvi to Gauṣūkti; Gauṣūkti to Jvālāyana; Jvālāyana to Śāṭyāyani; Śāṭyāyani to Rāma Krātujāteya Vaiyāghrapadya. The first section in the ninth lesson.

To Śaṅkha Bābhravya; Śaṅkha Bābhravya [received it] from Dakṣa Kātyāyani Ātreya; Dakṣa Kātyāyani Ātreya from Kaṃsa Vārakya; Kaṃsa Vārakya from Suyajña Śāṇḍilya; Suyajña Śāṇḍilya from Agnidatta Śāṇḍilya; Agnidatta Śāṇḍilya from Suyajña Śāṇḍilya; Suyajña Śāṇḍilya from Jayanta Vārakya; Jayanta Vārakya from Janaśruta Vārakya; Janaśruta Vārakya from Sudatta Pārāśarya. This is the Śāṭyāyanī Upaniṣad of the Gāyatra [Sāman]; thus it should be meditated upon. 17.2–3.
The second section in the ninth Anuvāka;
the ninth Anuvāka is completed.

By whom impelled does the mind fly forth when sent? By whom is the first breath joined and set in motion? By whom impelled do they utter this speech? And what god yokes the eye and the ear? The ear of the ear, the mind of the mind, that which is the speech of speech, and the breath of the breath, and the eye of the eye—the wise, having realized these, depart from this world and become immortal. The eye does not go there, nor does speech go there, nor the mind. We do not know, we do not understand, how one might instruct another regarding this.

"That is indeed other than the known, and moreover, above the unknown"—thus have we heard from those of old who explained it to us. (4) That which is not expressed by speech, but by which speech is expressed—know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which people worship here. (5) That which one does not think with the mind, but by which the mind is said to be thought—know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which people worship here. (6) That which one does not see with the eye, but by which the eyes are seen—know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which people worship here. (7)

That which one does not hear with the ear, by which this very ear is heard—that alone know thou to be Brahman, and not that which people here worship as an object. (8) That which one does not breathe with the breath, by which the breath is led forth—that alone know thou to be Brahman, and not that which people here worship as an object. (9) [End of the first section of the tenth lesson.]

If you think "I know it well," then surely you know only a very small portion of the form of Brahman—only that which is yours and that which is among the gods. Therefore, I believe that much remains to be investigated by you as yet unknown. "I do not think 'I know it well,' nor do I think 'I do not know it. And he among us who knows that he does not know it—he truly knows; he knows it. "He for whom it is not thought, by him it is thought; he who thinks he knows it, does not know it. It is unknown to those who understand, and known to those who do not understand. "That which is known through intuitive awakening—that is the thought [of Brahman]; for through that one finds immortality."

By oneself one finds strength; by knowledge one finds immortality. If one has known this here, then there is truth; if one has not known this here, there is great ruin. Having discerned [the Self] in every single being, the wise, after departing from this world, become immortal. Fifth Chapter, Ninth Section, Second Part.

Brahman indeed conquered for the gods. In that victory of Brahman, the gods exulted. They thought, "This victory is ours alone; this greatness is ours alone. He knew of their [thought], and he appeared before them. They did not recognize him, asking, "What is this spirit? (yakṣa) They said to Agni, "O Jātavedas, find out what this spirit is. "So be it," he replied. He ran toward it, and it spoke to him, saying, "Who are you? He said, "I am indeed Agni, the Jātavedas."

"I am he. "What power is there in you? "I could burn all this that is on the earth. He placed a blade of grass before him, saying, "Burn this. It flew toward it with all its speed, yet it was not able to burn it; it turned back from there, [saying], "I was not able to discern what this Yakṣa is. Then they said to Vāyu, "O Vāyu, find out what this Yakṣa is. "So be it," he replied. He ran toward it. It spoke to him, "Who are you? "I am Vāyu," he said.

"I am," said Mātariśvan, "I am indeed. "What power is there in you? "Even all this that is upon the earth, I could take it up. He placed a blade of grass before him, saying, "Take this up. He rushed toward it with all his speed, but he was not able to take it up. He turned back from that very spot, saying, "I was not able to discern what this Yakṣa is. Then they said to Indra, "O Maghavan, find out what this Yakṣa is. "So be it," he replied, and he went toward it.
He disappeared from that place. He came upon a woman in that very space, Uma Haimavatī, who was exceedingly beautiful; he said to her, "What is this spirit?
(End of the third section of the tenth lesson.)

"It is Brahman," he said. "It is in the victory of Brahman that you are being glorified. Then, indeed, he understood it to be Brahman. Therefore, these gods—Agni, Vāyu, and Indra—are, as it were, superior to the other gods; for they have touched this [Brahman] most closely, and they were the first to understand it as Brahman. Therefore, Indra is, as it were, superior to the other gods; for he has touched this [Brahman] most closely, and he was the first to understand it as Brahman. This is its instruction:

"That which flashed forth from the lightning—'Ah!'—and that which closed its eyes—'Ah!'"—this is with reference to the deities (adhidevatam). Now, with reference to the self (adhyātmam): that which the mind seems to go toward, and by means of which one repeatedly remembers this [Self], is volition (saṃkalpaḥ). That indeed is called "the Forest" (vanam); it should be meditated upon as "the Forest. He who knows this thus, all beings desire him. "Sir, tell us the Upaniṣad! "The Upaniṣad has been told to you. We have indeed told you the Upaniṣad pertaining to Brahman (brāhmī). "Its [observances] are austerity, self-control, and ritual action."

The Vedas are its foundation, all the auxiliary sciences are its limbs, and truth is its abode. He who knows this thus, having struck down evil, becomes established in the infinite, unconquerable heavenly world.
Fifth Section of the Tenth Anuvāka.
The Tenth Anuvāka is completed.

In the beginning, this world was indeed only hope (*āśā*). That became what was yet to be; it became those waters. Those waters performed austerity. While performing austerity, they breathed forth "huṣ" toward the east; that indeed became the out-breath (*prāṇa*). Having breathed out, they breathed in; that indeed became the in-breath (*apāna*). Having breathed in, they breathed across; that indeed became the diffused breath (*vyāna*). Having breathed across, they breathed together; that indeed became the equalizing breath (*samāna*). Having breathed together, they breathed up; that indeed became the upward breath (*udāna*). This [breath], being one alone, was a common food (*sadharmadya*), undifferentiated. He...

He created name-and-form; therefore, one who knows this is separated from evil by these two. 8. Now, that breath is yonder sun, Agni is the out-breathing, the waters are the diffused breath, the quarters are the equalizing breath, and the moon is the up-breathing. 9. That indeed became one—the breath itself. He who thus knows that it becomes one, thinking, "Thus indeed does this become one," becomes one among his own people as the most excellent. 10. Now, Agni is the breath and speech is the earth; Vāyu is the breath and speech is the intermediate space; Āditya is the breath...

"Speech"—the sky is speech; "breath"—the quarters are breath; "speech"—the ear is speech; "moon"—the mind is breath; "speech"—the male is breath; "speech"—the female is speech. 11. This world which was created by him was loose and insufficient. 12. He fashioned the form of *manas* (mind); by that he made it sufficient. Indeed, for one who knows this, this world which is created becomes firm, not loose, and sufficient. 13. 22. First section of the eleventh anuvāka.

This very [Upanishad] is established in four ways: the *udgītha*, the *sāman*, the *arkya*, and the *jyeṣṭhabrāhmaṇa*. 1. Breath indeed is the *ud*, speech is the *gī*; that is the *udgītha*. 2. Breath indeed is the *ā*, speech is the *mā*; that is the *sāman*. 3. Breath indeed is the *ka*, speech is the *ṛc*; that is the *arkya*. 4. Breath indeed is the *jyeṣṭha*, speech is the *brāhmaṇa*; that is the *jyeṣṭhabrāhmaṇa*. "Sir, tell me the Upanishad," he said. "The Upanishad has been told to you; those elements (*dhātu*) of yours have been told. It is threefold. "We have indeed told you the Upanishad as threefold. "This is white, this is black, and that is the color of the *sāman*."

Thus he said: "Whenever the white and black colors meet, that indeed seizes him; the tenth [month] is human. Thus it is threefold. He reflected: "Where now, while I lie stretched out, would these deities bring me tribute?
The second section of the eleventh anuvāka.

He chose the Puruṣa alone for refuge. He entered him from the front facing backward; for him, it became wide (*uru*), and that is why the chest is called *uraḥ*. Therefore, these deities bring tribute to him here: Agni brings tribute to him following speech as it is uttered; the Moon brings tribute to him following the mind as it moves; the Sun brings tribute to him following the eye as it sees; the Quarters bring tribute to him following the ear as it hears; and Vāyu brings tribute to him following the breath as it moves.

It carries him away. These vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are his dug-out paths for the draft-animals. Thus, these dug-out paths for the draft-animals lead him from every side; the vital breaths go forth for one who knows this. 9. This is that very throne of Brahman (*brahmāsandī*) upon which he has ascended. They bring the throne of Brahman for him, and he indeed ascends the throne of Brahman, he who knows this. 10. This is the glory of Brahman, surrounded by prosperity. Indeed, he becomes possessed of the glory and prosperity of Brahman, he who knows this. 11. This is its instruction:

That which is within the right eye—of that, what is white is the form of the *ṛc*s; what is black is the form of the *sāmans*; and what is, as it were, reddish-brown, is the form of the *yajus*es. This very person who is in the eye is Indra, this is Prajāpati. He is equal to the earth, equal to space, equal to heaven, equal to all beings. He shines beyond the sky; he indeed is to be meditated upon as "This All. [End of the third section of the eleventh anuvāka.]

Truth and untruth, untruth and truth; speech and mind, mind and speech; eye and ear, ear and eye; faith and austerity, austerity and faith—these are the sixteen. Brahman consists of sixteen parts. He who knows this Brahman of sixteen parts attains that very Brahman of sixteen parts. Veda is Brahman; its abode is truth, its support is tranquility and self-restraint. It is like one who, intending to depart tomorrow, [abstains] from evil action.

One should shrink from evil action day after day; one should shrink from improper time. Now, this Virāj consists of ten steps. There are ten heavens and hells within a person; those that have gone to heaven cause him to go to heaven, and those that have gone to hell cause him to go to hell.
The Fourth Section of the Eleventh Anuvāka.

The mind is hell; speech is hell; the vital breath is hell; the eye is hell; the ear is hell; the skin is hell; the hands are hell; the anus is hell; the generative organ is hell; the feet are hell. (1) Through the mind, one knows what is to be examined; thus one knows. (2) Through speech, one knows tastes; thus one knows. (3) Through the vital breath, one knows odors; thus one knows. (4) Through the eye, one knows forms; thus one knows. (5) Through the ear, one knows sounds; thus one knows. (6) Through the skin, one knows touches; thus one knows. (7) Through the two hands, one knows actions; thus one knows. (8)

With the belly one knows hunger; one knows it with the belly. 9. With the penis one knows women; one knows them with the penis. 10. With the two feet one knows roads; one knows them with the two feet. 11. A span above the Plakṣa tree Prāsravaṇa is the center of the earth; and where these Seven Seers are, that is the center of the sky. 12. Now, where these saline wastes are, that is the heart of the earth; and that which is black in the moon, that is the heart of the sky. 13. He who thus knows these two—the center and the heart of heaven and earth—[attains them].

One who is without desire does not depart from this world. Homage to Atisāma, Ayeta, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Pārthuśravasa; and those who protect the vital breath (prāṇa), may they protect me; "well-being" for the rite. "Peace" is the Gārhapatya fire; "tranquility" is the Āhavanīya fire; "self-control" is the Anvāhāryapacana fire. The fifth section of the eleventh anuvāka; the eleventh anuvāka is completed.

What is the Sāvitrī? Agni indeed is Savitṛ; the earth is the Sāvitrī. Where there is Agni, there is the earth; or where there is the earth, there is Agni. These two are two wombs; that is one couple. What is Savitṛ? What is the Sāvitrī? Varuṇa indeed is Savitṛ; the waters are the Sāvitrī. Where there is Varuṇa, there are the waters; or where there are the waters, there is Varuṇa. These two are two wombs; that is one couple. What is Savitṛ? What is the Sāvitrī? Vāyu indeed is Savitṛ; space (ākāśa) is the Sāvitrī. Where there is Vāyu, there is space; where...

Space and wind—these two are the womb; that is one couple. 6. Who is Savitṛ? What is Sāvitrī? The sacrifice itself is Savitṛ; the meters are Sāvitrī. 7. Where there is the sacrifice, there are the meters; where there are the meters, there is the sacrifice. These two are the womb; that is one couple. 8. Who is Savitṛ? What is Sāvitrī? Thunder itself is Savitṛ; lightning is Sāvitrī. 9. Where there is thunder, there is lightning; where there is lightning, there is thunder. These two are the womb; that is one couple. 10.

Who is the *kassavitā*? What is the *sāvitrī*? The Sun (*āditya*) is the *savitā*; the Sky (*dyauḥ*) is the *sāvitrī*. Where the Sun is, there is the Sky; or where the Sky is, there is the Sun. These two are two wombs (*yoni*); that is one couple (*mithuna*). Who is the *kassavitā*? What is the *sāvitrī*? The Moon (*candra*) is the *savitā*; the Constellations (*nakṣatrāṇi*) are the *sāvitrī*. Where the Moon is, there are the Constellations; or where the Constellations are, there is the Moon. These two are two wombs; that is one couple. Who is the *kassavitā*? What is the *sāvitrī*? The Mind (*manas*) is the *savitā*; Speech (*vāk*) is the *sāvitrī*. He...

Where there is mind, there is speech; where there is speech, there is mind. These two are the wombs; that is one couple. (16) Who is Savitṛ? Who is Sāvitrī? Man indeed is Savitṛ; woman is Sāvitrī. Where there is man, there is woman; or where there is woman, there is man. These two are the wombs; that is one couple. (17) The first section of the twelfth Anuvāka.

Of this [Gāyatrī], this is the first quarter: *bhūs tat savitur vareṇyam*. "Vareṇya" (the desirable) is indeed Agni; "vareṇya" is indeed the waters; "vareṇya" is indeed the moon. Of this, this is the second quarter: *bhuvo bhargo devasya dhīmahi*. "Bharga" is indeed Agni; "bharga" is indeed Āditya; "bharga" is indeed the moon. Of this, this is the third quarter: *svar dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt*. The sacrifice (*yajña*) indeed impels; for both woman and man procreate.

"Earth, atmosphere, that excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ, may we meditate upon. Agni indeed is the splendor; Āditya indeed is the splendor; the Moon indeed is the splendor. "May he inspire our thoughts"—the sacrifice indeed inspires; and both woman and man procreate. "Earth, atmosphere, heaven, that excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ, may we meditate upon; may he inspire our thoughts. Whoever knows this Sāvitrī thus, O Sāvitrī, crosses over death again.
Thus one conquers the same world as Sāvitrī; thus one conquers the same world. 6.28.
This is the second section of the twelfth Anuvāka; the twelfth Anuvāka is completed. Thus the Upaniṣad-Brāhmaṇa is completed.

Now begins the fourth chapter: O white-horsed one, beautiful to behold, you are like a green sapphire; you touch the green [grass], you who are awakened by the sun—do not harm me! You do not know me; run away! (1) When you, O prowler, approach the sleeping man who is ignorant, may Varuṇa shield me with an armor of stone! (2) When you, O prowler, approach the sleeping man who is ignorant, may Varuṇa shield me with an armor of iron! (3) When you, O prowler, approach the sleeping man who is ignorant, [may Varuṇa shield me] with an armor of bronze! (4)

May Varuṇa shield me within with his armor when you, O Abhyavacaraṇa, descend upon a sleeping man who is ignorant; may Varuṇa shield me within with armor made of silver. May Varuṇa shield me within with armor made of gold when you, O Abhyavacaraṇa, descend upon a sleeping man; may Varuṇa shield me within with armor made of gold. Life is your mother, thought is your father; homage to you, O Drying One! You are named the Seizer, the All-Living; to you, for all days, be homage! Homage to the Copper-hued One, homage to Varuṇa, homage to the one who seeks to strike down!
O King Yakṣman, do not harm me; O Yakṣman, O King, do not harm me. By the agreement of those two, may I attain a full lifespan. 8.1 The first section (anuvāka) is completed.

The sacrifice is indeed the person. His twenty-four years constitute the morning pressing (*prātassavana*). The *gāyatrī* consists of twenty-four syllables, and the morning pressing belongs to the *gāyatrī*. Those [deities] are the Vasus; the Vasus are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), for the vital breaths gather all this that is good (*vasu*) here. If anyone should afflict him at this time, he should say: "O Vasus, the vital breaths! This morning pressing of mine—extend it through the midday pressing! He will surely become free from disease. Now, as for those...

Forty-four years constitute that midday pressing; the *triṣṭubh* consists of forty-four syllables, and the midday pressing belongs to the *triṣṭubh*. 5. Those [deities] are the Rudras; the Rudras are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), for it is the vital breaths that make all this weep. 6. If, at this time, someone should afflict him with disease, he should say: "The Rudras are the vital breaths; may they extend this midday pressing of mine by means of the third pressing. Thus, he indeed becomes free from disease. 7. Now, as for those forty-eight [years]...

The rainy season is that third libation; the Jagatī meter consists of forty-eight syllables, and the third libation belongs to the Jagatī. (8) Those [deities] belong to the Ādityas; the Ādityas are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), for the vital breaths take up all this [world]. (9) If, at this time, someone should afflict him with a burning fever, he should say: "O Ādityas, who are the vital breaths, extend this third libation of mine along with my life-force! He shall indeed become free from disease. (10) Knowing this, the Brahmin Mahidāsa Aitareya said: "When one is afflicted by a burning fever, why do you afflict yourself thus?"

He who thinks, "May I not be sent away by this affliction," lived for sixteen hundred years; he lives for sixteen hundred years, and breath does not desert him before his full span of life, who knows thus.
The second section (anuvāka) is completed.

The threefold lifespan of Kaśyapa, the threefold lifespan of Jamadagni, the three flowers of immortality—thou hast granted these three lifespans to me. O life-giving father, enter us as one who brings peace and is gentle to the body. Those fires which have entered the earth as dwellers of the soil—you are the highest among them; impel us toward life.
The third section (anuvāka) is completed.

You are the calf of the forest, possessing all names, protecting all; you are the ripened [essence] of the waters, the messenger of Varuṇa, named "Invisibility. 1 Just as you, being immortal, are hidden from mortals, so do you hide us from those who seek to harm us. You are the invisibility against thieves. 2 The fourth section (anuvāka) is completed.

At dawn you become Savitṛ; as you are about to rise, Viṣṇu; as you rise, Puruṣa; once risen, Bṛhaspati; as you move forward, Maghavan Indra; at midday, Vaikuṇṭha; in the afternoon, Bhaga; as you grow red, the fierce god; at sunset, you become Yama. 1. In the eating [of food] you are King Soma; in the night, the King of the Fathers; in sleep, you enter into men, and with milk, into animals. 2. At the end of the night you become Bhava; in the latter part of the night, Aṅgiras; at the time of the Agnihotra, Bhṛgu. 3. Of him, this very solar orb is the udder; these two are his teats.
Whatever speech and breath there are—by means of those two, milk for me: study, the life of a student, offspring, cattle, the heavenly world, and preeminence among my kin. These blessings I pray for:
Bhūr, Bhuvas, Svar. When it has risen, I place that bright radiance within myself.
The fifth section is completed.

King Bhageratha, the descendant of Ikṣvāku, was about to perform the Kāmapra sacrifice. The Brahmins of the Kurus and Pañcālas heard of this and said, "This King Bhageratha, the descendant of Ikṣvāku, is about to perform the Kāmapra sacrifice; let us go there and have a conversation with him. They went to him, and when they had arrived, he paid them due honor. Then he approached them in the guise of a mendicant, having shaved off his hair and beard, clipped his nails, anointed himself with ghee, and carrying a staff and sandals. He spoke to them as follows:

"Venerable Brahmins, who among you knows this: 'When the call and the response have been exchanged, go to the gods'? (5) Then he said: "Who among you knows this: 'How it is that from one who knows, there arise a skilled Udgātṛ, a skilled Hotṛ, and a skilled Adhvaryu, as well as one who knows the ways of men'? (6) Then he said: "Who among you knows this: 'How the meters are employed, and how they all, when fully chanted, come together'? (7) Then he said: "Who among you knows this: 'As it is with the two final syllables of the Gāyatrī'? (8)
"Go back again to the sacrifice," he said. Then he asked: "Which of you knows this—how it is that the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās), once accepted, do not cause harm?
The first section of the sixth lesson.

He asked him these five questions. Among those people of the Kurus and Pañcālas, there was Baka Dālbhya, who was well-versed in sacred tradition (*anūcāna*). He said: "Regarding the statement, 'As the *āśrāvaṇa* and *pratyāśrāvaṇa* go to the gods'—O King, it is indeed in the eastern direction that the *āśrāvaṇa* and *pratyāśrāvaṇa* go to the gods; therefore, standing facing the east, one makes the *āśrāvaṇa*, and standing facing the east, one makes the *pratyāśrāvaṇa*. Then he said: "Regarding the statement, 'When a good *udgātṛ*, a good *hotṛ*, and a good *adhvaryu* are born, they are born as one who possesses excellent human knowledge'—who indeed is the human?"

"He knows the origin," he said, "for him there arises an excellent Udgātṛ, an excellent Hotṛ, an excellent Adhvaryu, and one who possesses excellent human knowledge. "O King, the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are indeed the origin of a human being. Then he said: "As for the meters that are employed, and how all of them, when fully praised, come together—O King, all the meters, when fully praised, come together in the *gāyatrī*. Then he said: "How do the two highest syllables of the *gāyatrī* return again to the sacrifice?"

"By means of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, O King, the *Gāyatrī* indeed returns again to the sacrifice at its two highest syllables. Then he said: "Just as sacrificial gifts, once accepted, do not cause harm. Sixth Anuvāka, Second Khaṇḍa.

"Whoever knows the mouth of the Gāyatrī," he said, "the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) received do not harm him. "Agni indeed, O King, is the mouth of the Gāyatrī; therefore, whatever one places into the fire becomes greater thereby and truly increases. In just this way, a Brāhmaṇa who knows this, while receiving gifts, becomes greater and truly increases. He said, "This Brāhmaṇa was indeed a learned scholar (anūcāna); I am coming to you with this sacrifice. "I shall chant the Udgītha for you in such a manner," he replied.

He said, "In such a way that you shall go to the heavenly world as a sole ruler. For him, he sang out with this *gāyatra* *udgītha*. He indeed became a sole ruler and went to the heavenly world. Whoever knows this, having become a sole ruler, goes to the heavenly world by means of this very same [singing]. "Oṃ vā"—these are two syllables; "oṃ vā" in the fourth [round]; "oṃ vā" in the sixth; "humbhā"; "oṃ vāk" in the eighth. With this very [singing], he sang out against Pratīdarśa, who was fearful and had no followers. He said to him, "What [did you do] for me?"

"I shall sing it," he said. "Let the two bay horses, my divine steeds, come to me," [the other] replied. "So be it. He sang them to him, and they both came to him. This indeed is that *udgītha* which is the fulfillment of desires: *oṃ vā3cauṃ vā3cauṃ vā3chumbhā oṃ vāk*. He who knows this thus becomes possessed of limbs, possessed of a body, and immortal; and so too does he for whom one who knows this sings the *udgītha*. Sixth Anuvāka, Third Khaṇḍa.

The sixth section is completed. Man, indeed, is the sacrifice; man, indeed, is the *udgītha*. Now, these are the very deaths: fire, wind, the sun, and the moon. They bind the man as he is being born with the fetters of death—fire binds his speech, wind his breath, the sun his sight, and the moon his hearing. Regarding this, they say: "Is there an *udgātṛ* who releases the fetters of death from the vital breaths of the sacrificer? He for whom one who knows thus performs the *prastāva*, [releases] that which is in his speech.

The noose of death is released from him alone. 4. Now, for whomsoever a singer who knows thus sings the *udgītha*, the noose of death that is in his breath (*prāṇa*) is released from him alone. 5. Now, for whomsoever a singer who knows thus performs the *pratihāra*, the noose of death that is in his eye is released from him alone. 6. Now, for whomsoever a singer who knows thus approaches the *nidhana*, the noose of death that is in his ear is released from him alone. 7. Thus indeed does a singer who knows thus release the nooses of death from the vital breaths of the sacrificer. 8. Regarding this, they say:

Or rather, it is the Udgātṛ who, having released the nooses of death from the vital breaths of the sacrificer, then rescues him—along with his limbs, his body, and his whole being—from all death. (9) This concludes the first section of the seventh chapter.

Thus, when one who knows this utters the *hiṅ* sound, he thereby delivers him from that noose of death which is in his hair. (1) Then, when one who knows this performs the *prastāva*, he thereby delivers him from that noose of death which is in his skin. (2) Then, when one who knows this takes up the *ādi*, he thereby delivers him from that noose of death which is in his flesh. (3) Then, when one who knows this sings the *udgītha*, he thereby delivers him from that noose of death which is in his sinews. (4) Then, when one who knows this... [the text continues].

The wise one performs the *pratihāra*; he thereby delivers him from whatever bond of death is in his limbs. 5. Then, for whomsoever the wise one performs the *upadrava*, he thereby delivers him from whatever bond of death is in his bones. 6. Then, for whomsoever the wise one approaches with the *nidhana*, he thereby delivers him from whatever bond of death is in his marrow. 7. Thus indeed does the Udgātṛ who knows this, having released the bonds of death from the sacrificer’s vital breaths, deliver him—along with his limbs, along with his body—from all death. 8.

Regarding this, they say: "The Udgātṛ is he who, having released the nooses of death from the vital breaths of the sacrificer, then places him—along with his limbs and his body—untouched by any death in the heavenly world, in seven ways. Now, this very Indra becomes Vaimṛdha as he rises; he is Savitṛ when risen; he is Mitra at the time of the gathering of cattle; he is Indro Vaikuṇṭha at midday; he is the god Śarva the fierce as he turns back; he is Prajāpati as he goes toward the redness [of twilight]; and he is indeed set when he has gone to rest. Therefore, for whomsoever one, knowing thus, utters the *hiṅ* sound...

Thus, for him who is rising [to perform the rite], heaven is his world; in that very world he places him. 11. Now, for him for whom one who knows thus chants the *prastāva*, heaven is his world when the sun has risen; in that very world he places him. 12. Now, for him for whom one who knows thus takes the beginning [of the chant], heaven is his world at the time of the *saṃgava*; in that very world he places him. 13. Now, for him for whom one who knows thus sings the *udgītha*, heaven is his world at midday; in that very world he places him. 14. Now, for him for whom one who knows thus performs the *pratihāra*...

In that very world which is his heavenly realm in the afternoon, he places him. (15) Now, for whomsoever one who knows thus approaches with the *upadrava*, in that very world which is his heavenly realm as the sun sets, he places him. (16) Now, for whomsoever one who knows thus enters upon the *nidhana*, in that very world which is his heavenly realm when the sun has set, he places him. (17) In this way indeed, the *udgātṛ* who knows thus, having released the bonds of death from the sacrificer’s vital breaths, and having touched him—along with his limbs, along with his body—from all sides by death, places him sevenfold in the heavenly world. (18) 10
The second section of the seventh lesson; the seventh lesson is completed.

There are indeed six self-existent deities: Agni, Vāyu, that [sun] yonder, Prāṇa, Food, and Speech. They disputed for preeminence, saying, "I am the best! I am the best! Worship me as the glory! They could not agree among themselves regarding who was the best. They said, "We shall certainly not abide by the superiority of one another; let us speak to these [deities] so that we may become the best. They said to Agni, "How are you the best? He replied, "I..."

"I am the mouth of the gods; through me the oblations are offered. I transform myself into the food of the gods and into the food of human beings. (5) "If I were not to exist, the gods would be mouthless, and other creatures would be mouthless. No oblations would be offered; neither the food of the gods nor that of human beings would be transformed. (6) "Consequently, this entire world would perish, and nothing at all would remain. (7) "So be it," they said. "Indeed, nothing at all would remain here if you were not to exist. (8) Then...

They said to Vāyu, "How are you the best? He replied, "I am the breath of the gods, and I am [the breath] of other creatures; for when I depart from it, then it perishes. If I were not present, then all this would perish, and nothing at all would remain. They said, "It is even so; if you were not present, nothing at all would remain here.
[End of the first section of the eighth anuvāka.]

Then they said to Āditya, "How are you the best? He replied, "When I rise, I become the day; when I set, I become the night. By me, as the eye, all actions are performed. If I were not to exist, there would be neither day nor night, and no actions would be performed. Then this entire universe would perish, and nothing at all would remain. They said, "It is even so; if you were not to exist, nothing at all would remain here. Then they said to Prāṇa, "How are you..."

"You are the best," [they said]. He replied: "Becoming breath, fire blazes; becoming breath, the wind pervades space; becoming breath, the sun rises; from breath comes food; from breath comes speech. "If I were not to exist, then all this would perish, and nothing at all would remain," he said. "It is even so," they replied. "If you were not to exist, nothing at all would remain here. Then they said to food: "How are you the best? He replied: "In me..."

"Fire blazes by being established in me; the wind pervades space by being established in me; the sun rises by being established in me; even life-breath and speech exist because of me. "If I were not to exist, then all this would perish, and nothing at all would remain," [he said]. "So be it," they replied, "but if you were not to exist, nothing at all would remain. Then they spoke to Speech: "How indeed are you the best? She said: "By me alone is this known; by me is that known."

"If I were not, this consciousness would not be known, nor would there be sound. Therefore, all this would perish; nothing at all would remain here. "It is just so," they said. "Nothing at all would remain here if you were not.
Fifth Anuvāka, Second Khaṇḍa.

They said, "Indeed, all these deities are each dependent on only one [of us]. Now, if not even one of all these deities were to remain, then all this would perish and nothing at all would be left. Come, let us come together and make that which is the best among us our own. They gathered together in this *prāṇa*, in the syllable *oṃ*, and in the syllable *vaṣaṭ*. Because they gathered together (*samāyan*), that is the essence of the *sāman* (the reason for its name). They said, "Those syllables of ours which are mortal, not free from evil, and impermanent—"

"Having extracted those [syllables] into the immortal, sinless, pure, imperishable [elements]—in fire, wind, sun, breath, food, and speech—we shall sing the Gāyatra chant. By that, having struck down death and having struck down evil, may we go to the heavenly world. 3. "Ā": this is the immortal, sinless, pure, imperishable [element] of fire; "gni": this is its mortal, non-sinless syllable. 4. "Vā": this is the immortal, sinless, pure, imperishable [element] of wind; "yu": this is its mortal, non-sinless syllable. 5. "Yā": this is the immortal, sinless, pure, imperishable [element] of the sun; "di": this is its mortal, non-sinless syllable.

"e"—this is the immortal, free from evil, pure, and imperishable of the sun; "tya"—this is its mortal, not free from evil, perishable syllable. 6. "pra"—this is the immortal, free from evil, pure, and imperishable of the vital breath (prāṇa); "ṇa"—this is its mortal, not free from evil, perishable syllable. 7. "e"—this is the immortal, free from evil, pure, and imperishable of food; "na"—this is its mortal, not free from evil, perishable syllable. 8. "va"—this is the immortal, free from evil, pure, and imperishable of speech; "gi"—this is its mortal, not free from evil, perishable syllable. 9. These are those [syllables].

Having extracted the mortal syllables—which are not free from evil—from the immortal, evil-free, pure syllables, they sang the *gāyatra* chant upon fire, wind, the sun, breath, food, and speech. By that, having struck down death and having struck down evil, they went to the heavenly world. (10) He who knows this, having struck down death and having struck down evil, goes to the heavenly world.
(11) Eighth Anuvāka, Third Khaṇḍa.

They said to Brahman, "Establishing ourselves in you, let us lift this up. Brahman said to them, "With your breath of the mouth, you shall attain me through the breath of the mouth. They, with this breath—the *oṃkāra*—intending to bring forth the syllable *a*, [produced] the syllable *bha* from the *hiṅkāra*; chanting the word *vāk* (speech) after the syllable *o*, they sang the *gāyatra* chant with both breaths: "Ovā3 ovā3 ovā3 chumbhā vo vā. Just as one with two feet stands firmly, even so did they stand firmly in the heavenly world. They stood firm.

He who knows this stands in the heavenly world. And indeed, he who, knowing this, departs from this world, becomes breath itself and enters into Vāyu; from Vāyu into the clouds, from the clouds into rain, and by means of rain he pervades this world. The seers once performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*). Again and again, with many various introductory verses, they could not at all discover the door to the heavenly world. Then, through toil, austerity, and the observance of vows, they won Indra over. To him—

"We have indeed desired the heavenly world, again and again, by many various paths; yet we have not found the door to the heavenly world. Teach us so that, having discerned the door to the heavenly world, we may go safely to the end of the year and reach the heavenly world unharmed. He said to them: "Who among you is the oldest?
*The Fourth Section of the Eighth Anuvāka*

"I am Agastya," he said. "Come," he replied. "I shall indeed tell you that by knowing which, having recognized the door of the heavenly world, you will go safely to the end of the year and reach the heavenly world, free from affliction. To him he spoke this secret doctrine (upaniṣad) concerning the Udgītha of the Gāyatra, regarding fire, wind, the sun, breath, food, and speech. Then, having recognized the door of the heavenly world, they went safely to the end of the year and reached it.

They went to the heavenly world. In this very way, one who knows thus, having discerned the door of the heavenly world, reaches the end of the year unharmed and in safety, and goes to the heavenly world.
Fifth section of the eighth lesson.
The eighth lesson is completed.

Thus indeed did Indra declare this secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) of the *udgītha* of the Gāyatra—immortality—to Agastya; Agastya to Iṣa Śyāvāśvi; Iṣa Śyāvāśvi to Gauṣūkti; Gauṣūkti to Jvālāyana; Jvālāyana to Śāṭyāyani; Śāṭyāyani to Rāma Krātujāteya Vaiyāghrapadya; and Rāma Krātujāteya Vaiyāghrapadya [taught it]. The first section in the ninth lesson.
The second section in the ninth chapter; the ninth chapter is completed.

By whom impelled does the mind fly forth when sent? By whom is the vital breath first joined and set in motion? By whom impelled do they utter this speech? And which god yokes the eye and the ear? The ear of the ear, the mind of the mind, that which is the speech of speech, and the breath of the breath, as well as the eye of the eye—the wise, having realized these, depart from this world and become immortal. The eye does not go there, nor does speech, nor the mind. We do not know, we do not understand, how one might instruct another regarding this.

"That is indeed other than the known, and moreover, above the unknown"—so we have heard from those of old who explained it to us. (4) That which is not expressed by speech, but by which speech is expressed—that alone know thou to be Brahman, not this which people worship here. (5) That which one does not think with the mind, but by which the mind is said to be thought—that alone know thou to be Brahman, not this which people worship here. (6) That which one does not see with the eye, but by which the eyes are seen—that alone know thou to be Brahman, not this which people worship here. (7)

If you think "I know it well," then surely you know only a small portion of the form of Brahman—only that which is yours and that which belongs to the gods. Therefore, I consider that which is unknown to you to be precisely what must be investigated. "I do not think 'I know it well,' nor do I think 'I do not know it'; yet he among us who knows that [truth] knows it, and he does not think 'I know it,' nor does he think 'I do not know it. That which is unthought is thought by him; that which is thought is not thought by him who does not know it. It is unknown to those who understand it, and known to those who do not understand it. When it is realized through awakening, it is known; for then one finds immortality.

By oneself one finds strength; by knowledge one finds immortality. If one has known this here, then there is truth; if one has not known this here, there is great destruction. Having discerned [the Self] in every single being, the wise, after departing from this world, become immortal. 5. 19. Second section of the tenth chapter.

Brahman indeed won a victory for the gods. In that victory of Brahman, the gods exulted. They thought, "This victory is ours alone; this greatness is ours alone. Brahman understood their intention and appeared before them. But they did not recognize him, wondering, "What is this spirit? (yakṣa). They said to Agni, "O Jātavedas, find out what this spirit is. "So be it," he replied. He ran toward it, and it spoke to him: "Who are you? "I am indeed Agni," he said, "I am Jātavedas."

"I am [that]. "What power is there in you? "I could burn all this that is on the earth. He placed a blade of grass before him, saying, "Burn this. It flew toward it with all its speed, but it was not able to burn it; it turned back from that very spot, saying, "I was not able to discern what this spirit (yakṣa) is. Then they said to Vāyu, "O Vāyu, find out what this spirit is. "So be it," he replied. He ran toward it, and it spoke to him, saying, "Who are you? "I am Vāyu," he said.

"I am," said Mātariśvan; "I am indeed," he replied. "What power is there in you? "I could take up all this that is on the earth. He placed a blade of grass before him, saying, "Take this up. He ran toward it with all his speed, but he was not able to take it up. He returned from right there, saying, "I was not able to discern what this Yakṣa is. Then they said to Indra, "O Maghavan, find out what this Yakṣa is. "So be it," he replied, and he ran toward it.
He disappeared from that place. He came upon a woman in that very space—Umā Haimavatī, who was exceedingly beautiful. He said to her: "What is this spirit?
(End of the third section in the tenth lesson.)

"It is Brahman," he said. "It is in the victory of Brahman that you rejoice. Thereupon, he indeed knew: "It is Brahman. Therefore, these gods—Agni, Vāyu, and Indra—are, as it were, superior to the other gods; for they touched it most closely, and they were the first to know: "It is Brahman. Therefore, Indra is, as it were, superior to the other gods; for he touched it most closely, and he was the first to know: "It is Brahman. This is its instruction:

"That which flashed forth like lightning—'A!'—and that which closed its eyes—'Ā!'"—this is with respect to the deities (adhidevatam). Now, with respect to the self (adhyātmam): that which the mind seems to go toward, and by means of which one repeatedly remembers this [Self], is volition (saṃkalpaḥ). That indeed is called "the Forest" (vana); it should be meditated upon as "the Forest. He who knows this thus, all beings desire him. "Tell us the Upanishad," they said. "The Upanishad has been told to you," he replied. "But the Upanishad of Brahman (brāhmī), tell us that! "Truly, we have told you the Upanishad of Brahman; austerity, self-control, and ritual action are its foundation."

The Vedas are the foundation, all the limbs [of the ritual] are the support, and truth is the abode. He who knows this thus, having struck down evil, becomes established in the infinite, unconquerable heavenly world.
Section 4 of the Tenth Anuvāka.
The Tenth Anuvāka is completed.

In the beginning, this world was indeed only hope; it became that which was yet to be, and it became those waters. Those waters performed austerity. While performing austerity, they breathed out "Hus!"—that indeed became the *prāṇa* (out-breath). Having breathed out, they breathed in—that indeed became the *apāna* (in-breath). Having breathed in, they breathed across—that indeed became the *vyāna* (diffused breath). Having breathed across, they breathed together—that indeed became the *samāna* (equalizing breath). Having breathed together, they breathed up—that indeed became the *udāna* (upward breath). This [world], being one alone, was a common food, undifferentiated. He...

He created name-and-form; therefore, one who knows this is separated from evil by these two. 8. Now, yonder sun is the out-breath (*prāṇa*), fire is the down-breath (*apāna*), the waters are the diffused breath (*vyāna*), the quarters are the equalizing breath (*samāna*), and the moon is the up-breath (*udāna*). 9. That indeed became one: namely, the out-breath itself. He who knows that it became one in this way—thinking, "In this way indeed does this become one"—becomes preeminent among his own people as a single unity. 10. Fire is the out-breath and speech is the earth; wind is the out-breath and speech is the intermediate space; the sun is the out-breath...

"Speech"—this is heaven; "breath"—this is the quarters; "speech"—this is the ear; "moon"—this is breath; "speech"—this is the mind; "male"—this is breath; "speech"—this is the female. 11. This world which was created by him was loose and insufficient. 12. He made for himself the form of Mind (*manas*); by that he made it sufficient. Indeed, for one who knows this, this world which is created becomes firm, not loose, and sufficient. 13. (End of the first section of the eleventh anuvāka.)

This very [Udgītha] is established in four ways: the Udgītha, the Sāman, the Arkya, and the Jyeṣṭhabrāhmaṇa. 1. Breath indeed is the *ud*, speech is the *gī*; that is the Udgītha. 2. Breath indeed is the *āma*, speech is the *sā*; that is the Sāman. 3. Breath indeed is the *ka*, speech is the *ṛc*; that is the Arkya. 4. Breath indeed is the *jyeṣṭha*, speech is the *brāhmaṇa*; that is the Jyeṣṭhabrāhmaṇa. "Tell me the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*)," he said. "The secret doctrine has been told to you; those elements (*dhātu*) of yours have been told. We have indeed told you the threefold secret doctrine. "This is white, black, and copper—the color of the Sāman."

Thus he said: "Whenever the copper-colored [sun] descends upon the white and the black, it indeed seizes that tenth human [portion]. Thus, possessing three layers, he reflected: "Where indeed shall these deities bring tribute to me as I lie stretched out? Section 2, Anuvāka 11.2.3.

He chose the Puruṣa alone for refuge. He entered him from the front facing backward; therefore, he became broad (uru), and that is the reason for the name *uraḥ* (chest). Because of this, these deities bring tribute to him here. Fire brings tribute to him following after speech; the Moon brings tribute to him following after the mind; the Sun brings tribute to him following after the eye; the Quarters bring tribute to him following after the ear; and Vāyu brings tribute to him following after the breath.

It carries him away. These vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are his dug-out paths and vehicles; thus, for one who knows this, these dug-out paths and vehicles carry him from every side. 9. This is that very throne of Brahman (*brahmāsandī*); they bring the throne of Brahman to him who knows this, and he indeed ascends the throne of Brahman. 10. This is the glory of Brahman, surrounded by prosperity; indeed, he becomes possessed of the glory and prosperity of Brahman who knows this. 11. This is its instruction:

That which is within the right eye—of that, what is white is the form of the *Ṛg* verses; what is black is the form of the *Sāman* chants; and what is as if coppery or brownish is the form of the *Yajus* formulas. This very person who is in the eye is Indra, this is Prajāpati. He is equal to the earth, equal to space, equal to heaven, equal to all beings. He shines beyond the sky; he alone is to be meditated upon as "This All. Section 3, Chapter 11.

Truth and untruth, untruth and truth; speech and mind, mind and speech; eye and ear, ear and eye; faith and austerity, austerity and faith—these are the sixteen. (1) This Brahman has sixteen parts. He who knows this Brahman with its sixteen parts attains that very Brahman with its sixteen parts. (2) The Veda is Brahman; Truth is its abode, and Tranquility and Self-restraint are its foundation. (3) Just as one about to depart on a journey tomorrow would shrink from evil action, even so should he do day by day.

One should recoil from evil action and from untimely [conduct]. Now, these [verses] constitute a ten-foot Virāj. There are ten heavens and hells within a person; those that have gone to heaven cause him to go to heaven, and those that have gone to hell cause him to go to hell. Fifth Khaṇḍa of the Eleventh Anuvāka.

The mind is hell; speech is hell; the vital breath is hell; the eye is hell; the ear is hell; the skin is hell; the hands are hell; the anus is hell; the genitals are hell; the feet are hell. (1) Through the mind, one knows what is to be examined; one knows it. (2) Through speech, one knows tastes; one knows them. (3) Through the vital breath, one knows odors; one knows them. (4) Through the eye, one knows forms; one knows them. (5) Through the ear, one knows sounds; one knows them. (6) Through the skin, one knows tactile sensations; one knows them. (7) Through the two hands, one knows actions; one knows them. (8)

With the belly one knows hunger; one knows it. With the penis one knows women; one knows it. With the two feet one knows roads; one knows them. One span north of the Plakṣa Prāsravaṇa is the center of the earth; and where these Seven Seers are, that is the center of the sky. Now, where these saline wastes are, that is the heart of the earth; and that which is black in the moon is the heart of the sky. He who thus knows the center and the heart of both heaven and earth—

"One who is without desire does not depart from this world. (14) "Homage to Atisāma, Aitu, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pārthuśravasa, and to those who protect the breath; may they protect me; may my work be auspicious. "Peace" is the Gārhapatya fire; "Tranquility" is the Āhavanīya fire; "Restraint" is the Anvāhāryapacana fire. (15) 27. Fifth section of the eleventh anuvāka. The eleventh anuvāka is completed.

What is the Sāvitrī? Agni is Savitṛ, and the earth is the Sāvitrī. Where there is Agni, there is the earth; and where there is the earth, there is Agni. These two are two wombs, and that is one couple. What is Savitṛ? What is the Sāvitrī? Varuṇa is Savitṛ, and the waters are the Sāvitrī. Where there is Varuṇa, there are the waters; and where there are the waters, there is Varuṇa. These two are two wombs, and that is one couple. What is Savitṛ? What is the Sāvitrī? Vāyu is Savitṛ, and space is the Sāvitrī. Where there is Vāyu, there is space; and where there is space, there is Vāyu.

These two are the wombs; that is one pair. Who is Savitṛ? What is Sāvitrī? The sacrifice is Savitṛ, and the meters are Sāvitrī. Where there is the sacrifice, there are the meters; or where there are the meters, there is the sacrifice. These two are the wombs; that is one pair. Who is Savitṛ? What is Sāvitrī? Thunder is Savitṛ, and lightning is Sāvitrī. Where there is thunder, there is lightning; or where there is lightning, there is thunder. These two are the wombs; that is one pair. Who is Savitṛ? What is Sāvitrī?

The Sun is Savitṛ, and the Sky is Sāvitrī. Where the Sun is, there is the Sky; and where the Sky is, there is the Sun. These two are the two wombs; that is one couple. Who is Savitṛ? Who is Sāvitrī? The Moon is Savitṛ, and the Constellations are Sāvitrī. Where the Moon is, there are the Constellations; and where the Constellations are, there is the Moon. These two are the two wombs; that is one couple. Who is Savitṛ? Who is Sāvitrī? Mind alone is Savitṛ, and Speech is Sāvitrī. Where the mind is, there is Speech; and where Speech is...

Speech and mind—these two are your wombs; that is one couple. (16) Who is Savitṛ? Who is Sāvitrī? Man indeed is Savitṛ, woman is Sāvitrī. Where there is a man, there is a woman; or where there is a woman, there is a man. These two are your wombs; that is one couple. (17) 27. First section of the twelfth Anuvāka.

Of this [Gāyatrī], this is the first foot: *bhūs tat savitur vareṇyam*. Fire is indeed the desirable; the waters are indeed the desirable; the moon is indeed the desirable. Of this, this is the second foot: *bhuvo bhargo devasya dhīmahi*. Fire is indeed the splendor (*bhargas*); the sun is indeed the splendor; the moon is indeed the splendor. Of this, this is the third foot: *svar dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt*. The sacrifice indeed impels; for both woman and man procreate.
The second section of the twelfth chapter; the twelfth chapter is completed.
Thus, the Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa is finished.
